name: Acetaminophen
uses: Pain and fever.
side: Liver effects at high doses. Toxic to cats.
how: Reduces pain and fever through effects in the brain.
avoid: People with liver disease or heavy alcohol use. Toxic to cats and dangerous for dogs.
drugClass: Pain reliever and fever reducer (analgesic, antipyretic)
about: Acetaminophen is one of the most widely used pain relievers and fever reducers in the world and has been available for decades in many over-the-counter and prescription products. Unlike NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, it does not reduce swelling and is gentler on the stomach. Prescribers may ask for it compounded when someone needs a dye-free or allergen-free capsule or a strength not sold in stores.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of liver injury, such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, upper right belly pain or unusual tiredness, or for a red, peeling or blistering skin rash. If you think you have taken too much, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 even if you feel fine.
interactions: Avoid taking it with other products that also contain acetaminophen, such as many cold, flu, sleep and prescription pain medicines, and limit alcohol; regular use can also raise the effect of the blood thinner warfarin. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Acetaminophen is often considered an option for pain or fever during pregnancy and breastfeeding when needed, but use it only as directed and check with your prescriber or OB first.
tips: It can be taken with or without food.
Read labels on other medicines so you don't take acetaminophen from two sources at once.
Keep it out of reach of pets; even a small amount can be deadly to cats and it is dangerous for dogs.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber may check liver tests if you take it regularly for a long time or have liver risk factors.
faqs: Can I drink alcohol while taking acetaminophen?
Alcohol and acetaminophen both stress the liver, so it is best to limit or avoid alcohol. People who have three or more drinks a day should ask their prescriber before using it.
What is the difference between acetaminophen and ibuprofen?

Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but does not reduce swelling, while ibuprofen is an NSAID that also reduces inflammation. Acetaminophen is easier on the stomach but can harm the liver in high amounts.
Can I give acetaminophen to my dog or cat?
No, not unless your veterinarian specifically tells you to. Acetaminophen is toxic to cats even in small amounts and can seriously harm dogs.

name: Acetazolamide
uses: Glaucoma, altitude sickness and some fluid conditions.
how: Blocks carbonic anhydrase, reducing fluid production in the eye and elsewhere.
avoid: People with a sulfa allergy, kidney or liver disease, or low sodium or potassium.
about: Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that has been used since the 1950s. It lowers fluid pressure inside the eye, helps the body adjust to high altitude and has a mild water-pill effect. A flavored or smooth oral liquid can help people who cannot swallow tablets and pets that need a precise amount. Veterinary use is off-label.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a skin rash, blistering or peeling skin, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever or sore throat, severe weakness or confusion, fast or deep breathing, or sharp side or back pain that could be a kidney stone.
interactions: Important interactions include high-dose aspirin, other diuretics or steroids that can lower potassium, lithium, and some seizure medicines such as topiramate and phenytoin. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Acetazolamide is usually avoided in pregnancy, especially early on, and small amounts pass into breast milk; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats taking acetazolamide by mouth may have panting, vomiting, weakness or low potassium, so veterinarians often prefer eye drops for long-term glaucoma care. Cats can be especially sensitive, so give it exactly as your veterinarian directs.
tips: Shake the liquid well and measure each dose with the syringe or cup provided.
It can be taken with food to reduce stomach upset.
Drink plenty of fluids unless your prescriber tells you otherwise, which may lower the risk of kidney stones.
For altitude sickness, your prescriber will tell you when to start before you travel.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check electrolytes such as potassium and sodium, kidney function and blood counts, especially with longer use.
faqs: Why does acetazolamide make my fingers tingle?
Tingling in the fingers, toes or around the mouth is a common and usually harmless side effect. Tell your prescriber if it is bothersome or does not go away.
Does acetazolamide make carbonated drinks taste strange?
Yes, many people notice that soda and other fizzy drinks taste flat or metallic while taking it. This goes away after the medicine is stopped.
Can I take acetazolamide if I am allergic to sulfa drugs?
Acetazolamide is a sulfonamide, so people with a sulfa allergy may react to it. Tell your prescriber about any sulfa allergy before starting.

name: Adapalene
uses: Acne.
how: A retinoid that normalizes skin cell turnover and calms inflammation.
avoid: Pregnancy. Increases sun sensitivity.
about: Adapalene is a third-generation topical retinoid, related to vitamin A, used for acne since the 1990s and now also sold over the counter in the US. It helps keep pores from clogging and calms inflamed breakouts. Dermatologists may request it compounded in a cream base or combined with ingredients such as azelaic acid or niacinamide to treat several concerns with one product.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling of the face or lips, or trouble breathing, or for severe burning, blistering or swelling of the treated skin.
interactions: Adapalene is applied to the skin, so drug interactions are unlikely, but using it with other drying or peeling products such as salicylic acid, strong exfoliants, alcohol-based toners or waxing can increase irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Adapalene is not recommended during pregnancy; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin, usually at night, and avoid the eyes, lips and corners of the nose.
Use a gentle moisturizer and a daily broad-spectrum sunscreen, since your skin may burn more easily.
Expect some dryness or a temporary flare in the first few weeks; this often settles as your skin adjusts.
Wash your hands after applying.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: How long does adapalene take to work?
Many people start to see changes after several weeks, and it can take about three months to see the full effect. Acne may look worse at first before it improves.
Is adapalene the same as tretinoin?
Both are topical retinoids used for acne, but they are different molecules. Adapalene is often described as gentler on the skin, and your prescriber decides which one fits you.

name: Alendronate
uses: Bone loss and, in cats, some types of high calcium.
side: Esophageal irritation; take with water as directed.
how: Slows the cells that break down bone.
avoid: People or pets with swallowing problems or esophageal disease; give with plenty of water.
about: Alendronate is a bisphosphonate, a group of medicines used since the 1990s to strengthen bones by slowing bone breakdown. In people it is used for osteoporosis, and veterinarians use it off-label for cats with high blood calcium of unknown cause. A flavored suspension can help with pets or people who have trouble with tablets, though careful swallowing steps still matter.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for chest pain, painful or difficult swallowing, new or worse heartburn, vomiting blood or refusing food, severe bone, joint or muscle pain, jaw pain or swelling, or new thigh or groin pain.
interactions: Calcium, antacids, iron, magnesium, other medicines and even food can block absorption, so keep them separate from alendronate as directed; NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen may add to stomach and esophagus irritation. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Alendronate is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In cats, alendronate is usually given on an empty stomach and followed right away by a small amount of water or food so it doesn't sit in the esophagus. Your veterinarian will explain the exact routine for your cat.
tips: Take it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach with a full glass of plain water, as directed.
Stay upright, sitting or standing, and wait before eating, drinking anything else or taking other medicines for the time your prescriber gives you.
Shake the suspension well before measuring.
If you miss a dose, follow your prescriber's instructions rather than taking it later in the day.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check calcium and vitamin D levels, kidney function and bone density over time; pets usually have repeat calcium checks.
faqs: Why do I have to stay upright after taking alendronate?
Lying down too soon can let the medicine flow back up and irritate the esophagus. Staying upright helps it move into the stomach.
How long do people usually take alendronate?
Many people take it for several years, and prescribers often review whether to continue or take a break after that. Your prescriber decides based on your bone health.
Should I see a dentist while on alendronate?
It is a good idea to tell your dentist you take it, especially before dental surgery or extractions. Rarely, bisphosphonates are linked to jaw bone problems.

name: Alpha lipoic acid
uses: Antioxidant supplement for nerve support. Toxic to cats.
how: An antioxidant involved in energy metabolism.
avoid: Cats (it is toxic to them). People with diabetes should monitor blood sugar.
about: Alpha lipoic acid is a natural antioxidant the body makes in small amounts and uses to turn food into energy. It has been studied for years for nerve health, especially in people with diabetes, and is widely sold as a supplement. A compounded oral liquid can help people who cannot swallow capsules or who need a dye-free or specific-strength product.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling or trouble breathing, or for signs of low blood sugar such as shakiness, sweating, confusion or a fast heartbeat.
interactions: Alpha lipoic acid may lower blood sugar, so it can add to the effect of insulin and other diabetes medicines, and it may affect thyroid hormone medicine. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is not enough safety information on alpha lipoic acid supplements in pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Taking it with food may ease stomach upset.
If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar more often when you start, as your prescriber directs.
Store it where pets cannot reach it; it is toxic to cats even in small amounts.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: If you have diabetes, your prescriber may want you to watch your blood sugar more closely; otherwise routine monitoring is usually not needed.
faqs: Is alpha lipoic acid safe for pets?
It is toxic to cats, even in small amounts, and should be kept well away from them. Don't give it to any pet unless your veterinarian approves.
Can alpha lipoic acid lower my blood sugar?
It may lower blood sugar somewhat, which matters if you take diabetes medicines. Your prescriber may adjust your plan or ask you to monitor more often.

name: Aluminum hydroxide
uses: Phosphate binder for pets with kidney disease.
how: Binds phosphorus in food so less is absorbed.
avoid: Long-term use needs monitoring; give with meals.
about: Aluminum hydroxide is an antacid that has been used for decades. In pets with kidney disease it is used off-label as a phosphate binder, because it holds onto phosphorus from food in the gut so less is absorbed. Many of the commercial liquid and gel products have become hard to find, so veterinarians often ask for capsules or a flavored suspension that can be mixed into food.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for severe constipation or straining, refusing food, repeated vomiting, unusual weakness, wobbliness or changes in behavior.
interactions: Aluminum hydroxide can bind many oral medicines, including doxycycline and other tetracyclines, fluoroquinolone antibiotics and some heart and thyroid medicines, so your veterinarian may ask you to space doses apart. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: It only works when it is in the gut with food, so it is usually mixed into or given with each meal. Cats with kidney disease are prone to constipation, so watch litter box habits and tell your veterinarian about any change.
tips: Give it with meals or mix it into food so it can bind phosphorus.
Shake the suspension well before measuring.
Keep feeding the kidney diet your veterinarian recommends, since the binder works together with diet.
If you miss a dose, give it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't give two doses at once.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck phosphorus and kidney values periodically and may adjust the plan based on the results.
faqs: Why does my pet need a phosphate binder?
When kidneys are not working well, phosphorus builds up in the blood and can make kidney disease worse. A binder lowers how much phosphorus is absorbed from food.
Can I give it at a different time than meals?
It works best mixed into or given right with food. Giving it on an empty stomach does little to lower phosphorus.

name: Amantadine
uses: Chronic pain in dogs and cats; Parkinson's in people.
how: Blocks NMDA receptors involved in chronic pain and increases dopamine.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease or seizures.
drugClass: NMDA receptor antagonist (antiviral and antiparkinson agent)
about: Amantadine was first introduced in the 1960s as an antiviral for influenza and was later found to help Parkinson's symptoms in people. Veterinarians use it off-label for long-term pain in dogs and cats, often added to an NSAID or gabapentin. Because pets need small, precise amounts and the capsules are bitter, it is commonly compounded as flavored liquids or treats.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for confusion, hallucinations, severe agitation, seizures, fainting, trouble urinating, or a skin rash.
interactions: Amantadine can add to the effects of anticholinergic medicines, stimulants and sedatives, and levels may rise with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim or some diuretics; it should not be given close to the live nasal flu vaccine. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Amantadine is usually avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In pets, amantadine is usually added to other pain medicines rather than used alone, and it may take a few weeks to see the full benefit. Some dogs have soft stools or restlessness at first, which often settles.
tips: It can be given with or without food; food may help if it causes stomach upset.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
Don't stop it suddenly in people with Parkinson's; ask your prescriber how to taper.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check kidney function, since amantadine is cleared by the kidneys, and will follow up on how well pain or symptoms are controlled.
faqs: How long does amantadine take to work for pain in dogs?
It is usually not a fast-acting pain reliever, and many veterinarians judge results after a few weeks. Your veterinarian will tell you what to watch for.
Can amantadine be given with my dog's NSAID or gabapentin?
Yes, veterinarians often combine amantadine with an NSAID or gabapentin for arthritis pain. Only combine medicines your veterinarian has prescribed together.
Is amantadine still used for the flu?
It is no longer recommended for influenza in the US because most flu viruses have become resistant to it. Today it is used mainly for Parkinson's in people and chronic pain in pets.

name: Amikacin
uses: Resistant bacterial infections, including vet ear preparations.
how: An aminoglycoside that stops bacteria from making proteins.
avoid: Ruptured eardrums (ear products) and kidney disease.
about: Amikacin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used since the 1970s for serious infections, including bacteria that resist other antibiotics such as Pseudomonas. In veterinary medicine it is often used in ear preparations and topical products, where it can act directly on the infection with little absorption into the body. Compounding lets veterinarians combine it with an antifungal or steroid in one ear product.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for a head tilt, loss of balance, circling, sudden deafness, or increased thirst and urination, which can signal ear or kidney effects.
interactions: Other medicines that can affect the kidneys or hearing, such as other aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, some NSAIDs and furosemide, add to risk, mainly when amikacin is absorbed into the body. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Before using an ear product, your veterinarian checks that the eardrum is intact, because aminoglycosides in the middle ear can damage hearing and balance. Cats may be more sensitive than dogs to these effects.
tips: Use the ear product exactly as directed and finish the full course even if the ear looks better.
Gently massage the base of the ear after applying, unless your veterinarian says otherwise.
Wash your hands after applying.
Do not clean the ear right after an ear pack is placed unless your veterinarian tells you to.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck the ears, and pets on oral or longer treatment may have kidney values monitored.
faqs: What is an ear pack?
An ear pack is a gel-like medicine your veterinarian places in the ear canal so it stays and releases medicine over days. It lets treatment continue without daily ear drops.
Is amikacin safe for cats?
Veterinarians do use it in cats, but cats can be more sensitive to hearing, balance and kidney effects. Your veterinarian decides if it is right for your cat.

name: Amitriptyline
uses: Nerve pain, sleep and mood in people; anxiety, itch and bladder pain in pets; also in topical pain creams.
how: A tricyclic that increases serotonin and norepinephrine and calms nerve pain signals.
avoid: People or pets with heart rhythm problems, glaucoma or urinary retention, and anyone on MAO inhibitors.
about: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant that has been used since the early 1960s. Today it is often prescribed at low amounts for nerve pain, headaches and sleep, and veterinarians use it off-label for anxiety, itch, overgrooming and bladder pain in pets. Compounding provides flavored liquids for pets, small-strength capsules, and topical creams or gels where it is combined with other pain ingredients.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast or irregular heartbeat, fainting, seizures, eye pain or vision changes, not being able to urinate, high fever with stiffness or agitation, or new or worsening thoughts of suicide in people.
interactions: Never combine it with MAO inhibitors, including selegiline and amitraz in some tick collars and dips for dogs, and use care with other serotonin medicines, some opioid pain medicines, alcohol, sedatives and drugs that affect heart rhythm. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; amitriptyline is used only when the benefit outweighs the risk, and you should not stop it suddenly on your own.
petNotes: Cats often get it for bladder pain or overgrooming and dogs for anxiety or itch, and a flavored suspension helps because the tablets are very bitter. Transdermal gels may be absorbed less reliably than oral forms in cats, so your veterinarian will watch the response.
tips: It is often given in the evening because it can cause drowsiness.
Wear gloves or wash your hands after applying creams or gels, and rotate application sites.
Don't stop it suddenly; your prescriber or veterinarian can explain how to taper.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check your heart rhythm (ECG) if you have heart risks or take higher amounts; pets on long-term treatment may have periodic blood work.
faqs: How long does amitriptyline take to work for nerve pain?
Some people notice better sleep within days, but pain relief often builds over several weeks. Your prescriber decides when to judge the result.
Can I drink alcohol while taking amitriptyline?
It is best to avoid alcohol, because it can add to drowsiness and dizziness and make side effects worse.
Will amitriptyline make my cat sleepy?
Drowsiness is a common effect in cats, especially at the start. Tell your veterinarian if your cat seems very sleepy, wobbly or stops eating.

name: Amlodipine
uses: High blood pressure in people and especially cats.
side: Ankle swelling, flushing, low blood pressure, gum overgrowth in dogs.
how: Relaxes blood vessels by blocking calcium from entering the muscle in their walls.
avoid: People or pets with very low blood pressure or severe heart valve narrowing.
about: Amlodipine is a long-acting calcium channel blocker used for high blood pressure and chest pain in people since the early 1990s. Veterinarians commonly use it off-label for high blood pressure in cats, which often goes along with kidney disease or an overactive thyroid. Cats need very small, exact amounts, so it is often compounded as flavored liquids, treats or transdermal gels.
conditions: High blood pressure from kidney disease in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, severe dizziness or weakness, collapse, chest pain that is new or worse, or swelling of the face, lips or tongue.
interactions: It can add to other blood pressure medicines, and some antifungals such as ketoconazole and itraconazole, certain antibiotics such as clarithromycin, and cyclosporine can change levels; prescribers may also limit simvastatin with it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited safety information about amlodipine in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In cats, high blood pressure can damage the eyes, kidneys, heart and brain, so steady daily treatment matters. Transdermal gel may be absorbed less than oral forms in cats, and dogs on long-term use can develop gum overgrowth.
tips: Give or take it at about the same time each day, with or without food.
Wear gloves to apply transdermal gel to the inner ear flap and switch ears as directed.
Get up slowly from sitting or lying down if you feel dizzy.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will recheck blood pressure, and pets with kidney disease usually have kidney values and eye exams followed over time.
faqs: How do I know if my cat needs amlodipine?
Your veterinarian measures your cat's blood pressure, much like in people, often along with checks of the eyes and kidneys. Signs such as sudden blindness or dilated pupils need an urgent visit.
Why do my ankles swell on amlodipine?
Ankle swelling is a common side effect caused by widened blood vessels, not by fluid from the heart. Tell your prescriber if it is bothersome.
Can I eat grapefruit while taking amlodipine?
Grapefruit has only a small effect on amlodipine for most people, but check with your prescriber if you eat a lot of it.

name: Ammonium chloride
uses: Acidifies urine to help dissolve or prevent certain bladder stones in pets.
how: Makes the urine more acidic.
avoid: Pets with liver or kidney disease.
about: Ammonium chloride is a salt that makes urine more acidic. Veterinarians have long used it in dogs and cats to help dissolve or prevent struvite bladder stones and crystals, which form more easily in alkaline urine. Commercial products for pets are limited, so it is often compounded as capsules in the amount a veterinarian orders. Its use is usually paired with diet changes.
conditions: Urinary acidification in cats and dogs
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for repeated vomiting, weakness, fast or labored breathing, confusion, unusual sleepiness, or straining to urinate with little or no urine.
interactions: Avoid combining it with other urine acidifiers, such as methionine or acidifying prescription diets, unless your veterinarian directs it, and it can change how some medicines leave the body through the urine. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: It is used for struvite stones, not for other stone types such as calcium oxalate or urate, which can be made worse by acidic urine. A male cat straining in the litter box with no urine is an emergency.
tips: Give it with food to lower the chance of stomach upset.
Encourage your pet to drink water, and follow any diet plan your veterinarian gives you.
If you miss a dose, give it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't give two doses at once.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck urine pH and urine tests, and may take X-rays and blood work to follow the stones and acid balance.
faqs: Will ammonium chloride dissolve all bladder stones?
No. It may help with struvite stones but is not used for calcium oxalate or urate stones. Your veterinarian identifies the stone type first.
Can my pet stay on ammonium chloride long term?
Some pets use it for a set time while others need longer prevention. Your veterinarian decides and will monitor urine and blood tests.

name: Amoxicillin
uses: Bacterial infections.
how: A penicillin antibiotic that breaks down bacterial cell walls.
avoid: Anyone with a penicillin allergy. Not for rabbits, guinea pigs and some other small mammals.
about: Amoxicillin is a penicillin-type antibiotic that has been widely used since the 1970s in both people and animals. It treats many common bacterial infections of the ears, sinuses, skin and urinary tract. Compounding can provide flavored liquids for children and pets, dye-free or allergen-free capsules, and special forms such as ear packs or troches when a prescriber needs them.
conditions: Skin infections in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, a blistering or peeling rash, or severe watery or bloody diarrhea, even weeks after finishing.
interactions: Important interactions include methotrexate, allopurinol (rash), and blood thinners such as warfarin. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Amoxicillin is commonly used during pregnancy and breastfeeding when an antibiotic is needed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats generally tolerate amoxicillin, and giving it with food can ease stomach upset. Never give it to rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils or chinchillas, because it can cause deadly gut problems.
tips: Finish the full course even if symptoms get better.
Shake liquid forms well and store them as the label directs, usually in the refrigerator.
It can be taken with or without food; food may help with stomach upset.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules, especially if symptoms do not improve.
faqs: How fast does amoxicillin start working?
Many people and pets begin to feel better within a few days. Call your prescriber if symptoms are not improving or get worse.
Does amoxicillin need to be refrigerated?
Liquid amoxicillin is usually kept in the refrigerator, but follow the storage directions on your label, since compounded forms can differ.
Can I drink alcohol while taking amoxicillin?
Alcohol does not directly interact with amoxicillin, but it can worsen stomach upset and may slow recovery from illness.

name: Amoxicillin/clavulanate
uses: Bacterial infections.
how: Amoxicillin plus clavulanate, which protects it from bacterial enzymes that would destroy it.
avoid: Anyone with a penicillin allergy. Not for rabbits and guinea pigs.
about: Amoxicillin/clavulanate pairs the antibiotic amoxicillin with clavulanate, which protects it from enzymes some bacteria use to resist penicillins. It has been used since the 1980s in people and is one of the most commonly prescribed antibiotics for dogs and cats. Compounded flavored liquids can help with dosing small pets, children and anyone who cannot swallow tablets.
conditions: Skin infections in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for hives, facial swelling, trouble breathing, a blistering rash, severe or bloody diarrhea, or yellowing of the skin, gums or eyes.
interactions: Important interactions include methotrexate, allopurinol and blood thinners such as warfarin. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Amoxicillin/clavulanate is often used during pregnancy and breastfeeding when needed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats usually tolerate it well, and giving it with a meal can reduce vomiting or diarrhea. It must never be given to rabbits, guinea pigs or other small herbivores.
tips: Give or take it at the start of a meal to reduce stomach upset.
Shake the liquid well and keep it refrigerated if the label says so.
Finish the full course even if things look better.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: What is the difference between amoxicillin and amoxicillin/clavulanate?
The clavulanate helps amoxicillin work against bacteria that make an enzyme that would otherwise break it down. Your prescriber chooses based on the likely infection.
Why does amoxicillin/clavulanate cause diarrhea?
It can upset the normal gut bacteria. Taking it with food may help, but call your prescriber or veterinarian if diarrhea is severe or bloody.

name: Amphotericin B
uses: Nasal and sinus rinses for fungal sinus conditions.
how: Binds fungal cell membranes and makes them leak.
avoid: Usually well tolerated as a nasal rinse; not for use without a prescriber's direction.
about: Amphotericin B is an antifungal medicine that has been used since the late 1950s, mainly by IV for serious infections. When used as a nasal spray or sinus rinse, it acts on the sinus lining with very little absorbed into the body. Because no commercial nasal product exists, ear, nose and throat specialists ask for it compounded, sometimes combined with other ingredients. These uses are off-label.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, or for heavy nosebleeds.
interactions: When used in the nose or sinuses very little reaches the bloodstream, so drug interactions are unlikely. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Little of a nasal rinse is absorbed, but data in pregnancy are limited; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Use the spray or rinse exactly as directed and clean the bottle or device after each use.
Store it as the label directs, which is often in the refrigerator and away from light.
Gently blow your nose before using it so the medicine reaches the sinus lining.
monitoring: Routine lab monitoring is usually not needed for nasal use, but keep follow-up visits, which may include a nasal scope, that your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Is amphotericin B nasal rinse the same as IV amphotericin?
It is the same ingredient, but a nasal rinse acts mainly on the sinus lining and very little is absorbed, so the serious side effects of IV use are not expected.
How long will I use an amphotericin B sinus rinse?
Length of treatment varies, and your ear, nose and throat specialist decides based on follow-up exams.

name: Anastrozole
uses: An aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen; used in breast cancer care and sometimes alongside testosterone therapy.
how: Blocks aromatase, the enzyme that converts testosterone into estrogen, lowering estrogen levels.
avoid: Premenopausal women (unless prescribed alongside other therapy), people with osteoporosis, and those who are pregnant.
about: Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor used since the mid-1990s in breast cancer care for postmenopausal women. By blocking the enzyme that turns testosterone into estrogen, it lowers estrogen levels. Some prescribers also use it off-label in men on testosterone therapy whose estrogen rises too high. Compounding allows small-strength capsules or a cream that can be matched to the prescriber's plan.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, a blistering skin rash, chest pain or shortness of breath, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a broken bone from a minor fall.
interactions: Estrogen-containing products and tamoxifen can work against anastrozole. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Anastrozole must not be used during pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby, and it is not used while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you could become pregnant.
tips: Take it at the same time each day, with or without food.
Wash your hands after applying the cream and keep treated skin away from partners and children.
Regular weight-bearing exercise and calcium and vitamin D, as your prescriber advises, help protect bones.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check estrogen levels, cholesterol and bone density over time.
faqs: Why is anastrozole used with testosterone?
Some testosterone is naturally converted to estrogen, and some men develop high estrogen on therapy. Prescribers may add anastrozole off-label when lab results and symptoms call for it.
Can anastrozole cause joint pain?
Yes, joint and muscle aches are common. Tell your prescriber, since there may be ways to manage them.

name: Apomorphine
uses: Induces vomiting in dogs after a toxic ingestion, given by a veterinarian.
how: Stimulates dopamine receptors in the brain's vomiting center.
avoid: Cats (usually), and pets that are unconscious, having seizures or swallowed something caustic or sharp.
about: Apomorphine is a dopamine agonist that veterinarians have used for many years to make dogs vomit quickly after they swallow something harmful. It is usually given in the clinic, often as a small troche placed in the pocket of the lower eyelid, so it can be rinsed out once vomiting starts. Compounded troches and capsules give clinics a convenient form, since commercial veterinary products are limited.
conditions: Swallowed foreign objects (when safe to vomit)
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for vomiting that continues after you get home, extreme drowsiness, weakness, trouble breathing, or red, irritated eyes after a visit.
interactions: Anti-nausea medicines such as maropitant and metoclopramide and sedatives such as acepromazine can block its effect, and sedatives or opioid pain medicines can add to drowsiness. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Apomorphine is generally used in dogs; it is often unreliable in cats, so veterinarians usually choose a different medicine for them. Never try to make your pet vomit at home without talking to a veterinarian or pet poison helpline first.
tips: Call your veterinarian or a pet poison helpline right away if your pet swallows something harmful; quick treatment matters.
Bring the package or a sample of what your pet swallowed to the clinic.
Your pet may be sleepy for a short time afterward; keep them quiet and watch them at home.
monitoring: Your veterinarian watches your pet in the clinic while the medicine works and may recommend follow-up care or blood tests depending on what was swallowed.
faqs: Can I give apomorphine to my dog at home?
No. It is given by a veterinarian, who first decides whether vomiting is safe. Some swallowed items, such as caustic chemicals or sharp objects, can do more harm coming back up.
Why is apomorphine placed in the eye?
The tissue under the eyelid absorbs it quickly, and the veterinarian can rinse it out once the dog vomits to limit lingering side effects.

name: Aripiprazole
uses: Mood disorders and, in low doses, other conditions as prescribed.
how: Partially activates dopamine and serotonin receptors, stabilizing their signals.
avoid: Older adults with dementia and people with a history of seizures.
about: Aripiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic first approved in the US in 2002. It partly turns on dopamine and serotonin receptors, which helps balance their signals. It is prescribed for several mood and thought disorders and, sometimes at very low amounts, for other conditions as the prescriber decides, which can be off-label. Compounded capsules can provide small or uncommon strengths that are hard to get from commercial tablets.
serious: Get medical help right away for high fever with stiff muscles and confusion, uncontrolled movements of the face or body, fainting, seizures, new or worsening thoughts of suicide, or strong urges you can't control, such as gambling or binge eating.
interactions: Medicines that change how the liver breaks it down, such as fluoxetine, paroxetine, ketoconazole and carbamazepine, can raise or lower levels, and alcohol, sedatives and blood pressure medicines can add to dizziness. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; aripiprazole may affect newborns when used late in pregnancy, and you should not stop it on your own.
tips: Take it at the same time each day, with or without food.
Stand up slowly and avoid overheating or getting dehydrated.
Don't stop it suddenly without talking to your prescriber.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check how you are doing and may check weight, blood sugar and cholesterol over time, and look for any unusual movements.
faqs: How long does aripiprazole take to work?
Some effects may be noticed within a week or two, while full benefit can take several weeks. Your prescriber will follow your progress.
Can I drink alcohol while taking aripiprazole?
It is best to avoid alcohol, because it can add to drowsiness and dizziness and may make mood symptoms worse.
What is low-dose aripiprazole?
Some prescribers use much smaller amounts than usual for certain conditions, which can be off-label. Compounded capsules can make these small strengths possible.

name: Atenolol
uses: High blood pressure and heart rhythm or heart muscle conditions in people and cats.
side: Tiredness, slow heart rate, low blood pressure.
how: A beta-blocker that slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.
avoid: People or pets with asthma, very slow heart rate or uncontrolled heart failure. Do not stop suddenly.
about: Atenolol is a beta-blocker that has been used since the 1970s. It slows the heart rate and lowers blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline on the heart. Veterinarians use it off-label in cats with thickened heart muscle and in pets with fast heart rhythms or high blood pressure. Compounding provides flavored liquids, treats and small capsules for precise pet dosing.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a very slow pulse, fainting or collapse, trouble breathing or wheezing, cold or pale limbs, or sudden weight gain and swelling that could signal heart failure.
interactions: Other medicines that slow the heart, such as diltiazem, verapamil and digoxin, can add to its effect, NSAIDs may weaken it, and it can hide signs of low blood sugar in people taking insulin or other diabetes medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Atenolol may affect a baby's growth during pregnancy and passes into breast milk; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats with heart disease often need small, precise amounts, which is why flavored liquids and treats are helpful. Transdermal gel may be absorbed less reliably than oral forms, so your veterinarian may check heart rate to see how well it is working.
tips: Give or take it at the same times each day.
Never stop it suddenly; stopping quickly can cause a fast heartbeat or chest pain, so your prescriber or veterinarian will explain how to taper.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check heart rate and blood pressure, and pets with heart disease may have repeat heart ultrasounds or ECGs.
faqs: Why can't I stop atenolol suddenly?
Stopping a beta-blocker all at once can cause a rebound fast heartbeat, high blood pressure or chest pain. Tapering under your prescriber's direction is safer.
Is atenolol safe for cats?
Veterinarians use it off-label in cats, especially for heart muscle disease and fast heart rates. Your veterinarian decides if it fits your cat's condition.
Can I take atenolol if I have asthma?
Beta-blockers can tighten the airways, so people with asthma need extra care. Your prescriber decides whether it is appropriate.

name: Azathioprine
uses: Immune-mediated diseases in dogs.
side: Vomiting, bone marrow and liver effects; requires monitoring. Not for cats.
how: Interferes with the growth of immune cells.
avoid: Cats (it can cause serious bone marrow suppression), pregnancy, and people or dogs with low TPMT enzyme activity.
about: Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant that has been used since the 1960s to calm an overactive immune system. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs with immune-mediated diseases, often so the amount of steroid can be lowered. Compounding helps provide exact capsule sizes or a flavored suspension for dogs of different sizes. It is not used in cats.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for fever, pale gums, unusual bruising or bleeding, yellow gums or eyes, repeated vomiting, belly pain or not eating.
interactions: Allopurinol can greatly raise azathioprine levels and should be avoided unless your veterinarian directs otherwise, and other medicines that suppress the bone marrow or immune system add to the risk; live vaccines may need to wait. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Cats are very sensitive to azathioprine and can develop serious bone marrow suppression, so it is a dogs-only medicine. People who are pregnant or trying to become pregnant should wear gloves when handling it.
tips: Give it with food if it upsets your dog's stomach.
Wear disposable gloves when handling capsules or the suspension and wash your hands afterward.
Store it away from other pets, especially cats.
If you miss a dose, give it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't give two doses at once.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check blood counts and liver values often at first and then periodically for as long as your dog takes it.
faqs: How long does azathioprine take to work in dogs?
It often takes a few weeks to reach its full effect, which is why it is usually started alongside a faster-acting steroid.
Why can't cats take azathioprine?
Cats break it down poorly and can develop severe, sometimes life-threatening bone marrow suppression even at small amounts.

name: Azelaic acid
uses: Acne, rosacea and dark spots.
how: Reduces acne bacteria, calms redness and slows pigment production.
avoid: People with a history of cold sores near the application area.
drugClass: Topical dicarboxylic acid (anti-acne and skin-brightening agent)
about: Azelaic acid is a naturally occurring acid, found in grains such as wheat and barley, that has been used on the skin for decades. It helps with acne and the bumps and redness of rosacea and can fade uneven dark spots. Dermatologists often ask for it compounded in a custom cream or combined with ingredients like niacinamide or tranexamic acid.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling of the face or trouble breathing, or for severe burning, blistering or noticeable lightening of normal skin.
interactions: Azelaic acid is used on the skin and has very few known drug interactions, but combining it with other strong acids or exfoliants may increase irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Very little azelaic acid is absorbed through the skin, and it is often considered an option in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but check with your prescriber first.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin and avoid the eyes, mouth and inside the nose.
Mild tingling is common at first and usually fades within a few weeks.
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen daily, especially when treating dark spots.
Wash your hands after applying.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: How long does azelaic acid take to work?
Many people see changes in acne or rosacea after about a month, and dark spots often take a few months to fade.
Can I use azelaic acid with retinoids?
Many people use them together, often at different times of day, but this may add to dryness. Ask your prescriber how to fit them into your routine.

avoid: Sun exposure, which makes melasma worse. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Azelaic acid, kojic acid and vitamin C each slow pigment production, and niacinamide reduces the transfer of pigment to the skin surface.
name: Azelaic acid and kojic acid melasma cream
side: Stinging, itching, redness or dryness, usually mild and early in treatment.
uses: Melasma and dark spots, without hydroquinone. Made with azelaic acid 18%, kojic acid 4%, niacinamide 3% and vitamin C 2%.
about: This compounded cream combines four skin-brightening ingredients so that people with melasma or dark spots can treat several steps of pigment formation with one product, without using hydroquinone. Azelaic acid and kojic acid have long been used for uneven pigment, while niacinamide and vitamin C are popular in skin care. Dermatologists may choose it for people who don't tolerate or want to avoid hydroquinone.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing, or for severe burning, blistering or patches of skin that become lighter than your normal skin tone.
interactions: Used on the skin, this cream has very few drug interactions, but layering it with other acids, retinoids or exfoliants can increase stinging and dryness. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Azelaic acid is often considered acceptable in pregnancy, but there is limited information on kojic acid, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin over the dark areas as directed, avoiding the eyes and lips.
Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen and a hat every day; sun exposure can undo progress.
Wash your hands after applying.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber may take photos at follow-up visits to track changes.
faqs: How long before I see results for melasma?
Melasma tends to fade slowly, and changes often take two to three months of steady use with daily sun protection.
Why is this cream made without hydroquinone?
Some people get irritation from hydroquinone or want to avoid it for long-term use. This combination uses other ingredients that also act on pigment production.
Will melasma come back after I stop?
Melasma often returns, especially with sun, heat or hormone changes, so many people need ongoing sun protection and a maintenance plan from their prescriber.

avoid: Sun exposure, which makes melasma worse. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Tranexamic acid calms the signals that switch on pigment cells. Azelaic acid and kojic acid slow pigment production, and niacinamide reduces the transfer of pigment to the skin surface.
name: Azelaic acid and tranexamic acid melasma cream
side: Stinging, itching, redness or dryness, usually mild and early in treatment.
uses: Melasma and dark spots, without hydroquinone. Made with azelaic acid 12%, tranexamic acid 5%, kojic acid 4% and niacinamide 3%.
about: This compounded cream combines tranexamic acid with azelaic acid, kojic acid and niacinamide to address melasma and dark spots without hydroquinone. Tranexamic acid has been used for decades as a medicine to control bleeding, and dermatologists more recently began applying it to the skin, off-label, for melasma. Putting these ingredients in one cream lets people treat pigment from several angles with a single step.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing, or for severe burning, blistering or patches of skin that become lighter than your normal skin tone.
interactions: Very little is absorbed through the skin, so drug interactions are unlikely, but using it with other acids, retinoids or exfoliants can add to irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on using topical tranexamic acid and kojic acid in pregnancy, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin over the dark areas as directed, avoiding the eyes and lips.
Use broad-spectrum sunscreen every day, and reapply when outdoors.
Wash your hands after applying.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Is topical tranexamic acid the same as tranexamic acid pills?
It is the same ingredient, but applied to the skin very little reaches the bloodstream. Its use on the skin for melasma is off-label.
How long does it take to see results?
Pigment usually fades slowly over a few months, and daily sunscreen is needed to protect results.

name: Azithromycin
uses: Bacterial and some respiratory and parasitic infections.
how: A macrolide antibiotic that stops bacteria from making proteins.
avoid: People or pets with liver disease or heart rhythm problems.
about: Azithromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used since the early 1990s for many respiratory, skin and sexually transmitted infections. It stays in the body's tissues for a long time, which allows short courses. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs, cats and other animals for certain respiratory, skin and parasitic infections, and flavored suspensions or pastes make dosing easier.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast or irregular heartbeat, fainting, signs of an allergic reaction, a blistering rash, severe or bloody diarrhea, or yellowing of the skin or eyes.
interactions: Use care with other medicines that affect heart rhythm, such as some antiarrhythmics and antipsychotics, as well as warfarin, digoxin and cyclosporine; separate it from aluminum or magnesium antacids. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Azithromycin is often used during pregnancy and breastfeeding when an antibiotic is needed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats often tolerate azithromycin well, and its long action can mean fewer doses than other antibiotics. Vomiting or diarrhea are the most common problems, and giving it with a little food may help.
tips: Shake the suspension well before measuring each dose.
Finish the full course even though courses are often short.
It can be given with or without food; food may help with stomach upset.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses; people with heart rhythm problems may need an ECG.
faqs: Why is a course of azithromycin so short?
Azithromycin stays in the body's tissues for days after the last dose, so it keeps working after you finish.
Can I drink alcohol with azithromycin?
There is no major direct interaction, but alcohol can worsen stomach upset and may slow recovery.
Is azithromycin safe for cats?
Veterinarians commonly use it off-label in cats for some respiratory and other infections. Your veterinarian decides the amount and length of treatment.

name: Baclofen
uses: Muscle spasm, including in topical pain and vaginal creams.
how: Activates GABA-B receptors to relax muscle spasm.
avoid: People with kidney disease or seizures. Toxic to dogs in overdose; keep away from pets.
about: Baclofen is a muscle relaxant used since the 1970s, mainly for muscle spasm from conditions such as multiple sclerosis and spinal cord injury. Compounded topical creams combine it with other ingredients for local muscle and nerve pain, and vaginal creams or suppositories are prescribed off-label for pelvic floor muscle spasm. Applying it where it is needed may lower the amount that reaches the rest of the body.
conditions: Spasticity from MS or spinal cord injury
serious: Get medical help right away for extreme drowsiness, confusion, slow or shallow breathing, hallucinations, seizures or severe weakness.
interactions: Alcohol, sedatives, sleep aids, opioid pain medicines, some antihistamines and other muscle relaxants can add to drowsiness and slowed breathing. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; baclofen is used in pregnancy only when the benefit outweighs the risk.
tips: Apply creams only to the area your prescriber directs and wash your hands afterward.
Use vaginal creams or suppositories at bedtime if directed, since lying down helps them stay in place.
Avoid driving or other risky tasks until you know how it affects you.
Keep it away from dogs and cats, which can be poisoned by small amounts.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for topical or vaginal use, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Is baclofen cream as strong as baclofen tablets?
Creams are used to act mainly where they are applied, and usually less reaches the bloodstream than with tablets. Your prescriber decides which form fits your needs.
Can I drink alcohol while using baclofen?
It is best to avoid alcohol, since both can cause drowsiness and dizziness.
What should I do if my dog licks baclofen cream?
Call your veterinarian or a pet poison helpline right away. Dogs are very sensitive to baclofen, and even a small amount can cause serious problems.

name: BEG nasal spray
uses: A compounded nasal spray combining mupirocin (Bactroban), EDTA and gentamicin, prescribed for chronic sinus infections, often after sinus surgery.
side: Nasal stinging, burning or irritation, and occasional nosebleeds.
how: EDTA helps break up bacterial biofilms, the protective layers bacteria form in the sinuses, so the antibiotics mupirocin and gentamicin can reach the bacteria.
avoid: People allergic to mupirocin or aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin. Use only as long as directed and follow up with your prescriber.
about: BEG nasal spray is a compounded spray named for its ingredients: Bactroban (mupirocin), EDTA and gentamicin. Ear, nose and throat specialists may prescribe it off-label for chronic sinus infections that keep coming back, especially after sinus surgery. Because the antibiotics are applied right to the sinus lining, the goal is to reach the infection while limiting how much enters the bloodstream. No commercial version exists.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing, or for ringing in the ears, hearing loss, dizziness or balance problems, or heavy nosebleeds.
interactions: Little reaches the bloodstream, but tell your prescriber if you take other aminoglycoside antibiotics or medicines that can affect the kidneys or hearing. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside, a group of antibiotics that can affect a baby's hearing when taken by mouth or injection, so talk to your prescriber before using this spray if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Gently blow your nose or rinse with saline first, if directed, so the spray reaches the sinus lining.
Aim the nozzle toward the outer wall of the nostril, away from the center.
Store it as the label directs and don't share the bottle.
Use it only for the time your prescriber sets.
monitoring: Your ear, nose and throat specialist will usually see you for follow-up, which may include a nasal scope or culture.
faqs: What does BEG stand for?
BEG stands for Bactroban (mupirocin), EDTA and gentamicin, the three ingredients in the spray.
Why is EDTA in BEG spray?
EDTA helps break up biofilms, slimy layers bacteria build to protect themselves, so the antibiotics can reach them better.

name: Benazepril
uses: High blood pressure, heart failure and kidney protein loss, especially in cats and dogs.
side: Low blood pressure, decreased appetite, changes in kidney values.
how: An ACE inhibitor that relaxes blood vessels and reduces protein loss through the kidneys.
avoid: Pregnancy, and people or pets with dehydration or high potassium.
about: Benazepril is an ACE inhibitor used in people since the early 1990s for high blood pressure. It relaxes blood vessels and lowers pressure inside the kidney's filters. Veterinarians use it widely for cats and dogs with protein loss through the kidneys, high blood pressure and heart failure, often off-label in the US. Compounded flavored liquids and transdermal gels help with small or hard-to-pill pets.
conditions: Protein in the urine from kidney disease in cats and dogs
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, fainting or collapse, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, severe weakness, or much less urine than usual.
interactions: Potassium supplements, salt substitutes and spironolactone can raise potassium, NSAIDs can strain the kidneys and weaken its effect, and it can raise lithium levels and add to other blood pressure medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Benazepril is not used in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby; talk to your prescriber right away if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats and dogs usually tolerate it well, and it can be given with or without food as your veterinarian directs. Make sure your pet keeps drinking, since dehydration from vomiting or diarrhea can raise kidney values.
tips: Give or take it at the same time each day.
Wear gloves to apply transdermal gel and rotate between ears as directed.
Call your prescriber or veterinarian if vomiting, diarrhea or not drinking leads to dehydration.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check kidney values, potassium and blood pressure, often within a couple of weeks of starting and then periodically.
faqs: Why is benazepril given to cats with kidney disease?
In cats that lose protein through the kidneys, benazepril may lower the pressure in the kidney's filters and reduce protein loss. Your veterinarian decides based on urine tests.
Can benazepril cause a cough?
A dry cough is a known side effect of ACE inhibitors in people. Tell your prescriber if it is bothersome.

name: Benzocaine
uses: Numbing agent in topical anesthetic creams.
side: Local irritation; rare blood oxygen problem (methemoglobinemia).
how: Blocks nerve signals to numb the skin or mouth.
avoid: Children under 2 and people with methemoglobinemia.
about: Benzocaine is an ester-type local anesthetic that has been used for more than a century in over-the-counter numbing products for the skin and mouth. It works quickly on the surface of the skin. In compounded numbing creams it is usually combined with lidocaine and tetracaine to numb the skin before procedures such as injections, laser treatments or tattooing.
serious: Get medical help right away for pale, gray or blue skin, lips or nail beds, shortness of breath, headache, lightheadedness, a fast heartbeat or unusual tiredness, which can be signs of methemoglobinemia, a rare blood oxygen problem.
interactions: Other numbing products and medicines linked to methemoglobinemia, such as dapsone, nitrates and prilocaine, may add to the risk. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber before using numbing creams with benzocaine if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only to the area and for the time your prescriber or provider directs.
Don't cover it with plastic wrap or a heating pad unless directed, since that increases absorption.
Wash your hands after applying and keep it away from children and pets.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Why shouldn't benzocaine be used in young children?
Children under 2 are at higher risk of methemoglobinemia, a rare but dangerous drop in blood oxygen, so benzocaine is not used in them.
How long does benzocaine numbing last?
Numbing from benzocaine starts fast but tends to wear off sooner than some other anesthetics, which is why it is often combined with lidocaine and tetracaine.

name: Betahistine
uses: Vertigo and Meniere's disease.
how: Acts on histamine receptors and may improve blood flow in the inner ear.
avoid: People with active stomach ulcers, asthma or pheochromocytoma.
about: Betahistine is a histamine-like medicine prescribed in many countries since the 1970s for vertigo and Meniere's disease. It is not sold as a commercial product in the US, so prescribers who want to use it ask for compounded capsules. It is thought to improve blood flow in the inner ear and calm balance signals. Its use is as decided by the prescriber.
conditions: Ringing in the ears with Meniere's
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling or trouble breathing, wheezing, or black or bloody stools.
interactions: Antihistamines may weaken its effect, and MAO inhibitors may raise its levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is little information on betahistine in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so it is usually avoided; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Taking it with food can help reduce stomach upset.
Keep a symptom diary of vertigo attacks to share with your prescriber.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber will follow up on how often vertigo attacks happen.
faqs: Why is betahistine compounded in the US?
Betahistine is sold commercially in many other countries but not in the US, so compounding is how US prescribers can get it for patients.
Can I take betahistine with allergy medicines?
Antihistamines may work against betahistine. Ask your prescriber before using allergy medicines.

name: Betamethasone
uses: Potent steroid for inflamed skin and nipple cream formulas.
how: A potent steroid that reduces inflammation.
avoid: Untreated skin infections; avoid long use on the face or thin skin.
about: Betamethasone is a potent corticosteroid that has been used on the skin since the 1960s. It calms redness, itching and swelling from many skin conditions in people and pets. Compounding lets prescribers choose a specific base or combine it with an antibiotic such as mupirocin, for example in nipple creams for breastfeeding parents or treatment for infected, inflamed skin.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of a spreading skin infection, such as increasing redness, warmth, pus or fever, or for vision changes if used near the eyes.
interactions: Applied to the skin, it has few drug interactions, but using it with other steroid creams or pills can add to steroid effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Use only as directed on the smallest area for the shortest time during pregnancy, and if used on the nipples, follow your prescriber's directions on wiping off before feeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Pets often lick creams off, which can reduce benefit and cause stomach upset, so your veterinarian may suggest a cone or a covering. Wear gloves when applying to your pet.
tips: Apply a thin layer only to the affected area and rub in gently.
Don't cover with a tight bandage unless directed.
Wash your hands after applying unless your hands are being treated.
Avoid the face, groin and underarms unless your prescriber directs it.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short use, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules, especially with long-term use.
faqs: Can betamethasone thin my skin?
Long-term use of potent steroids can thin the skin, cause stretch marks or small visible blood vessels. Using it only as directed lowers this risk.
Is betamethasone cream safe to use on nipples while breastfeeding?
Prescribers sometimes use it in nipple creams. Follow your prescriber's directions about the amount and whether to wipe it off before feeding.

name: Bethanechol
uses: Helps the bladder empty in people and pets.
how: Stimulates the bladder muscle to contract.
avoid: People or pets with urinary or bowel blockages, asthma or slow heart rate.
about: Bethanechol is a cholinergic medicine used since the 1940s to help the bladder muscle contract and empty. In people it is used for urinary retention after surgery or childbirth or from nerve problems. Veterinarians use it in dogs and cats that cannot empty the bladder fully, often along with medicines that relax the urethra. Compounded liquids help with small or exact doses.
conditions: Urinary retention in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, wheezing or trouble breathing, a very slow heartbeat, heavy sweating or drooling, or severe belly cramping and vomiting.
interactions: Other cholinergic drugs such as pyridostigmine can add to its effects, while anticholinergic medicines such as atropine work against it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is little safety information on bethanechol in pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats may drool, vomit or have diarrhea, which often means the amount needs adjusting, so call your veterinarian if this happens. Bethanechol only helps if the urethra is not blocked; a male cat straining without passing urine is an emergency.
tips: It is usually taken on an empty stomach to reduce nausea, unless your prescriber or veterinarian says otherwise.
Shake the liquid well before measuring.
Stand up slowly if you feel lightheaded.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check how well the bladder empties, sometimes with an ultrasound, and may test urine for infection.
faqs: How long does bethanechol take to work?
Effects on the bladder can begin within an hour, though finding the right plan may take some adjustment.
Is bethanechol safe for cats?
Veterinarians use it in cats that cannot empty their bladder fully. It is not used when there is a blockage, so your veterinarian checks for that first.

name: Biest (estriol + estradiol)
uses: A combination of estriol and estradiol, usually 80/20 or 50/50, for menopausal hormone therapy.
how: Combines two estrogens, estriol and estradiol, to replace estrogen after menopause.
avoid: People with a history of breast or uterine cancer, blood clots, stroke, liver disease or unexplained vaginal bleeding.
about: Biest is a compounded blend of two estrogens, estriol and estradiol, that has long been used in bioidentical hormone therapy. It is made only by compounding pharmacies, so prescribers can choose the ratio, strength and form, such as creams, capsules or troches. It is prescribed to manage hot flashes, night sweats and vaginal dryness after menopause. No commercial Biest product exists.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of a blood clot or stroke, such as leg pain or swelling, chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, sudden severe headache, vision changes, or weakness or numbness on one side, and for a new breast lump, unusual vaginal bleeding or yellowing of the skin or eyes.
interactions: Some seizure medicines, rifampin and St. John's wort can lower estrogen levels, and estrogen can change the needs for thyroid hormone and affect blood thinners. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Biest is not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you could be pregnant.
tips: Apply creams to the area your prescriber directs and let them dry before dressing.
Keep children and pets from touching treated skin, and wash your hands after applying.
People with a uterus usually also need progesterone with estrogen; ask your prescriber.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will follow up on symptoms and may check hormone levels, along with regular mammograms, pelvic exams and blood pressure checks.
faqs: What is the difference between Biest and Triest?
Biest contains estriol and estradiol, while Triest adds a third estrogen, estrone. Your prescriber chooses based on your needs.
Do I need progesterone with Biest?
People who still have a uterus are usually prescribed progesterone too, to protect the lining of the uterus. Your prescriber decides.
Can my partner or pet be exposed to Biest cream?
Yes, hormone creams can transfer through skin contact. Wash your hands, cover the area once dry and keep children and pets from touching it.

name: Biotin
uses: Hair, skin and nail support supplement.
side: Can interfere with some lab tests.
how: A B vitamin used by enzymes that support hair, skin and nails.
avoid: Tell your lab before blood tests, since biotin can skew some results.
about: Biotin is a water-soluble B vitamin the body uses to process fats, carbohydrates and protein. It is found in foods such as eggs, nuts and seeds and is a popular supplement for hair, skin and nails. Prescribers and veterinarians sometimes include it in compounded capsules, alone or with other hair and nail ingredients. True biotin deficiency is uncommon.
conditions: Skin and coat support in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing. In an emergency, tell the care team you take biotin, since it can cause false results on some heart and thyroid blood tests.
interactions: Biotin has few drug interactions, but some seizure medicines such as carbamazepine and phenytoin may lower biotin levels, and biotin can skew some lab tests. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Biotin is a normal part of prenatal vitamins, but check with your prescriber before taking extra supplements if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Biotin is commonly given to dogs and cats for skin, coat and claw health and is generally well tolerated. Check that any pet product is free of xylitol and other ingredients that are unsafe for pets.
tips: It can be taken with or without food.
Tell your lab and prescriber you take biotin before blood tests; you may be asked to pause it first.
Hair and nail changes take time, often a few months, since they grow slowly.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How long does biotin take to work for nails?
Nails grow slowly, so any change usually takes a few months to notice.
Why does biotin affect lab tests?
Some lab tests use biotin as part of how they measure results, so extra biotin in the blood can make results falsely high or low, including some thyroid and heart tests.

name: BLT numbing cream
uses: A strong topical anesthetic combining benzocaine, lidocaine and tetracaine, applied before cosmetic and skin procedures such as injections, laser treatments and tattooing.
side: Redness, swelling or paleness of the skin. Using too much, on large areas or under a wrap can cause serious reactions affecting the heart or blood oxygen.
how: All three ingredients block sodium channels in nerve endings, stopping pain signals from traveling.
avoid: Applying to large areas, broken skin or under a wrap unless directed; people with methemoglobinemia or an allergy to local anesthetics. Keep away from children and pets.
about: BLT numbing cream is a compounded topical anesthetic named for its three ingredients: benzocaine, lidocaine and tetracaine. Combining them gives both fast-starting and longer-lasting numbing for cosmetic and skin procedures, such as injections, laser treatments and tattooing. It is stronger than over-the-counter numbing products, so it should be used only as the prescriber or provider directs. No commercial version exists.
serious: Get medical help right away for an irregular or slow heartbeat, dizziness, ringing in the ears, a metallic taste, numb lips or tongue, confusion, seizures, or pale, gray or blue skin, lips or nail beds.
interactions: Using other numbing products at the same time, some heart rhythm medicines and medicines linked to methemoglobinemia, such as dapsone and nitrates, can add to the risk of serious reactions. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber before using BLT cream if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only to the area to be treated and only for the time directed, usually at the provider's office.
Don't cover with plastic wrap or apply heat unless your provider tells you to.
Wash your hands well after applying and keep it out of reach of children and pets.
Remove it as directed before the procedure.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your provider will watch you during the procedure.
faqs: What does BLT stand for in numbing cream?
BLT stands for benzocaine, lidocaine and tetracaine, the three numbing ingredients combined in the cream.
How long does BLT cream take to work?
Numbing usually builds over the time your provider leaves it on before the procedure. Follow their directions rather than leaving it on longer.
Can I use BLT cream at home on a large area?
No. Using it on large areas, broken skin or under a wrap can lead to dangerous reactions. Use it only as your prescriber or provider directs.

name: Boric acid
uses: Vaginal suppositories for recurrent yeast and bacterial vaginosis.
how: Makes the vaginal environment hostile to yeast and some bacteria.
avoid: Pregnancy, and never take by mouth.
about: Boric acid is a mild acid with antifungal and antibacterial effects that has been used as a vaginal treatment for many years. Prescribers may recommend vaginal suppositories, off-label, for yeast infections that keep coming back or don't respond to usual antifungals, and sometimes for recurring bacterial vaginosis. It is never taken by mouth. Compounded suppositories allow a measured amount in a form made for vaginal use.
serious: Get medical help right away for severe burning, blistering, fever, pelvic pain or unusual discharge with a bad odor. If anyone swallows boric acid, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.
interactions: Used vaginally, boric acid has few known drug interactions, but avoid using other vaginal products at the same time unless your prescriber directs it. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Boric acid is not used during pregnancy because it may harm a developing baby; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Insert suppositories at bedtime and consider wearing a panty liner for any discharge.
Never take boric acid by mouth, and store it out of reach of children and pets.
Avoid sex during treatment unless your prescriber says otherwise, since it can irritate a partner.
Wash your hands before and after inserting.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber may test for the type of yeast or bacteria and follow up if symptoms return.
faqs: How long does it take boric acid suppositories to work?
Many people notice relief within a few days, but finish the full course your prescriber gives you.
Can I have sex while using boric acid suppositories?
