interactions: Ketoconazole, itraconazole, erythromycin, diltiazem and grapefruit can raise cyclosporine levels, and phenobarbital, rifampin and St. John's wort can lower them. Avoid live vaccines unless your prescriber approves. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Cyclosporine is used in pregnancy only when the benefit outweighs the risk and passes into breast milk, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: Cats should be tested or kept indoors to avoid toxoplasmosis, since cyclosporine can make that infection worse. Vomiting is common at first; giving it with a small meal or freezing capsules may help, and gum overgrowth should be reported to your veterinarian.
tips: Give it the same way each day, either always with food or always on an empty stomach, as your prescriber or veterinarian directs.
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.
Wear gloves when handling capsules or applying gel and wash your hands afterward.
Shake the suspension well before each dose.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood levels, kidney and liver values, and blood pressure, especially with long-term use.
faqs: How long does cyclosporine take to work for dog allergies?
It often takes several weeks before itching improves. Your veterinarian may use another medicine at first while cyclosporine starts to work.
Why does my pet vomit after cyclosporine?
Stomach upset is common in the first weeks. Ask your veterinarian about giving it with a small meal or other ways to reduce it.
Can I eat grapefruit while taking cyclosporine?
No. Grapefruit can raise cyclosporine levels in the blood and increase side effects.

name: Cyproheptadine
uses: Allergies in people; appetite stimulation in cats.
side: Drowsiness, dry mouth, excitability in cats.
how: Blocks histamine and serotonin receptors, which reduces allergy symptoms and stimulates appetite.
avoid: People or pets with glaucoma or urinary retention.
about: Cyproheptadine is a first-generation antihistamine that also blocks serotonin. It has been used for decades to relieve allergy symptoms and itching in people. Veterinarians use it off-label as an appetite stimulant in cats, and it is also used for serotonin-related problems. Commercial tablets can be hard to divide for small patients, so a flavored suspension helps with dosing.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast heartbeat, trouble urinating, seizures, severe confusion or agitation, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Alcohol, sedatives, opioid pain medicines and other antihistamines add to drowsiness. It can reduce the effect of SSRI antidepressants and MAO inhibitors can increase its side effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Cyproheptadine should be used in pregnancy only if your prescriber recommends it, and it is generally avoided while breastfeeding.
petNotes: In cats it is used off-label to encourage eating, and some cats become hyperactive or vocal rather than sleepy. Tell your veterinarian if your cat still will not eat, since appetite loss can be dangerous in cats.
tips: Shake the suspension well before each dose.
Give it with or without food; for appetite, your veterinarian may time it before meals.
Avoid driving until you know how drowsy it makes you.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your veterinarian will follow your cat's appetite and weight.
faqs: How fast does cyproheptadine increase a cat's appetite?
Some cats start showing interest in food within a few hours. If your cat still is not eating, call your veterinarian.
Why is my cat hyper on cyproheptadine?
Some cats become restless or vocal instead of sleepy. Let your veterinarian know if this happens.

name: D-Penicillamine
uses: Copper storage disease and some stone types.
how: Binds copper and some other metals so the body can remove them.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease or a penicillin allergy.
about: D-penicillamine is a chelating agent that binds copper and certain other substances so they can be removed in urine. It has been used since the 1950s for Wilson's disease in people and cystine kidney stones. Veterinarians use it off-label for copper storage liver disease in dogs and some types of bladder stones. Compounded capsules allow doses that fit small dogs and people who need specific strengths.
conditions: Copper storage liver disease in dogs
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fever, sore throat, mouth sores, unusual bruising or bleeding, rash, blood in urine, swelling, or yellow skin or eyes.
interactions: Antacids, iron and zinc can reduce absorption, so separate them by a few hours. Other medicines that affect the bone marrow or kidneys can add to its risks. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Penicillamine can harm a developing baby, so talk to your prescriber right away if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dog breeds prone to copper storage disease include Bedlington terriers, Labrador retrievers and Doberman pinschers. Vomiting is common; your veterinarian may suggest giving it with a small snack if an empty stomach causes nausea.
tips: Take or give it on an empty stomach, usually an hour before or two hours after meals, unless directed otherwise.
Separate it from minerals, antacids and iron supplements.
Keep a consistent schedule each day.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check blood counts, urine protein, kidney function and copper or liver values regularly.
faqs: Why is penicillamine taken on an empty stomach?
Food and minerals can greatly reduce how much is absorbed. If it causes nausea, your prescriber or veterinarian may adjust how it is given.
How long do dogs take penicillamine for copper liver disease?
Treatment often lasts months, and your veterinarian uses liver tests to decide when to change or stop it.

name: Dexamethasone
uses: Inflammation and allergic conditions; used in mouthwashes and ear preparations.
side: Increased thirst and appetite, mood changes.
how: A long-acting, potent steroid that calms inflammation.
avoid: People or pets with diabetes, infections or ulcers.
about: Dexamethasone is a long-acting corticosteroid that has been used since the late 1950s. It is many times stronger than hydrocortisone and is used for inflammation, allergic reactions, swelling and some cancers. Compounded liquids, mouthwashes and veterinary ear preparations let it be used where it is needed, such as for mouth sores or ear inflammation, often combined with other ingredients.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, signs of infection, extreme thirst and urination, severe mood changes, vision changes, or swelling of the legs.
interactions: Taking it with NSAIDs raises the risk of stomach ulcers, and it can raise blood sugar and change the effect of diabetes medicines. Some seizure medicines and antifungals change its levels, and live vaccines should be avoided during high-dose use. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Dexamethasone is used in pregnancy only for specific reasons decided by your prescriber, so tell them if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Never give dexamethasone with NSAIDs such as carprofen or meloxicam in dogs and cats. It is much stronger than prednisone, so follow the label exactly, and it can increase thirst, urination and appetite.
tips: Take or give oral forms with food to protect the stomach.
For mouthwash, swish and spit as directed, and avoid eating or drinking for a short time afterward unless told otherwise.
Do not stop long-term use suddenly; your prescriber or veterinarian will taper it.
Shake liquids well before each dose.
monitoring: With longer use, your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood sugar, blood pressure, bone health or adrenal function.
faqs: What is the difference between dexamethasone and prednisone?
Both are corticosteroids, but dexamethasone is much stronger and lasts longer. Your prescriber or veterinarian chooses based on the condition.
Can dexamethasone mouthwash be swallowed?
Usually it is swished and spit out, though some prescribers direct swish and swallow. Follow the label instructions.
Why does my dog drink so much water on dexamethasone?
Steroids commonly increase thirst and urination. Keep fresh water available and tell your veterinarian if it is extreme.

name: DHEA
uses: A hormone precursor sometimes prescribed for low DHEA levels and in vaginal preparations for menopause-related dryness.
side: Acne, oily skin, hair growth, mood changes.
how: DHEA is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that the body converts into testosterone and estrogen.
avoid: People with hormone-sensitive cancers, polycystic ovary syndrome or liver disease, and those who are pregnant.
about: DHEA, or dehydroepiandrosterone, is a hormone made mainly by the adrenal glands that the body turns into testosterone and estrogen. Levels drop with age. A vaginal insert containing DHEA, called prasterone, is used for painful intercourse after menopause, and compounded creams, capsules and vaginal preparations allow prescribers to order specific strengths or combine it with other hormones.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, shortness of breath, leg pain or swelling, a racing heartbeat, severe mood changes, yellow skin or eyes, or a new breast lump.
interactions: DHEA can add to the effects of estrogen and testosterone therapy and may interact with some antidepressants, seizure medicines and blood thinners. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: DHEA is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding because it can affect hormone levels in the baby.
tips: Use it at the same time each day.
For creams or gels, let the area dry and wash your hands so hormones are not passed to others.
For vaginal preparations, use at bedtime unless directed otherwise.
Tell your prescriber about acne, oily skin or new hair growth.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check DHEA-S, testosterone or estrogen levels and review symptoms after starting or adjusting it.
faqs: Is DHEA a steroid?
DHEA is a natural hormone that acts as a building block for testosterone and estrogen. It is not the same as a corticosteroid like prednisone.
How long does vaginal DHEA take to work?
Many people notice improvement in dryness after several weeks of regular use. Your prescriber will check how it is working.

name: Diazoxide
uses: Low blood sugar from insulin-secreting tumors in dogs.
how: Blocks insulin release from the pancreas, raising blood sugar.
avoid: Pets with heart failure or low blood pressure.
about: Diazoxide raises blood sugar by stopping the pancreas from releasing insulin. Oral diazoxide has been used for decades in people with low blood sugar from too much insulin. Veterinarians use it off-label for dogs with insulinoma, a tumor that makes too much insulin. Commercial oral products can be hard to find or dose for dogs, so it is often compounded into a liquid.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for weakness, wobbling, seizures or collapse, which may mean low blood sugar, or for severe vomiting, excessive thirst, or trouble breathing.
interactions: Thiazide diuretics can increase its effect on blood sugar, and it can add to the effect of blood pressure medicines. Steroids such as prednisone also raise blood sugar and may be used with it on purpose. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: It is used in dogs alongside frequent small meals and sometimes prednisone. Keep a sugar source such as corn syrup on hand for signs of low blood sugar, and call your veterinarian if you need to use it.
tips: Give it with food to reduce vomiting.
Shake the liquid well before each dose.
Feed several small meals a day as your veterinarian directs.
Avoid hard exercise and long gaps between meals.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check blood sugar regularly and may monitor blood counts and other bloodwork.
faqs: How does diazoxide help dogs with insulinoma?
It reduces insulin release from the pancreas, which helps keep blood sugar from dropping too low. It controls symptoms but does not remove the tumor.
What should I do if my dog has a low blood sugar episode?
Rub a little corn syrup or honey on the gums if your dog can swallow safely, then call your veterinarian right away.

name: Diclofenac
uses: Anti-inflammatory for joint and muscle pain, including topical creams.
side: Skin irritation; stomach and kidney effects with oral use.
how: An NSAID that blocks COX enzymes to reduce inflammation and pain.
avoid: People with stomach ulcers, kidney disease or heart disease, and late pregnancy. Toxic to pets.
about: Diclofenac is an NSAID that has been used for decades to reduce pain and inflammation. Applied to the skin, less of it reaches the bloodstream than when taken by mouth, which can lower the risk of stomach and heart side effects. Compounded creams let a prescriber combine diclofenac with other pain ingredients, such as lidocaine, gabapentin or capsaicin, in one product for a specific area.
conditions: Arthritis of the knees and hands
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side, slurred speech, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, swelling, a blistering rash, or yellow skin or eyes.
interactions: Avoid other NSAIDs and aspirin unless directed. Blood thinners, steroids, lithium, methotrexate, diuretics and some blood pressure medicines can interact. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: NSAIDs like diclofenac should be avoided after about 20 weeks of pregnancy unless your prescriber directs otherwise; ask before using it if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply cream to clean, dry, unbroken skin and rub it in gently.
Wash your hands after applying unless you are treating your hands.
Do not cover with heat or tight bandages, and avoid sun on treated skin.
Keep pets away from treated skin and the tube, since diclofenac is toxic to dogs and cats.
monitoring: For long-term oral use, your prescriber may check blood pressure, kidney and liver function; topical use usually needs less monitoring.
faqs: Is diclofenac cream dangerous for pets?
Yes. Licking treated skin or chewing a tube can cause serious kidney and stomach problems in dogs and cats. Keep it out of reach and cover treated areas.
Can I use diclofenac cream with ibuprofen?
Using two NSAIDs together increases the risk of side effects. Ask your prescriber before combining them.
How long does diclofenac cream take to work?
Some relief may come within days, but full benefit for arthritis can take a week or more of regular use.

name: Diethylstilbestrol (DES)
uses: Estrogen-responsive urinary incontinence in spayed female dogs.
side: Bone marrow effects at high doses; requires monitoring.
how: A synthetic estrogen that strengthens the urethral sphincter in spayed female dogs.
avoid: Intact female dogs and cats. Doses are kept low and infrequent because high doses can suppress bone marrow.
about: Diethylstilbestrol, or DES, is a synthetic estrogen. It was withdrawn from human use decades ago, but veterinarians still use it off-label to treat urinary incontinence in spayed female dogs, where low estrogen can weaken the urethral sphincter. Because commercial products are no longer made, it is available only by compounding.
conditions: Urinary incontinence in spayed female dogs
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for pale gums, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever, lethargy, a swollen vulva, or signs of heat in a spayed dog.
interactions: Other estrogen-containing products can add to its effects. Phenylpropanolamine is sometimes used with it on purpose under veterinary supervision. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: It is usually given on a schedule that tapers to the lowest effective dose to protect the bone marrow. Pregnant people and children should avoid handling it, so wear gloves.
tips: Follow your veterinarian's schedule exactly, since it is often not given every day.
Wear gloves when handling capsules or treats, and wash your hands afterward.
Keep track of accidents so your veterinarian can adjust the plan.
Store it out of reach of children and other pets.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may check complete blood counts periodically to watch for bone marrow effects.
faqs: Why is DES given only a few times a week?
Lower and less frequent doses reduce the risk of bone marrow problems. Your veterinarian finds the lowest schedule that controls leaks.
How long does DES take to work for incontinence?
Many dogs improve within a few days to a couple of weeks. Your veterinarian will adjust the schedule based on how your dog does.

name: Diltiazem
uses: Heart rhythm and blood pressure; topical forms for anal fissures.
side: Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, headache.
how: Blocks calcium channels in the heart and blood vessels, slowing heart rate and relaxing muscle.
avoid: People or pets with very low blood pressure or certain heart block conditions.
about: Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker that has been used since the early 1980s to treat high blood pressure, chest pain and fast heart rhythms. Applied as an ointment or cream, it relaxes the anal sphincter muscle, which helps anal fissures heal; this topical use is compounded and off-label. Veterinarians also use oral diltiazem for some heart conditions in dogs and cats.
conditions: Heart disease in cats and dogs
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, a very slow heartbeat, severe dizziness, shortness of breath, or swelling of the legs or face.
interactions: Beta-blockers, digoxin and other heart rate-lowering medicines can slow the heart further. It can raise levels of some statins, cyclosporine and other medicines broken down by CYP3A4. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Diltiazem is generally not recommended during pregnancy and passes into breast milk, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: Topical forms for people should be kept away from pets. Oral diltiazem for heart conditions in pets is prescribed separately, and your veterinarian sets the plan.
tips: For anal fissures, apply a small amount to the area with a gloved or covered finger as directed.
Wash your hands well after applying.
Headache is common when starting; tell your prescriber if it persists.
Keep stools soft with fiber and fluids to help healing.
monitoring: For topical use, your prescriber will check healing at follow-up visits; with oral use, heart rate and blood pressure are checked periodically.
faqs: How long does diltiazem ointment take to heal a fissure?
Many people notice less pain within a couple of weeks, and healing often takes several weeks of regular use.
Can diltiazem ointment cause headaches?
Headache can happen, but it is usually less common than with nitroglycerin ointment. Tell your prescriber if it is bothersome.
Why is diltiazem used for fissures?
It relaxes the anal sphincter muscle and improves blood flow, which helps the tear heal.

name: Diphenhydramine
uses: Allergies and itch; a common ingredient in mouthwash blends.
how: A sedating antihistamine that blocks H1 receptors.
avoid: People or pets with glaucoma, urinary retention or heart disease, and older adults.
about: Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine available since the 1940s. It relieves allergy symptoms, itching and hives and causes drowsiness, which is why it is in many sleep aids. It is a common ingredient in compounded mouthwashes for mouth sores. Veterinarians also use it off-label in pets for allergic reactions and itching.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast or irregular heartbeat, seizures, severe confusion or agitation, trouble urinating, or very deep sleepiness.
interactions: Alcohol, sleep aids, sedatives, opioid pain medicines and other antihistamines add to drowsiness. It can increase side effects of other medicines with drying effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Diphenhydramine has been used in pregnancy, but it can pass into breast milk and may reduce milk supply, so ask your prescriber first.
petNotes: Use only plain diphenhydramine products in pets; avoid combination products with decongestants, acetaminophen or xylitol. Cats may drool from the bitter taste, so flavored liquids help.
tips: Avoid driving until you know how drowsy it makes you.
For mouthwash, swish and spit as directed; the label will say whether to swallow.
Older adults should ask their prescriber before using it because of confusion and fall risk.
Shake liquids well before each dose.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Can I give my dog Benadryl?
Veterinarians often use plain diphenhydramine in dogs. Ask your veterinarian first, and never use products with decongestants, acetaminophen or xylitol.
Why is diphenhydramine in magic mouthwash?
It has a mild numbing and anti-inflammatory effect that can soothe painful mouth sores.

name: Diphenoxylate/atropine
uses: Diarrhea.
how: Slows movement of the intestines; atropine is added to discourage misuse.
avoid: Children, and people or pets with infectious diarrhea or liver disease.
about: Diphenoxylate with atropine is a prescription antidiarrheal that has been used since the 1960s. Diphenoxylate slows the movement of the intestines so stools become less frequent, and a small amount of atropine is added to discourage misuse. Veterinarians sometimes use it off-label in dogs. A compounded flavored suspension can help with dosing when tablets are not practical.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a swollen or painful belly, severe constipation, fever, bloody diarrhea, a fast heartbeat, trouble breathing or extreme sleepiness.
interactions: Alcohol, sedatives, opioid pain medicines and other medicines that cause drowsiness add to its effects. MAO inhibitors should not be used with it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is not well established, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: It is used off-label mostly in dogs; cats can become excited from this type of medicine, so it is used with caution in cats. Do not use in pets with diarrhea from infection or poisoning unless your veterinarian says to.
tips: Shake the suspension well and measure carefully.
Drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.
Stop and call your prescriber if diarrhea lasts more than a couple of days or your belly swells.
Keep it out of reach of children; accidental use can be dangerous.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber or veterinarian will follow how the diarrhea responds.
faqs: Why does this medicine contain atropine?
A small amount of atropine is added to discourage taking more than prescribed; it causes unpleasant effects at high amounts.
Is Lomotil safe for dogs?
Veterinarians sometimes use it off-label in dogs. Use only as directed by your veterinarian.

name: DMSA (succimer)
uses: A chelating agent that binds heavy metals such as lead so the body can remove them.
side: Nausea, diarrhea, rash, changes in liver values; requires monitoring.
how: Binds heavy metals such as lead so they can be removed through the urine.
avoid: People or pets with kidney or liver disease. Needs lab monitoring.
about: DMSA, also called succimer, is an oral chelating agent that has been used since the early 1990s to treat lead poisoning, especially in children. It binds lead so the body can remove it through the urine. Veterinarians use it off-label for lead poisoning in dogs, cats and birds. Compounded capsules allow doses that fit smaller patients.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a rash, fever, sore throat, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or severe vomiting or diarrhea.
interactions: Avoid using other chelating agents at the same time unless directed. Iron and other mineral supplements may need to be timed separately. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information on DMSA in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: In pets it is used off-label, and removing the lead source, such as paint chips or fishing weights, is an important part of treatment. Capsules can be opened and mixed with a small amount of food if your veterinarian approves.
tips: Take it with plenty of water.
Remove the lead source from the home before or during treatment.
Take it at the same times each day for the full course.
A sulfur-like smell to urine or breath can be normal.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check blood lead levels, blood counts and liver values during and after treatment.
faqs: How long does DMSA treatment last?
Courses are often a few weeks, and blood lead levels are checked to see if more treatment is needed.
Does DMSA remove other metals?
It is mainly used for lead, though it may bind some other heavy metals. Your prescriber decides when it is appropriate.

name: DMSO
uses: Carrier that helps medications absorb through the skin.
side: Garlic-like breath or taste, skin irritation.
how: A solvent that carries other medicines through the skin.
avoid: Apply only to clean skin, since it can carry other substances in with it.
about: DMSO, or dimethyl sulfoxide, is a solvent that easily passes through skin and can carry other ingredients with it. A bladder instillation product is approved for interstitial cystitis in people, and it has been used in veterinary practice for decades. In compounding, it is used as a carrier in creams to help medications absorb through the skin.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe skin redness, blistering, swelling or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Because DMSO carries substances through the skin, anything on the skin, including lotions, chemicals or other medicines, may be absorbed. Apply it only as part of the prescribed formula. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information on DMSO in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: Wear gloves when applying DMSO products to pets, since they can carry medicine into your skin. Keep pets from licking the area until it dries.
tips: Apply only to clean, dry skin, free of lotions or chemicals.
Wear gloves or wash your hands right after applying.
A garlic-like taste or breath odor is common and harmless.
Avoid applying it to broken or irritated skin unless directed.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Why does DMSO cause garlic breath?
The body breaks it down into a compound with a garlic-like odor. This can happen even when it is used on the skin.
Why is DMSO in my cream?
It helps the active medicines pass through the skin so they reach the target area.

name: Doxycycline
uses: Bacterial and tick-borne infections, acne and rosacea.
side: Stomach upset, sun sensitivity; give with water or food.
how: A tetracycline antibiotic that stops bacteria from making proteins; also calms inflammation in acne and rosacea.
avoid: Children under 8 and pregnancy. Give with water and food to protect the esophagus, especially in cats.
about: Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic that has been used since the late 1960s. It treats many bacterial infections, tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis, and, at lower doses, acne and rosacea through its anti-inflammatory effects. Veterinarians use it often in dogs and cats. Compounded flavored liquids and other forms help pets and people who cannot take tablets.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble swallowing or chest pain, a severe headache with vision changes, severe sunburn or rash, bloody or watery diarrhea, or yellow skin or eyes.
interactions: Antacids, calcium, iron, zinc and magnesium products can block absorption, so space them a few hours apart. It can increase the effect of warfarin and may reduce the effect of some birth control pills. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Doxycycline is usually avoided in pregnancy and during breastfeeding because it can affect a baby's teeth and bones; talk to your prescriber.
petNotes: In cats, tablets or capsules can lodge in the esophagus and cause narrowing, so always follow each dose with water or food. Flavored liquids or treats make it easier to give.
tips: Take it with a full glass of water and stay upright for at least 30 minutes afterward.
Take it with food if it upsets your stomach, but avoid dairy close to the dose.
Use sunscreen and limit sun exposure.
Finish the full course even if symptoms improve.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses; with long-term use, your prescriber or veterinarian may check liver values.
faqs: Can I take doxycycline with milk?
Dairy can reduce how much is absorbed. Take it with water and food, and separate dairy by a couple of hours if possible.
Why does my cat need water after doxycycline?
Doxycycline can stick in a cat's esophagus and cause irritation or scarring. A small amount of water or food after the dose helps move it along.
How long does doxycycline take to work for acne?
Acne usually improves over several weeks. Your prescriber will decide how long to continue.

name: Drospirenone
uses: A progestin used in hormone therapy and contraception.
side: Headache, breast tenderness, nausea; can raise potassium.
how: A progestin that acts like progesterone and also has mild anti-androgen and water-balancing effects.
avoid: People with kidney or adrenal problems, liver disease, or a history of blood clots, and those taking medicines that raise potassium.
about: Drospirenone is a progestin related to spironolactone. Besides acting like progesterone, it has mild anti-androgen and water-balancing effects. It has been used in birth control pills since the early 2000s, alone or combined with estrogen, and in menopause hormone therapy. Compounded capsules allow strengths that are not available commercially, as ordered by your prescriber.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, shortness of breath, leg pain or swelling, sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness on one side, or signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat.
interactions: Medicines that raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements and NSAIDs, can increase potassium further. Some seizure medicines, rifampin and St. John's wort can lower its levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Drospirenone is not used during pregnancy; tell your prescriber if you are pregnant or breastfeeding.
tips: Take it at the same time each day.
Avoid potassium supplements or salt substitutes unless your prescriber approves.
Report any unusual bleeding or spotting to your prescriber.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check potassium levels, especially if you take other medicines that raise potassium.
faqs: Why does drospirenone affect potassium?
It is related to spironolactone, which helps the body keep potassium. Your prescriber may check your level, especially with certain other medicines.
Is drospirenone the same as progesterone?
No. It is a synthetic progestin that acts like progesterone but also has mild anti-androgen and water-balancing effects.

name: Duloxetine
uses: Depression, anxiety and nerve or chronic pain.
how: Increases both serotonin and norepinephrine, which affect mood and pain signals.
avoid: People with liver disease, heavy alcohol use or uncontrolled glaucoma, and those on MAO inhibitors.
about: Duloxetine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, or SNRI, that has been prescribed since 2004. It is used for depression and anxiety and also for several types of chronic pain, including nerve pain from diabetes and fibromyalgia. Compounded capsules can help people who need a strength or form that is not available commercially.
serious: Get medical help right away for thoughts of suicide or self-harm, worsening mood or agitation, signs of serotonin syndrome such as high fever, stiff muscles or confusion, yellow skin or eyes, unusual bleeding, or a severe rash.
interactions: Never take it with MAO inhibitors, and use caution with other serotonin medicines such as SSRIs, triptans and some pain medicines. Fluvoxamine and ciprofloxacin can raise its levels, and NSAIDs and blood thinners increase the risk of bleeding. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Duloxetine may affect a newborn when used late in pregnancy and passes into breast milk, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Swallow capsules whole; do not crush or chew them.
Do not stop it suddenly; your prescriber will taper it to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
Limit alcohol, which can increase the risk of liver problems.
If you miss a dose, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will follow your mood and pain and may check blood pressure and liver function.
faqs: How long does duloxetine take to work?
Some improvement may be seen in one to two weeks, but full effects often take several weeks.
Can I drink alcohol with duloxetine?
Heavy drinking increases the risk of liver problems with duloxetine. Talk to your prescriber about whether any alcohol is safe for you.
What happens if I stop duloxetine suddenly?
Stopping suddenly may cause dizziness, nausea, irritability or other withdrawal symptoms. Your prescriber will reduce it slowly.

name: Dutasteride
uses: Hair loss and enlarged prostate.
how: Blocks both forms of the enzyme that converts testosterone into DHT.
avoid: Anyone who is or may become pregnant should avoid handling it. People with liver disease.
about: Dutasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor first approved as Avodart capsules for enlarged prostate in the early 2000s. Because it blocks both the type 1 and type 2 forms of the enzyme, it lowers DHT more fully than finasteride, and some prescribers use it off-label for male-pattern hair loss. Compounded capsules or a scalp solution may be requested when a strength or form is needed that is not available commercially.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or lips, or trouble breathing, or for a breast lump, breast pain or nipple discharge.
interactions: Strong CYP3A4 blockers such as ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin and some HIV medicines can raise dutasteride levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not for anyone who is pregnant or may become pregnant, because it can harm the development of a male baby; pregnant people should not touch leaking capsules or the scalp solution, and it is not used while breastfeeding.
tips: Swallow capsules whole; do not chew or open them, because the contents can irritate the mouth and throat.
Apply the solution to a dry scalp, let it dry fully, and wash your hands right after.
Do not donate blood while taking dutasteride and for at least 6 months after your last dose, so the blood never reaches a pregnant person.
If a dose is missed, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check a PSA blood test, since dutasteride lowers PSA results, and will review hair or urinary progress over several months.
faqs: How long does dutasteride take to work for hair loss?
Hair grows slowly, so many people need 6 to 12 months of steady use before judging results. Your prescriber decides how long to continue.
What is the difference between dutasteride and finasteride?
Both block the enzyme that makes DHT, but dutasteride blocks two forms of it while finasteride mainly blocks one. Dutasteride also stays in the body much longer after it is stopped.
Can I donate blood while taking dutasteride?
No. Men taking dutasteride should wait at least 6 months after the last dose before donating blood.

name: Ear packs (veterinary)
uses: Long-acting ear preparations that combine an antibiotic, antifungal and steroid, applied by the veterinarian or at home as directed.
how: Combines medicines that kill bacteria and yeast with a steroid that calms inflammation, held in the ear canal for days.
avoid: Pets with a ruptured eardrum, unless the veterinarian has confirmed it is safe.
about: Ear packs are long-acting ear gels that a veterinarian places in a pet's ear canal, usually right after a thorough cleaning, so the medicine stays in contact with the infection for days. They typically combine an antibiotic, an antifungal and a steroid. Compounded packs let the veterinarian pick the ingredients, such as enrofloxacin, amikacin or imipenem for resistant bacteria, based on ear cytology or culture results and the needs of each dog or cat.
conditions: Outer ear infections in dogs (otitis externa)
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for a head tilt, loss of balance, walking in circles, flicking eye movements, a drooping face, sudden hearing loss, or severe ear pain or swelling.
interactions: Ear packs act mostly inside the ear canal, so drug interactions are uncommon; do not add ear cleaners or other ear drops during treatment unless your veterinarian says to. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Many packs are placed in the clinic, and the gel slowly breaks down and works its way out of the ear over the following days to weeks. Cats can be more sensitive to some ear medicines, so the veterinarian chooses ingredients with that in mind.
tips: Do not clean or flush the ears after the pack is placed unless your veterinarian tells you to.
Keep the ears dry: avoid baths, swimming and grooming that wets the ears during treatment.
A little gel or waxy material coming out of the ear is normal; gently wipe the outer ear with a soft cloth.
Keep the recheck appointment so your veterinarian can confirm the infection has cleared.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck the ears, often with a repeat ear cytology or culture, after treatment to make sure the infection is gone.
faqs: Is head shaking normal after an ear pack?
Some head shaking or scratching for a day or two is common as the pet gets used to the gel. Call your veterinarian if it is severe, lasts longer, or your pet loses balance.
Why use an ear pack instead of daily ear drops?
A pack keeps medicine in the ear canal for days, which helps pets who resist drops and owners who find daily treatment hard. Your veterinarian decides which option fits your pet.
Should I clean my dog's ears after an ear pack is placed?
Usually not. Cleaning can remove the medicine early, so follow your veterinarian's instructions.

name: EDTA (tris-EDTA)
uses: Helps topical, nasal and ear antibiotics work better against biofilms.
how: Binds calcium and magnesium in bacterial cell walls and biofilms, making bacteria easier to kill.
avoid: Ruptured eardrums (ear products).
about: EDTA is a chelating agent, meaning it binds metals such as calcium and magnesium. Tris-EDTA, a buffered form, has been used for many years in veterinary ear flushes alongside antibiotics, especially for hard-to-treat infections such as Pseudomonas. In compounded nasal sprays it may be paired off-label with an antibiotic or antifungal for chronic sinus infections, where it helps break up the biofilms that protect bacteria.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing, or for nosebleeds, severe burning, ear pain, loss of balance or hearing changes after use.
interactions: Used in the nose, ear or on the skin, very little EDTA is absorbed and drug interactions are unlikely; it is meant to be used together with the antibiotic or antifungal your prescriber or veterinarian chose. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Very little is absorbed from nasal or topical use, but information in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited, so talk to your prescriber first.
petNotes: In dogs and cats, tris-EDTA is most often used as an ear flush or ear-medicine partner, especially for Pseudomonas infections. Ear products should be used only after a veterinarian has confirmed the eardrum is intact.
tips: Shake and prime the nasal spray before first use, and gently blow your nose before each dose.
Point the spray tip slightly toward the outer side of the nostril, away from the center wall.
Do not share the spray bottle, and wipe the tip after each use.
Use it with your antibiotic or antifungal exactly as directed, even if symptoms improve.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Is EDTA an antibiotic?
No. EDTA does not kill bacteria well on its own; it weakens bacterial walls and biofilms so that antibiotics can work better.
Why is EDTA added to a sinus spray?
Chronic sinus infections often involve biofilms, a protective slime that shields bacteria. EDTA may help antibiotics reach the bacteria inside these biofilms.

name: Enalapril
uses: High blood pressure, heart failure and protein loss through the kidneys.
side: Low blood pressure, cough in people, changes in kidney values.
how: An ACE inhibitor that relaxes blood vessels and reduces protein loss through the kidneys.
avoid: Pregnancy, and people or pets with severe kidney disease, dehydration or high potassium.
about: Enalapril is an ACE inhibitor that has been used since the 1980s for high blood pressure and heart failure in people. Veterinarians also use it widely in dogs and cats with heart disease, high blood pressure or protein loss through the kidneys. Compounded flavored liquids or a transdermal gel may be requested for small pets, cats that refuse pills, or people who need a dose not available in a commercial tablet.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, fainting or collapse, very little urine, or signs of high potassium such as muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat.
interactions: Potassium supplements, salt substitutes, potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, NSAIDs, lithium and other blood pressure medicines can raise potassium, lower kidney function or drop blood pressure too far. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby, especially later in pregnancy; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In dogs it is often given with pimobendan and furosemide for heart failure, and in cats it may be used for kidney protein loss. NSAID pain relievers should only be given with your veterinarian's approval while a pet takes enalapril.
tips: Give it at about the same time each day, with or without food.
Shake flavored suspensions well and measure each dose with the oral syringe provided.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to the inner ear flap, and alternate ears.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check blood pressure, kidney values and potassium after starting and periodically during treatment.
faqs: Why does enalapril cause a cough?
ACE inhibitors can cause a dry, tickly cough in some people because of a buildup of a natural substance called bradykinin. Tell your prescriber if it bothers you; don't stop on your own.
Can dogs take enalapril with pimobendan?
Yes, veterinarians commonly prescribe them together for heart failure, often with a diuretic. Your veterinarian decides the combination and doses.
How long does enalapril take to work?
It begins lowering blood pressure within hours, but the full benefit for heart failure or kidney protein loss builds over weeks.

name: Enclomiphene
uses: A form of clomiphene prescribed off-label to help men's bodies make more of their own testosterone while preserving fertility.
side: Headache, hot flashes, mood changes, visual disturbances.
how: Blocks estrogen's signal in the brain, prompting the pituitary to release hormones that stimulate natural testosterone production.
avoid: People with liver disease, vision problems or high red blood cell counts.
about: Enclomiphene is one of the two mirror-image forms that make up clomiphene (Clomid), a fertility medicine used since the 1960s. It was studied as a separate product for men with low testosterone, but no enclomiphene product is FDA-approved in the US. Prescribers may order it compounded, off-label, for men who want to raise their own testosterone while keeping sperm production, something testosterone therapy itself can suppress.
serious: Get medical help right away for blurred vision, spots or flashes in your vision, signs of a blood clot such as leg swelling, chest pain or sudden shortness of breath, or yellowing of the skin or eyes.
interactions: Testosterone and other hormone therapies, aromatase inhibitors such as anastrozole, and other SERMs such as clomiphene or tamoxifen can overlap with its effects. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: It is prescribed for men and is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding; anyone who is pregnant should avoid handling opened capsules.
tips: Take it at about the same time each day, with or without food.
Stop and call your prescriber right away if you notice any change in your vision.
Do not combine it with other hormone products unless your prescriber has planned it.
If a dose is missed, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check testosterone, estradiol, LH, FSH and a blood count before and during treatment.
faqs: What is the difference between enclomiphene and clomiphene?

Clomiphene is a mix of two forms, enclomiphene and zuclomiphene. Enclomiphene is the form mainly responsible for raising the hormones that signal testosterone production, and zuclomiphene lingers longer in the body.
Does enclomiphene affect fertility like testosterone therapy?
Testosterone therapy can lower sperm production. Enclomiphene works by signaling the body to make its own testosterone, which is why prescribers may choose it when fertility matters.
How long does it take to raise testosterone?
Levels often change within a few weeks, and your prescriber will recheck blood work to decide next steps.

name: Enrofloxacin
uses: Bacterial infections in pets, including ear packs.
side: Stomach upset; not for young, growing animals.
how: A fluoroquinolone that blocks bacterial DNA copying.
avoid: Young growing dogs (cartilage damage) and cats at high doses (vision damage).
about: Enrofloxacin is a veterinary fluoroquinolone antibiotic that has been used in dogs and cats since the late 1980s, sold commercially as Baytril. It works against many bacteria that cause urinary, skin, ear and respiratory infections. Compounded flavored liquids, chewable treats, capsules or transdermal gel help with cats and small dogs that need a smaller strength or refuse tablets, and it is a common ingredient in veterinary ear packs.
conditions: Urinary tract infections in dogs and cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for dilated pupils, bumping into things or other vision changes (especially in cats), seizures, severe wobbliness, limping or joint swelling in a young animal, or facial swelling or hives.
interactions: Antacids, sucralfate and supplements with calcium, iron, zinc or magnesium can block absorption if given at the same time; it can also raise theophylline levels, and NSAIDs may add to seizure risk. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Cats can develop retinal damage and blindness when doses run too high, so dosing in cats must follow your veterinarian exactly. It is generally avoided in growing puppies, especially large breeds, because it can damage developing cartilage.
tips: Give the full course, even if your pet seems better.
Give it a couple of hours apart from dairy, antacids or mineral supplements.
Giving it with a small meal may help if it upsets your pet's stomach.
Shake liquids well, and wear gloves when applying transdermal gel.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may recheck your pet or repeat a urine, skin or ear culture at the end of treatment to confirm the infection is gone.
faqs: Why do cats need special care with enrofloxacin?
Cats are sensitive to its effects on the retina, which can lead to vision loss at high doses. Your veterinarian sets a cat-specific dose and you should never increase it.
How quickly does enrofloxacin start working?
Many pets start to feel better within a few days, but the full course is needed to clear the infection.
Is enrofloxacin safe for puppies?
It is usually avoided in young, growing dogs because it can harm developing joints. Your veterinarian will choose a different antibiotic when possible.

name: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2)
uses: Vitamin D supplement.
how: Vitamin D2, which the body converts to active vitamin D.
avoid: Too much can cause high calcium.
about: Ergocalciferol is vitamin D2, a form of vitamin D made from plants and yeast. The liver and kidneys convert it into the active hormone that helps the body absorb calcium and keep bones strong. High-strength prescription capsules have been used for decades to correct low vitamin D, and compounded capsules may be requested for a specific strength or a version without certain dyes or fillers.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of high calcium such as nausea, vomiting, constipation, strong thirst, frequent urination, confusion, weakness or an irregular heartbeat.
interactions: Thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide, calcium supplements and digoxin need care because of calcium levels, while cholestyramine, mineral oil and some seizure medicines can lower vitamin D absorption or levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Normal vitamin D intake is important in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but high-dose prescription vitamin D should be used only as your prescriber directs.
petNotes: Dogs and cats are very sensitive to vitamin D overdose, and human supplements, some rodent poisons and vitamin D psoriasis creams can poison pets. Store capsules out of reach and call your veterinarian if a pet swallows extra.
tips: Take it with a meal that has some fat to help absorption.
If you take it once a week, mark the day on a calendar or phone reminder.
Do not add other vitamin D supplements unless your prescriber says to.
If a dose is missed, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually recheck vitamin D (25-hydroxy vitamin D) and calcium levels after a few months of treatment.
faqs: What is the difference between vitamin D2 and vitamin D3?
D2 (ergocalciferol) comes from plants and yeast, and D3 (cholecalciferol) is the form made in skin and found in animal foods. Both raise vitamin D levels, and your prescriber decides which to use.
How long does it take to raise vitamin D levels?
It usually takes several weeks to a few months of steady use, which is why levels are often rechecked after about 3 months.

name: Ergoloid mesylates
uses: Circulation-supporting ingredient used in topical sexual-health creams.
how: Ergot-derived compounds that increase blood flow in small vessels.
avoid: People with low blood pressure or slow heart rate, and those taking other ergot medicines.
about: Ergoloid mesylates are a mix of three modified ergot alkaloids that were sold for decades as Hydergine tablets for age-related changes in thinking in older adults; oral use is now uncommon. Prescribers may include it off-label in compounded topical sexual-health creams, alongside ingredients such as sildenafil, pentoxifylline and theophylline, to support blood flow in the area where the cream is applied.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, fainting, a very slow heartbeat, numbness, coldness or color changes in the fingers or toes, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Other ergot medicines, triptans for migraine, strong CYP3A4 blockers such as some HIV medicines, clarithromycin and azole antifungals, and blood pressure medicines should be reviewed before use. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Ergot medicines are not used in pregnancy; do not use this cream if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding unless your prescriber says it is safe.
tips: Apply only the amount prescribed to clean, dry skin in the area directed.
Wash your hands after applying, and keep the cream away from your eyes.
Stop using it and call your prescriber if you get burning, a rash or lasting irritation.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Is ergoloid the same as ergotamine?
No. Both come from ergot, but ergotamine is a strong blood vessel narrower used for migraines, while ergoloid mesylates have milder effects and are used in small amounts in creams.
Can both men and women use a cream with ergoloid?
Compounded sexual-health creams are prescribed for both men and women, and the ingredients are chosen by the prescriber for each person.

name: Erythromycin
uses: Bacterial infections and slow stomach emptying.
how: A macrolide antibiotic; at low doses it also stimulates the stomach to empty.
avoid: People or pets taking cisapride or other drugs it interacts with.
about: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used since the 1950s for respiratory, skin and other bacterial infections. At low doses it also acts like motilin, a natural gut hormone, which is why it is used off-label to help the stomach empty in people with gastroparesis and in dogs and cats with slow stomach emptying. Compounded capsules let prescribers and veterinarians choose small strengths that commercial products do not offer.
conditions: Slow stomach emptying in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe watery or bloody diarrhea, fainting or a fast or irregular heartbeat, yellowing of the skin or eyes, hearing loss, or a severe rash or swelling.
interactions: Erythromycin blocks the liver enzyme CYP3A4 and can raise levels of many drugs, including simvastatin and lovastatin, colchicine, theophylline, warfarin, digoxin, cyclosporine and some heart rhythm medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Erythromycin is generally considered an option in pregnancy and breastfeeding when an antibiotic is needed, but your prescriber decides; the estolate salt form is usually avoided in pregnancy.
petNotes: Dogs and cats may vomit or have diarrhea, so it is often given with a small meal. It should not be given to rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters or other small herbivores, because it can upset their gut bacteria and cause life-threatening illness.
tips: Follow the label on whether to take it with food; taking it with a small snack can ease stomach upset.
When used for stomach emptying, it is usually given before meals as directed.
For infections, finish the full course even if you feel better.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses; with long-term use, your prescriber may check liver tests or a heart tracing (ECG) if you take other heart-related medicines.
faqs: How does erythromycin help the stomach empty?

At low doses it triggers the same receptors as motilin, a gut hormone that starts the muscle waves that move food along. The effect may fade with long-term use, so your prescriber reviews how well it is working.
Why does erythromycin upset my stomach?
The same gut-stimulating effect that helps stomach emptying can cause cramps, nausea or diarrhea. Taking it with a small amount of food may help if your prescriber agrees.

name: Estradiol
uses: Estrogen replacement for menopause symptoms such as hot flashes and vaginal dryness.
side: Breast tenderness, bloating, nausea, headache, spotting. Estrogen therapy carries boxed-warning risks your prescriber will review.
how: Replaces estradiol, the main estrogen the ovaries make before menopause.
avoid: People with a history of breast or uterine cancer, blood clots, stroke, heart attack, liver disease or unexplained vaginal bleeding, and those who are pregnant.
about: Estradiol is the main estrogen the ovaries make before menopause. It has been used since the 1970s in FDA-approved tablets, patches, gels, vaginal tablets and rings. Prescribers may order compounded estradiol when they want a strength, base or route that is not available commercially, such as a troche or a cream combined with estriol, progesterone or testosterone, or when a patient reacts to an ingredient in a commercial product.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, pain or swelling in one leg, a sudden severe headache, vision loss, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, a new breast lump, or unusual vaginal bleeding.
interactions: Carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampin and St. John's wort can lower estradiol levels, while ketoconazole and some other antifungals can raise them; thyroid hormone doses may need adjusting. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy, and it may lower milk supply while breastfeeding; tell your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply creams and gels to clean, dry skin, rotate sites, and let it dry before dressing.
Wash your hands after applying, and keep treated skin away from children and pets, since estrogen can transfer by touch.
Let troches dissolve fully between the cheek and gum; do not chew or swallow them whole.
If you still have a uterus, use the progesterone your prescriber ordered with your estrogen.
monitoring: Your prescriber will review symptoms regularly and may recommend mammograms, pelvic exams and sometimes blood levels; any unexpected vaginal bleeding should be checked.
faqs: Do I need progesterone with estradiol?
If you still have a uterus, prescribers usually add progesterone, because estrogen alone can thicken the uterine lining and raise the risk of uterine cancer. Your prescriber decides what you need.
Can estradiol cream transfer to my partner, children or pets?
Yes. Skin-to-skin contact with treated areas can pass estrogen to others, so wash your hands and cover the area once it is dry.
How long does estradiol take to help hot flashes?
Many people notice changes within a few weeks, with fuller relief over 2 to 3 months. Your prescriber may adjust the dose based on how you feel.

name: Estriol
uses: A milder estrogen used mainly in vaginal and topical preparations for menopause-related dryness and skin changes.
side: Vaginal irritation or discharge, breast tenderness, spotting.
how: A weaker estrogen that acts mainly on vaginal and skin tissue at the doses usually prescribed.
avoid: People with a history of estrogen-sensitive cancer, blood clots or unexplained vaginal bleeding.
about: Estriol is a weaker natural estrogen that the body makes in large amounts during pregnancy. It has been used for decades in vaginal creams in Europe, but no FDA-approved estriol product exists in the US, so it is available here only as a compounded preparation. Prescribers may order it alone for vaginal or skin dryness after menopause, or combined with estradiol (often called Bi-est) and other hormones.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, pain or swelling in one leg, a sudden severe headache, vision loss, weakness or numbness on one side, slurred speech, a new breast lump, or unusual vaginal bleeding.
interactions: Seizure medicines such as carbamazepine, rifampin and St. John's wort may lower estrogen levels, and other hormone products add to its effects. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding; tell your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Using vaginal cream or suppositories at bedtime helps them stay in place.
Wash the applicator with warm soapy water after each use, and wash your hands.
Use a panty liner if you notice leakage after vaginal use.
Let troches dissolve fully in the mouth without chewing.
monitoring: Your prescriber will review symptoms regularly, recommend routine breast and pelvic care, and want to know right away about any vaginal bleeding.
faqs: What is the difference between estriol and estradiol?
Estradiol is the strongest natural estrogen, while estriol is much weaker and acts mainly on vaginal and skin tissue at usual doses. Prescribers sometimes combine them.
What is Bi-est?
Bi-est is a compounded mix of estriol and estradiol in a ratio your prescriber chooses. It is not a commercial product.
Is estriol safer than other estrogens?
Estriol is weaker, but it is still an estrogen and its long-term safety has not been studied as much, so the same precautions generally apply.

avoid: Pregnancy. People who have been told to avoid estrogen, such as those with an estrogen-sensitive cancer, unless their prescriber approves. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Estriol, a mild estrogen, supports skin thickness, collagen and moisture. Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover, and hyaluronic acid holds moisture.
name: Estriol and tretinoin anti-aging cream
side: Dryness, peeling or sun sensitivity. Estriol is a hormone, and a small amount can be absorbed through the skin.
uses: Aging skin and fine lines on the face and neck. Made with estriol 0.3%, hyaluronic acid 0.5% and tretinoin 0.02%.
about: This compounded face cream combines three ingredients that each target a different part of skin aging: estriol, a mild estrogen; tretinoin, a vitamin A retinoid; and hyaluronic acid, a moisture-holding molecule. No commercial product contains this combination. It is prescribed mainly for people whose skin has become thinner, drier and more lined after menopause, when falling estrogen affects collagen and moisture.
conditions: Loss of skin firmness on the neck
serious: Get medical help right away for severe blistering, swelling or burning, signs of an allergic reaction such as facial swelling or trouble breathing, a new breast lump, or unexpected vaginal bleeding.
interactions: Avoid using other strong exfoliants, benzoyl peroxide, salicylic or glycolic acid, and drying acne products on the same areas unless your prescriber approves, and tell your prescriber about any hormone therapy, since estriol adds to it. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because tretinoin and estriol may affect a developing baby, and it is not recommended while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber first.
tips: Apply a small amount at night to clean, completely dry skin.
Keep it away from the eyes, the corners of the nose and the lips.
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen every morning, since tretinoin makes skin burn more easily.
If skin gets dry or flaky, use a gentle moisturizer and ask your prescriber about using it less often at first.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: How long before I see results?
Changes in fine lines and skin texture often take 2 to 3 months of regular use, and some dryness or peeling may come first.
Why is there a hormone in an anti-aging cream?
After menopause, lower estrogen can thin the skin and reduce collagen. A small amount of estriol applied to the skin is used to support skin thickness and moisture.
Can I use this cream with my other skin care?
Gentle cleansers, moisturizers and sunscreen are usually fine. Ask your prescriber before using acids, scrubs or other retinoids at the same time.

name: Famciclovir
uses: Herpes infections in people and feline herpesvirus in cats.
how: Converted to penciclovir, which stops herpesviruses from copying their DNA.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease (lower dose).
about: Famciclovir is an antiviral approved in the 1990s for shingles, cold sores and genital herpes in people. The body converts it to penciclovir, its active form. Veterinarians use it off-label for feline herpesvirus, a common cause of eye and upper respiratory problems in cats. Because the tablets taste very bitter, compounded flavored suspensions or chewable treats can make it much easier to give to cats.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, facial swelling or trouble breathing, confusion, severe vomiting, or a large drop in urination.
interactions: Probenecid can raise famciclovir levels, and other medicines that strain the kidneys need extra care; other interactions are uncommon. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so it is used only when your prescriber decides the benefit outweighs the risk.
petNotes: Cats most often receive it for herpes flare-ups that cause eye inflammation, corneal ulcers or sneezing. It is generally well tolerated in cats, though some get mild stomach upset.
tips: For shingles or cold sores, start it as soon as symptoms begin, as your prescriber directed.
It can be given with or without food; with food may help an upset stomach.
Shake the suspension well and finish the full course.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed; cats are often rechecked so the veterinarian can see how the eyes are healing, and kidney values may be checked in older pets or people with kidney disease.
faqs: Is famciclovir safe for cats?
Veterinarians commonly prescribe it off-label for cats with herpesvirus, and most cats tolerate it well. Your veterinarian decides the dose and how long to give it.
Does famciclovir cure herpes?
No. Herpes viruses stay in the body for life; famciclovir helps control flare-ups by slowing the virus while it is active.
How soon should famciclovir be started for shingles?
It is usually started as early as possible, ideally within 3 days of the rash appearing. Contact your prescriber as soon as you notice symptoms.

name: Famotidine
uses: Reduces stomach acid for reflux and ulcers.
how: Blocks histamine (H2) receptors in the stomach to reduce acid.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease (lower dose).
about: Famotidine is an H2 blocker that has been used since the 1980s to lower stomach acid, and it is now widely sold over the counter. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats for stomach upset, acid reflux and ulcers. Compounded flavored suspensions, capsules and chewable treats help when a pet or person needs a smaller dose, a liquid, or a form that is easier to give.
conditions: Acid reflux in dogs and cats (off-label)
Vomiting and stomach upset in pets (off-label)
Ulcer prevention during NSAID or steroid use
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for confusion or unusual behavior (more likely with kidney disease), a fast or irregular heartbeat, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: By lowering stomach acid, famotidine can reduce absorption of medicines that need acid, such as ketoconazole, itraconazole and some HIV and cancer medicines; antacids given at the same time may reduce its effect. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Famotidine is generally considered an option in pregnancy and breastfeeding when an acid reducer is needed, but check with your prescriber first.
petNotes: Pets often get it before the first meal of the day. Its acid-lowering effect may weaken with continued daily use over a few weeks, so veterinarians sometimes switch to another medicine for longer treatment.
tips: It can be taken with or without food; to prevent heartburn, take it before meals that trigger symptoms.
Shake the suspension well and measure with the oral syringe.
Separate it from antacids by about an hour or two.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How fast does famotidine work?
It usually starts lowering stomach acid within about an hour, and the effect lasts for several hours.
Can dogs and cats take famotidine?
Veterinarians commonly prescribe it off-label for dogs and cats. Ask your veterinarian before giving any product meant for people, since dose and ingredients matter.
What is the difference between famotidine and omeprazole?
Famotidine blocks one signal that triggers acid, while omeprazole shuts down the acid pumps themselves and usually lowers acid more strongly. Your prescriber or veterinarian decides which fits.

name: Finasteride
uses: Hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) and enlarged prostate, including topical formulas for hair.
side: Decreased libido, sexual side effects, breast tenderness.
how: Blocks the enzyme that converts testosterone into DHT, the hormone behind male-pattern hair loss and prostate growth.
avoid: Anyone who is or may become pregnant should not handle crushed tablets or topical forms, since it can affect a developing baby.
about: Finasteride blocks the type 2 form of 5-alpha reductase, the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT. It was approved as Proscar for enlarged prostate in 1992 and as Propecia for male-pattern hair loss in 1997. Compounded topical solutions, often combined with minoxidil, are applied to the scalp so the medicine acts where hair grows; a flavored liquid may help people who cannot swallow tablets. Topical finasteride is not FDA-approved.
serious: Get medical help right away for a breast lump, breast pain or nipple discharge, signs of an allergic reaction, or depressed mood or thoughts of harming yourself.
interactions: Finasteride has few known drug interactions, but it lowers PSA test results, so tell any doctor ordering a PSA test that you use it. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not for anyone who is pregnant or may become pregnant, because it can harm the development of a male baby; they should not touch the topical solution or crushed or broken tablets, and it is not used while breastfeeding.
tips: Apply the topical solution to a dry scalp and let it dry before bed or putting on a hat.
Wash your hands after applying, and avoid letting a partner touch treated areas until dry.
Shake the oral suspension well and measure each dose carefully.
Use it every day; hair gained usually starts to be lost again within months if you stop.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check PSA and review hair progress, often with photos, every few months.
faqs: What is the difference between topical and oral finasteride?

Both block DHT production. The topical form is applied to the scalp and is intended to act mostly where it is applied, while oral finasteride works through the whole body. Your prescriber decides which fits.
How long does finasteride take to work for hair loss?
Most people need 3 to 6 months of daily use to see changes, and up to a year to judge the full result.
Can women use finasteride?
It must not be used by anyone who is or could become pregnant. Prescribers occasionally use it off-label for women after menopause, and only your prescriber can decide.

name: Fluconazole
uses: Fungal and yeast infections.
how: Blocks the fungal enzyme needed to build the fungal cell membrane.
avoid: People with liver disease or heart rhythm problems, and pregnancy.
about: Fluconazole is a triazole antifungal used since 1990 for yeast and other fungal infections. It is absorbed well by mouth and reaches many body tissues, including the brain and urine. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats for fungal infections such as cryptococcosis. Compounded flavored suspensions help when a pet needs a small or specific dose, or a person needs a liquid in a particular strength or flavor.
conditions: Fungal infections in cats and dogs (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe stomach pain, fainting or a fast or irregular heartbeat, or a severe rash with blistering or peeling.
interactions: Fluconazole raises levels of many medicines, including warfarin, some statins, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, phenytoin, sulfonylureas for diabetes and medicines that affect heart rhythm; it should never be combined with cisapride. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Generally avoided in pregnancy, especially at high doses or for long courses, because it has been linked to birth defects; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats usually tolerate it well, and treatment for deep fungal infections such as cryptococcosis in cats can last months. Pets with kidney disease may need dose changes.
tips: It can be given with or without food.
Shake the suspension well before each dose.
Finish the full course, even after symptoms clear.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: For longer courses, your prescriber or veterinarian may check liver tests periodically.
faqs: How long does fluconazole take to work for a yeast infection?
Many people feel better within a few days, though symptoms can take up to a week to fully clear.
Is fluconazole safe for cats?
Veterinarians commonly prescribe it off-label for cats with fungal infections, and it is usually well tolerated. Your veterinarian sets the dose and monitoring.

name: Fluorouracil
uses: Precancerous skin spots and warts, as prescribed.
how: Blocks DNA production in rapidly dividing abnormal skin cells.
avoid: Pregnancy. Extremely toxic to dogs and cats, even in small amounts; store securely.
about: Fluorouracil, often called 5-FU, is a chemotherapy medicine that has been used as a skin cream since the 1960s. On the skin, it targets fast-growing abnormal cells in precancerous spots and some superficial skin cancers while leaving most normal skin alone. Compounded creams may combine it off-label with calcipotriene for sun-damaged skin or with salicylic acid for warts.
serious: Get medical help right away for open sores or signs of skin infection, a severe allergic reaction, or rarely severe diarrhea, mouth sores, fever or bleeding, which can happen in people with a DPD enzyme deficiency.
interactions: Very little is absorbed, but avoid other irritating skin products on treated areas, and tell your prescriber if you take warfarin, capecitabine or other cancer medicines. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby, and it is not recommended while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply with a gloved finger or cotton swab, or wash your hands right after.
Keep it away from the eyes, nose and mouth.
Avoid sun exposure on treated skin and use sunscreen once healed.
Store it where pets can't reach, wipe up any spills, and don't let pets lick treated skin.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check the treated skin during and after treatment to make sure the spots have cleared and the skin is healing.
faqs: Is it normal for the skin to look worse during treatment?
Yes. Redness, crusting and tenderness are expected as abnormal cells are destroyed. Call your prescriber if it becomes very painful or looks infected.
Why is fluorouracil so dangerous to dogs and cats?

Pets can be poisoned by licking or chewing a tube or treated skin, causing vomiting, seizures and death even from small amounts. Call your veterinarian or an animal poison control line right away if exposure happens.
How long does it take for skin to heal after treatment?
Most skin heals within a few weeks after stopping, although some pinkness can last longer.

name: Fluoxetine
uses: Depression and anxiety in people; anxiety, aggression and compulsive behaviors in dogs and cats.
side: Nausea, decreased appetite, sleep changes, restlessness.
how: An SSRI that increases serotonin available in the brain.
avoid: Anyone taking MAO inhibitors, tramadol or other serotonin medicines; pets with seizures. Takes several weeks to reach full effect.
about: Fluoxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that has been prescribed for depression and anxiety since 1987. A chewable form, Reconcile, has been approved for separation anxiety in dogs, and veterinarians also use fluoxetine off-label for other behavior problems in dogs and cats. Compounded flavored liquids, treats, small capsules and transdermal gel help with cats and small dogs that need a smaller dose or refuse pills.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for new or worsening thoughts of suicide or self-harm, fever with agitation, muscle stiffness or twitching, confusion, seizures, unusual bleeding or bruising, or sudden aggression in a pet.
interactions: Never combine it with MAO inhibitors, including selegiline and amitraz tick collars in pets, and use care with other serotonin medicines, triptans, opioid pain medicines, NSAIDs, blood thinners and some heart rhythm medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
