pregnancy: Use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is a decision to make with your prescriber, since there may be risks to the baby but stopping suddenly can also cause problems; don't stop on your own.
petNotes: In dogs and cats the full effect usually builds over 4 to 6 weeks and is usually paired with a behavior plan. Some pets have less appetite or are sleepy at first; tell your veterinarian if your pet has ever had a seizure.
tips: Give it at about the same time each day; giving it with food may reduce stomach upset.
Do not stop it suddenly; your prescriber or veterinarian will taper it if needed.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel, and shake liquids well.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check in during the first weeks for mood changes; veterinarians may recheck behavior and bloodwork for pets on long-term treatment.
faqs: How long does fluoxetine take to work in dogs?
Some changes may appear in the first couple of weeks, but the full effect usually takes 4 to 6 weeks. Behavior training remains an important part of treatment.
Can fluoxetine be stopped suddenly?
Avoid stopping it suddenly. Fluoxetine leaves the body slowly, but your prescriber or veterinarian should plan any change in dose.
Can cats take fluoxetine?
Veterinarians prescribe it off-label for cats with urine marking, anxiety or compulsive behaviors. Cats are often given a flavored liquid or small capsule at a cat-specific dose.

name: Furosemide
uses: Fluid buildup from heart failure and other conditions.
how: A loop diuretic that makes the kidneys remove more salt and water.
avoid: People or pets who are dehydrated or have low potassium; needs kidney monitoring.
about: Furosemide is a loop diuretic, or water pill, used since the 1960s to remove extra fluid from the body. It acts quickly and strongly on the kidneys, which makes it a key medicine for fluid in the lungs from heart failure in people, dogs and cats. Compounded flavored liquids, chewable treats and capsules help with small dogs and cats that need precise doses, and transdermal gel may be used for pets that cannot be pilled.
conditions: Fluid buildup from liver or kidney disease
Heart failure in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe weakness, muscle cramps, dizziness or fainting, very little urine, extreme thirst, confusion, ringing in the ears or hearing loss, or breathing that becomes faster or harder.
interactions: NSAIDs, other blood pressure medicines, lithium, digoxin, steroids, aminoglycoside antibiotics such as gentamicin or amikacin, and other medicines that lower potassium can add risk. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It is used in pregnancy only if clearly needed, and it may lower milk supply while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: For pets with heart failure, counting the resting breathing rate while your pet sleeps helps your veterinarian adjust treatment. Always leave fresh water out, and know that cats can become dehydrated more easily than dogs.
tips: Give morning doses early so extra urination doesn't disturb sleep, unless directed otherwise.
Keep fresh water available at all times.
Shake liquids well, and wear gloves when applying transdermal gel.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check kidney values and electrolytes such as potassium and sodium after starting and periodically during treatment.
faqs: Why does my pet drink and urinate so much on furosemide?
That is how the medicine works: it makes the kidneys release more water, so pets feel thirstier. Never limit water, and call your veterinarian if your pet stops drinking or seems weak.
What is a resting breathing rate and why does it matter?
It is the number of breaths your pet takes in one minute while sleeping. A rising rate can be an early sign of fluid in the lungs, so your veterinarian may ask you to track it.
How quickly does furosemide work?
By mouth, it usually starts increasing urination within about an hour.

name: Gabapentin
uses: Nerve pain and seizures in people; pain, anxiety before vet visits and seizures in dogs and cats; also used in topical pain creams.
how: Binds calcium channels on nerve cells and reduces the release of pain and excitement signals.
avoid: People with kidney disease (dose adjustment needed). Liquids made for people may contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs; pet formulations are made without it.
about: Gabapentin was approved in 1993 for seizures and later for nerve pain after shingles. It is now one of the most common off-label medicines in veterinary practice, used for chronic pain in dogs and cats and to calm cats before vet visits. Compounded forms include xylitol-free flavored liquids and treats for pets, small capsules, and creams, vaginal preparations or suppositories that combine it with other pain or hormone ingredients.
conditions: Chronic pain in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble breathing or very slow breathing, extreme sleepiness, new or worsening depression or thoughts of self-harm, a rash with swelling or fever, or a pet that cannot stand or walk.
interactions: Opioid pain medicines, sedatives, alcohol and other drugs that cause drowsiness can add to sleepiness and slow breathing, and antacids with aluminum or magnesium reduce absorption if given within about 2 hours. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Information in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited, so talk to your prescriber so the benefits and risks can be weighed.
petNotes: Human gabapentin liquids can contain xylitol, which is very dangerous to dogs, so give only pet-specific prescriptions. Cats often receive a dose before a vet visit, and older pets or pets with kidney disease may be more wobbly.
tips: Do not stop it suddenly, especially if it is used for seizures; your prescriber will taper it.
Avoid driving until you know how it affects you.
Shake liquids well, and wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to pets.
Give it about 2 hours apart from antacids.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check kidney function, since gabapentin is cleared by the kidneys, and review how well pain or anxiety is controlled.
faqs: Does gabapentin make dogs and cats sleepy?
Yes, sleepiness and wobbliness are the most common effects, especially when starting. They often ease within a few days; call your veterinarian if your pet can't walk normally.
Can I give my own gabapentin to my dog or cat?
No. Human products may contain xylitol and come in strengths not suited to pets. Your veterinarian needs to prescribe a pet-specific dose and form.
Can gabapentin be stopped suddenly?
Stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms or seizures in some people and pets, so dose changes should be guided by your prescriber or veterinarian.

name: Gemfibrozil
uses: High triglycerides, including in dogs with high blood fats.
how: Lowers triglycerides by activating PPAR-alpha in the liver.
avoid: People or pets with liver, kidney or gallbladder disease, or taking statins.
about: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate medicine used since the early 1980s to lower triglycerides, the main fat carried in the blood. Very high triglycerides raise the risk of pancreatitis. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs with high blood fats that do not respond to a low-fat diet, a problem seen especially in Miniature Schnauzers. Compounded capsules let veterinarians choose a dose suited to a dog's size.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, dark urine, severe stomach pain with nausea or vomiting, or yellowing of the skin or eyes.
interactions: Gemfibrozil should not be combined with statins, repaglinide or selexipag, and it can strengthen the effect of warfarin and some diabetes medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding unless your prescriber decides it is needed.
petNotes: In dogs it is used together with a low-fat diet, which remains the main treatment. It is rarely used in cats.
tips: For people, it is usually taken about 30 minutes before meals, as directed.
Keep following the low-fat diet your prescriber or veterinarian recommends.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check triglycerides and liver tests, and sometimes a blood count, after starting and periodically.
faqs: Can I take gemfibrozil with a statin?
Gemfibrozil and statins together raise the risk of serious muscle damage, so the combination is usually avoided. Your prescriber decides the safest plan.
Is diet still important while taking gemfibrozil?
Yes. A low-fat diet and other lifestyle steps remain the foundation for lowering triglycerides in people and dogs.

name: Gentamicin
uses: Topical and ear and nasal preparations for bacterial infections.
how: An aminoglycoside that stops bacteria from making proteins.
avoid: Ruptured eardrums (ear products), and kidney disease if absorbed.
about: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used since the 1960s. It is poorly absorbed through the gut and skin, which makes it useful in topical ointments, ear medicines and eye drops. Compounded forms include nasal sprays used off-label for chronic sinus infections, ointments, and veterinary ear packs where it may be combined with an antifungal and a steroid, as well as with EDTA to help it reach bacteria in biofilms.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for ringing in the ears, hearing loss, dizziness or loss of balance, a head tilt in pets, much less urine, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: If absorbed, risk to the kidneys and ears rises with other medicines that can harm them, such as other aminoglycosides, vancomycin, loop diuretics like furosemide and some chemotherapy. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Little is absorbed from nasal or skin use, but gentamicin given by injection can harm a baby's hearing, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Ear products containing gentamicin can damage hearing or balance if the eardrum is torn, so the veterinarian checks the eardrum first. Cats may be more sensitive to these effects than dogs.
tips: Shake and prime nasal sprays before first use, and wipe the tip after each use.
Clean and dry the area before applying ointment, and wash your hands after.
Use it for the full time prescribed, even if symptoms improve.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short topical use; with long or widespread use, your prescriber may check kidney function or hearing.
faqs: Can gentamicin cause hearing loss?
When given by injection or absorbed in large amounts, gentamicin can harm the inner ear. With nasal, skin or ear use the risk is lower, but report any ringing, hearing change or dizziness right away.
Why use gentamicin in a nasal spray?
Applying it in the nose puts the antibiotic directly where a sinus infection is while keeping very little in the bloodstream. Your prescriber decides whether this approach fits.

name: Glycolic acid
uses: Exfoliation for skin tone and texture.
how: An alpha hydroxy acid that loosens dead skin cells.
avoid: Sensitive or broken skin. Increases sun sensitivity.
about: Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid (AHA), originally derived from sugarcane. Its small size lets it work into the top layer of skin, where it loosens the bonds between dead skin cells so they shed more evenly. It has been used in skin care products and in-office peels for decades. Compounded creams may combine it with tretinoin, hydroquinone or vitamin C for dark spots and rough texture.
conditions: Dark spots and melasma (with other agents)
serious: Get medical help right away for severe burning, blistering, swelling or oozing, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives or trouble breathing.
interactions: Used on the skin, glycolic acid has no meaningful drug interactions, but using it with tretinoin, benzoyl peroxide, other acids, or waxing can increase irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Topical glycolic acid is generally considered low risk in pregnancy and breastfeeding because little is absorbed, but check with your prescriber, especially if it is combined with tretinoin or hydroquinone.
tips: Start by using it every other night, then increase as your skin tolerates it.
Keep it away from the eyes, lips and any broken skin.
Wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day, since it makes skin more sun-sensitive.
Stop it a few days before waxing, laser treatments or chemical peels.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Can I use glycolic acid with tretinoin?
Prescribers sometimes combine them, but together they can be irritating. Use them only in the way your prescriber directs.
Is tingling normal with glycolic acid?
Mild tingling for a minute or two is common. Rinse it off and call your prescriber if you have strong burning, blistering or lasting redness.

name: Gonadorelin
uses: A synthetic form of the hormone that signals the pituitary gland, prescribed off-label to support natural testosterone and fertility signaling, often alongside testosterone therapy.
side: Headache, flushing, nausea, mouth irritation with troches.
how: Mimics GnRH, the brain hormone that signals the pituitary to release LH and FSH.
avoid: People with hormone-sensitive cancers or pituitary conditions.
about: Gonadorelin is a synthetic version of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain hormone that signals the pituitary gland to release LH and FSH. A commercial injection, Factrel, was once used to test pituitary function but is no longer available. Some prescribers order it compounded, off-label, for men on testosterone therapy to help keep their own hormone signaling active. Research on gonadorelin used this way is limited.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, or for a sudden severe headache with vision changes.
interactions: Testosterone, estrogens, progestins, steroid medicines, spironolactone and levodopa can change how the pituitary responds to gonadorelin. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: In this use it is prescribed for men and is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Let the troche dissolve fully between the cheek and gum; do not chew or swallow it.
Avoid eating or drinking until it has completely dissolved.
Alternate sides of the mouth to limit irritation, and store troches as the label directs.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check testosterone, estradiol, LH and FSH, and sometimes a semen analysis, during treatment.
faqs: Why is gonadorelin used with testosterone therapy?

Testosterone therapy tells the brain to slow its own hormone signals, which can shrink the testicles and lower sperm production. Gonadorelin is prescribed off-label to help keep that signaling active.
What is the difference between gonadorelin and hCG?
Gonadorelin acts on the pituitary gland, prompting it to release LH and FSH. hCG acts directly on the testicles, mimicking LH.

name: Griseofulvin
uses: Ringworm and fungal infections.
how: Stops fungal cells from dividing.
avoid: Pregnancy, cats with FIV, and people with liver disease or porphyria.
about: Griseofulvin is one of the oldest oral antifungal medicines, first made from a Penicillium mold and used since the late 1950s. It collects in the outer layers of skin, hair and nails, where it stops ringworm fungi from spreading into new growth. Compounded flavored suspensions can help with children, kittens and other pets who need a liquid in a specific strength.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for yellowing of the skin or eyes, a severe rash or blisters, fever or sore throat, unusual bruising, or in pets weakness, pale gums or loss of appetite.
interactions: It can make birth control pills and warfarin less effective, phenobarbital can lower its levels, and alcohol may cause flushing and a fast heartbeat. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby; people who can become pregnant need reliable birth control during treatment and for a month after, and men should avoid fathering a child for 6 months after treatment.
petNotes: Kittens and cats with FIV are prone to dangerous drops in blood counts, so many veterinarians choose other antifungals for them. It should not be given to pregnant animals.
tips: Give it with a fatty meal, which helps the body absorb it.
Shake the suspension well before each dose.
Avoid strong sun, since it can make skin more sensitive.
Continue for the full course, which often lasts weeks to months.
monitoring: On longer courses, your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood counts and liver tests periodically; cats usually have blood counts checked.
faqs: Why should griseofulvin be taken with fatty food?
It dissolves poorly in water, and fat in the meal helps the body absorb much more of it.
How long does ringworm treatment take?
Skin ringworm often needs several weeks, scalp infections longer, and nail infections months. Treatment continues until your prescriber or veterinarian confirms the infection is gone.

name: GS-441524
uses: Antiviral used to treat feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) in cats. Not FDA-approved; compounded only from a veterinarian's prescription for a specific cat, following FDA's policy.
side: Mild stomach upset and changes in liver values; dosing is weight-based and set by your veterinarian.
how: A nucleoside analog that stops the feline coronavirus that causes FIP from copying its genetic material.
avoid: Treatment must be directed by a veterinarian with weight-based dosing and regular checkups, usually for at least 12 weeks.
about: GS-441524 is an antiviral nucleoside analog, closely related to remdesivir, that blocks the feline coronavirus responsible for feline infectious peritonitis (FIP). FIP was long considered almost always fatal, and research at veterinary schools has made GS-441524 a central part of how veterinarians approach the disease. It is not FDA-approved for cats; it is compounded from a veterinarian's prescription for an individual cat as a flavored oral suspension.
conditions: FIP affecting the eyes or brain
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for trouble breathing, new seizures, wobbliness or behavior changes, yellow gums or eyes, refusal to eat for more than a day, or a belly that swells again.
interactions: Information on drug interactions is limited, so give other medicines or supplements only with your veterinarian's approval. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Because doses are based on weight, weigh your cat regularly, especially growing kittens, and report changes to your veterinarian. Giving every dose on time matters, since missed doses may raise the risk of relapse.
tips: Give it at the same time every day, and set a phone reminder.
Shake the suspension well and measure each dose with the oral syringe.
Weigh your cat weekly on a home or baby scale and share the results with your veterinarian.
Do not stop early, even if your cat looks well; your veterinarian decides when treatment ends.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually check bloodwork such as blood counts, protein levels (globulin and albumin), liver and kidney values, plus weight, before, during and after treatment.
faqs: How long does FIP treatment last?
Treatment usually lasts at least 12 weeks, and your veterinarian may extend it based on bloodwork and how your cat is doing.
What happens after treatment ends?
Your veterinarian will keep checking your cat for several weeks or months to watch for signs of relapse. Call right away if old symptoms return.
Is GS-441524 the same as remdesivir?
No, but they are closely related. Remdesivir is converted in the body into GS-441524, and veterinarians may use either as part of FIP treatment.

name: Guaifenesin
uses: Loosens chest congestion.
how: Thins mucus so it is easier to clear.
avoid: Usually well tolerated; check combination products for other ingredients.
about: Guaifenesin is an expectorant that has been used since the 1950s and is found in many over-the-counter cough and cold products. It thins mucus in the airways so a cough can bring it up more easily. A compounded flavored suspension may be prescribed when someone needs a version free of dyes, sugar, alcohol or extra cold-medicine ingredients, or when a veterinarian wants a pet-safe liquid without harmful additives.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, trouble breathing, a cough that lasts more than a week, or a cough with high fever, rash or a lasting headache.
interactions: Guaifenesin has few interactions on its own, but many cough and cold products also contain decongestants, cough suppressants or pain relievers, so check labels to avoid doubling up. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Ask your prescriber before using it in pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, or while breastfeeding.
petNotes: Human cough and cold products can contain xylitol, acetaminophen or decongestants, which can poison dogs and cats, so use only a formula your veterinarian prescribes. Ask your veterinarian before giving any cough medicine to a cat.
tips: Drink plenty of water, which helps thin mucus.
Shake the suspension well and measure with the oral syringe.
Give it with food if it upsets the stomach.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Does guaifenesin stop a cough?
No. It loosens mucus so coughing is more productive; it does not suppress the cough itself.
Can I give my dog Mucinex?
Do not give human cough products to pets without your veterinarian's approval. Many contain extra ingredients that are dangerous to dogs and cats.

name: Guanfacine
uses: ADHD and blood pressure.
side: Drowsiness, low blood pressure, dry mouth.
how: Stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brain, lowering blood pressure and improving focus.
avoid: People with slow heart rate or low blood pressure. Do not stop suddenly.
about: Guanfacine acts on alpha-2A receptors in the brain. It was approved as Tenex for high blood pressure in 1986, and an extended-release form, Intuniv, was approved in 2009 as a non-stimulant treatment for ADHD in children and teens. Extended-release tablets cannot be crushed, so a compounded oral liquid may be prescribed for children or adults who cannot swallow tablets; a liquid is immediate-release, so the prescriber sets dosing with that in mind.
serious: Get medical help right away for fainting, a very slow heartbeat, severe dizziness, or a pounding headache, nervousness or fast heartbeat after doses are missed or stopped.
interactions: Ketoconazole and other strong CYP3A4 blockers can raise levels, rifampin and carbamazepine can lower them, and alcohol, sedatives and other blood pressure medicines add to drowsiness and low blood pressure; it may also raise valproic acid levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Information in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Measure each dose with the oral syringe, never a kitchen spoon.
Do not stop it suddenly; your prescriber will lower the dose gradually.
Stand up slowly and drink fluids, especially in hot weather, to reduce dizziness.
If a dose is missed, take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check blood pressure and heart rate, and in children height and weight, during treatment.
faqs: Is guanfacine a stimulant?
No. Guanfacine is a non-stimulant that works on a different brain pathway than stimulant ADHD medicines, and it is sometimes used together with them.
How long does guanfacine take to work for ADHD?
Some effects may appear within a week or two, but it often takes several weeks of adjusting the dose to see the full benefit.
What happens if guanfacine is stopped suddenly?
Stopping suddenly can cause blood pressure to rise sharply, along with headache and nervousness. Always ask your prescriber before stopping.

name: Hyaluronic acid
uses: Moisture for skin and vaginal tissue in creams.
how: A natural sugar molecule that holds water in skin and tissue.
avoid: Usually well tolerated.
about: Hyaluronic acid is a natural sugar molecule found in skin, joints and eyes, where it holds large amounts of water. It is widely used in skin care, eye drops, joint injections and vaginal moisturizers. In compounding it is added to creams, serums, gels, vaginal suppositories and nasal sprays, often alongside estriol, estradiol or tretinoin, to add moisture and help reduce dryness or irritation.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or lips, or trouble breathing.
interactions: Used on the skin, in the vagina or in the nose, hyaluronic acid has no known meaningful drug interactions; check with your prescriber before using it with other vaginal products. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Topical hyaluronic acid is generally considered low risk in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but check with your prescriber, especially when it is combined with hormones or tretinoin.
tips: Apply serums and creams to slightly damp skin, then follow with a moisturizer.
Use vaginal suppositories or gels at bedtime, and wear a panty liner if there is leakage.
Prime the nasal spray before first use and wipe the tip after each use.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Is hyaluronic acid a hormone?
No. It is a natural moisture-holding molecule, not a hormone, although it is sometimes combined with hormones in compounded products.
Can hyaluronic acid be used with estrogen cream?
Yes, prescribers often combine them, and hyaluronic acid adds moisture while estrogen supports the tissue. Use them as your prescriber directs.

name: Hydrochlorothiazide
uses: Blood pressure, fluid buildup and prevention of some urinary stones.
how: A thiazide diuretic that increases salt and water removal and reduces calcium in the urine.
avoid: People or pets with severe kidney disease, low potassium or gout.
about: Hydrochlorothiazide, often called HCTZ, is a thiazide diuretic used since 1959 for high blood pressure and fluid retention. It also lowers the amount of calcium in the urine, which is why it is used to help prevent some calcium kidney stones in people and, off-label, calcium oxalate stones in dogs and cats. A compounded oral liquid helps children and small pets that need precise doses or cannot take tablets.
conditions: Calcium oxalate stones in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe dizziness or fainting, muscle cramps or weakness, extreme thirst with confusion, sudden eye pain or vision changes, a hot, painful swollen joint, or a severe rash.
interactions: Lithium, NSAIDs, digoxin, steroids, diabetes medicines, other blood pressure medicines, and calcium or vitamin D supplements can all interact with it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Generally avoided in pregnancy unless clearly needed, and it may lower milk supply while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In dogs with recurring calcium oxalate stones it is used together with a special diet, and pets should always have fresh water. Watch for weakness or poor appetite, which can mean low potassium.
tips: Give it in the morning so extra urination doesn't disturb sleep.
Shake the liquid well and measure each dose carefully.
Use sunscreen and protective clothing, since it can make skin more sensitive to the sun.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check electrolytes, kidney function, and sometimes blood sugar, uric acid and calcium during treatment.
faqs: Does hydrochlorothiazide make you sensitive to the sun?
Yes. It can increase sunburn risk, and long-term use has been linked to a higher risk of some non-melanoma skin cancers, so daily sun protection and regular skin checks are wise.
Why is a water pill used for kidney stones?
Hydrochlorothiazide helps the kidneys hold on to calcium, so less calcium ends up in the urine where it can form stones.

name: Hydrocortisone
uses: Mild steroid for itchy, inflamed skin and in barrier ointments.
how: A mild steroid that reduces skin inflammation and itch.
avoid: Skin infections that are not being treated. Avoid long use on the face or thin skin.
about: Hydrocortisone is the same molecule as cortisol, the natural steroid hormone made by the adrenal glands. It has been used since the 1950s, both as a mild steroid on the skin and by mouth as hormone replacement when the adrenal glands do not make enough. Compounded creams, ointments and suppositories combine it with ingredients such as lidocaine, nystatin or hydroquinone, and oral liquids or capsules provide small, precise doses for children and pets.
conditions: Itchy skin in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for skin that looks infected, with pus, spreading redness or fever, a rash that keeps getting worse, or, with oral forms, severe weakness, vomiting, dizziness or confusion during an illness.
interactions: Topical forms have few interactions; with oral forms, NSAIDs raise the risk of stomach ulcers, it can raise blood sugar, rifampin and some seizure medicines can lower its levels, and ketoconazole can raise them. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Low-strength topical hydrocortisone is commonly used in pregnancy and breastfeeding for short periods, but check with your prescriber, and do not apply it to the breast right before nursing.
petNotes: Pets often lick off creams, so cover the area or distract your pet for a few minutes after applying. Oral hydrocortisone may be used in dogs with Addison's disease, where steady daily dosing matters.
tips: Apply a thin layer to the affected skin only, and wash your hands after.
Do not cover treated skin with tight bandages or diapers unless your prescriber says to.
Take oral forms with food, and never stop them suddenly.
If you take it for adrenal insufficiency, ask your prescriber what to do on sick days.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short topical use; with oral replacement therapy, your prescriber or veterinarian will check symptoms, blood pressure, electrolytes and, in children, growth.
faqs: Can I use hydrocortisone cream on my face?
Short-term use on the face is sometimes recommended, but the skin there is thin, so use it only as long as your prescriber directs.
How long can I use hydrocortisone cream?
For self-treatment, about a week is a common limit. Longer use should be guided by your prescriber, since steroids can thin the skin over time.
Is hydrocortisone safe for dogs?
Veterinarians prescribe hydrocortisone for dogs in both topical and oral forms. Use only the product and amount your veterinarian recommends.

name: Hydroquinone
uses: Dark spots and melasma.
how: Blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes skin pigment.
avoid: Long-term continuous use, which can darken skin. Use sunscreen.
about: Hydroquinone has been used for decades to lighten dark patches of skin by slowing pigment production. Since 2020 it is no longer sold over the counter in the US and is available only by prescription. Compounded creams often combine it with tretinoin and a mild steroid, an approach known as the Kligman formula, or with niacinamide, vitamin C or kojic acid, so prescribers can choose a strength and mix for each patient.
conditions: Dark marks after acne or inflammation
serious: Get medical help right away for blistering, cracking or severe redness, signs of an allergic reaction, or a blue-black darkening of the skin.
interactions: Avoid using it with benzoyl peroxide or hydrogen peroxide products, which can briefly stain the skin, and with other harsh or drying products on the same areas unless your prescriber approves. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Usually avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding because more of it is absorbed through the skin than many other topical products; talk to your prescriber first.
tips: Test a small area for a few days before applying it more widely.
Apply it only to the dark spots, not the surrounding skin.
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen daily, since even brief sun exposure can undo progress.
Follow your prescriber's plan for how long to use it and when to take breaks.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check your progress after a few months and decide when to stop or take a break.
faqs: Why is hydroquinone prescription-only now?
A 2020 change in federal law ended over-the-counter sales of hydroquinone products in the US, so it now requires a prescription.
How long can I use hydroquinone?
It is usually used in courses of a few months followed by a break, because long continuous use can cause dark discoloration. Your prescriber sets the schedule.
Why does sunscreen matter so much with hydroquinone?
Sunlight triggers pigment production, which can quickly undo progress, so daily sunscreen is a key part of treatment.

avoid: Pregnancy. Long-term continuous use, which can darken or thin the skin. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Hydroquinone blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes skin pigment. Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover and helps hydroquinone work, hydrocortisone calms irritation, and niacinamide reduces the transfer of pigment to the skin surface.
name: Hydroquinone 12% melasma cream
side: Irritation, redness, peeling and sun sensitivity. For limited-duration use with close prescriber follow-up.
uses: Stubborn melasma and dark spots. A high-strength cream made with hydroquinone 12%, tretinoin 0.05%, niacinamide 2% and hydrocortisone 2.5%.
about: This is a high-strength compounded cream for melasma and dark spots that have not responded to milder treatments. It builds on the well-known triple combination approach of hydroquinone, tretinoin and a mild steroid, and adds niacinamide. No commercial product contains this strength or combination. Because hydroquinone is used at a high strength, it is meant for short courses under close prescriber supervision.
conditions: Dark spots not helped by milder creams
serious: Get medical help right away for blistering, cracking or severe redness, signs of an allergic reaction, or a blue-black darkening of the skin.
interactions: Avoid using it with benzoyl peroxide or hydrogen peroxide products, which can briefly stain the skin, and with other harsh or drying products on the same areas unless your prescriber approves. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because of the tretinoin and the amount of hydroquinone absorbed through the skin, and it is not recommended while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber first.
tips: Apply a small amount only to the dark areas, usually at night, as directed.
Keep it away from the eyes, the corners of the nose and the lips.
Wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day and limit sun exposure.
Stop and call your prescriber if your skin becomes very red, cracked or painful.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually see you every few months while you use this high-strength cream, to check results and watch for irritation, thinning or darkening of the skin.
faqs: Why use a 12% cream instead of a lower strength?
Some melasma does not respond to lower strengths. Your prescriber may choose a higher strength for a short course when milder creams have not helped.
Can I use it all over my face?
It is usually applied only to the dark areas. Ask your prescriber exactly where to apply it.
What happens when I stop?
Melasma can come back, especially with sun exposure, so prescribers often switch to a milder cream and daily sunscreen to maintain results.

avoid: Long-term continuous use, which can darken skin. Pregnancy. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Hydroquinone blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes skin pigment. Vitamin C also slows pigment production, and niacinamide reduces the transfer of pigment to the skin surface.
name: Hydroquinone 5% melasma cream
side: Irritation or redness. For limited-duration use.
uses: Melasma and dark spots. Made with hydroquinone 5%, niacinamide 3% and vitamin C 1%.
about: This compounded cream pairs a moderate strength of hydroquinone with niacinamide and vitamin C, three ingredients that work on different steps of skin pigmentation. It does not contain a retinoid or steroid, so it may suit people who want a gentler mix for melasma and dark spots. No commercial product contains this exact combination, and it is intended for limited courses under prescriber guidance.
serious: Get medical help right away for blistering, cracking or severe redness, signs of an allergic reaction, or a blue-black darkening of the skin.
interactions: Avoid using it with benzoyl peroxide or hydrogen peroxide products, which can briefly stain the skin, and with other harsh or drying products on the same areas unless your prescriber approves. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy, and usually avoided while breastfeeding because some hydroquinone is absorbed through the skin; talk to your prescriber first.
tips: Apply a thin layer only to dark areas, as directed.
Wear a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day and reapply when outdoors.
Keep it away from the eyes and lips, and wash your hands after applying.
Store it away from heat and light, which can break down hydroquinone and vitamin C.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check your progress after a few months and decide when to stop or take a break.
faqs: How long does it take to see results?
Lightening is gradual and often takes several weeks to a few months of steady use with daily sunscreen.
Is this cream gentler than a 12% hydroquinone cream?
It uses a lower strength of hydroquinone and no tretinoin or steroid, so it is often less irritating. Your prescriber decides which strength fits your skin.

name: Hydroxyzine
uses: Itch and anxiety.
how: An antihistamine that also has calming effects.
avoid: People with heart rhythm problems, and during early pregnancy.
about: Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine that has been used since the 1950s. Besides blocking histamine to relieve itching, it has calming effects, so it is prescribed for anxiety and to relax people before procedures. Veterinarians use it off-label for allergic itch in dogs and cats. Compounded flavored suspensions or capsules help when a child or pet needs a specific dose or a form that is easier to give.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting or a fast, pounding or irregular heartbeat, seizures, a severe rash with blisters or pus-filled bumps, extreme drowsiness, or unusual excitement in a pet.
interactions: Opioid pain medicines, sedatives, alcohol and other antihistamines add to drowsiness, and medicines that affect heart rhythm, such as some antibiotics, antidepressants and heart rhythm drugs, can raise the risk of rhythm problems. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Not used in early pregnancy and generally avoided while breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs may become sleepy or, less often, excitable. Tell your veterinarian if your pet has seizures or heart disease, and expect your veterinarian to judge results over a trial period.
tips: Avoid driving or other risky tasks until you know how it affects you.
Sugar-free gum or sips of water can ease dry mouth.
Shake the suspension well before each dose.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Is hydroxyzine addictive?
Hydroxyzine is not considered habit-forming, which is one reason it is sometimes chosen for anxiety. It can still cause drowsiness, so use it as directed.
How fast does hydroxyzine work?
It usually starts working within about an hour.
Can dogs take hydroxyzine?
Veterinarians prescribe it off-label for allergic itch in dogs. Do not give a human product without your veterinarian's dose and approval.

name: Hyoscyamine
uses: Stomach and bowel cramping.
how: Blocks acetylcholine to relax smooth muscle in the gut and bladder.
avoid: People with glaucoma, bowel blockage or urinary retention.
about: Hyoscyamine is a belladonna alkaloid, a close relative of atropine, that has been used for decades to relax cramping muscles in the stomach, bowel and bladder. It blocks acetylcholine, a nerve signal that makes these muscles contract and glands secrete. In compounding it may be included as an ingredient in preparations such as magic mouthwash or combined with lidocaine, as the prescriber directs.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for confusion, hallucinations, a fast heartbeat, eye pain with blurred vision, being unable to urinate, a swollen belly with severe constipation, or overheating with hot, dry skin.
interactions: Other anticholinergic medicines, such as some antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants and bladder medicines, add to side effects, antacids can reduce absorption, and it may increase stomach injury from solid potassium chloride tablets. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber before using it in pregnancy; it passes into breast milk and may lower milk supply.
petNotes: Pets may get dry mouth, constipation or a faster heart rate. It is not used in pets with glaucoma, and pets should stay cool in hot weather because it reduces their ability to shed heat.
tips: Take it before meals if it is prescribed for cramping with eating, as directed.
Avoid overheating: it reduces sweating, so take care in hot weather and during exercise.
Separate it from antacids by about an hour.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Can hyoscyamine cause overheating?
Yes. It reduces sweating, so the body has a harder time cooling down. Stay hydrated and avoid heavy exertion in hot weather.
Why does hyoscyamine cause dry mouth?
The same nerve signal it blocks to relax the gut also controls saliva. Sugar-free gum or sips of water can help.

name: Ibuprofen
uses: Pain and inflammation.
how: An NSAID that blocks COX enzymes to reduce inflammation and pain.
avoid: People with ulcers, kidney disease or late pregnancy. Toxic to dogs and cats.
about: Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) introduced in the 1960s and sold over the counter in the US since 1984. It relieves pain, lowers fever and reduces inflammation. A compounded oral liquid may be prescribed when someone needs a particular strength, flavor, or a version without certain dyes, sugars or other ingredients, such as for children or for people who use a feeding tube.
serious: Get medical help right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness on one side or slurred speech, swelling with much less urine, or a severe rash or skin blistering.
interactions: Blood thinners, aspirin, other NSAIDs, steroids, SSRI antidepressants, lithium, methotrexate, diuretics and blood pressure medicines can all interact with ibuprofen. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Avoid it from 20 weeks of pregnancy onward unless your prescriber directs it, because it can affect the baby's kidneys and heart; small amounts pass into breast milk, so check with your prescriber.
tips: Take it with food or milk to protect your stomach.
Measure each dose with the oral syringe, and don't take more than prescribed.
Store it where pets can't reach it; even small amounts can poison dogs and cats.
Check other medicines you take for hidden ibuprofen or other NSAIDs.
monitoring: For long-term use, your prescriber may check blood pressure, kidney function and blood counts.
faqs: Can I alternate ibuprofen and acetaminophen?
Some prescribers recommend alternating them for fever or pain, but follow their exact schedule so you don't take too much of either.
Why is ibuprofen dangerous for dogs and cats?
Pets are much more sensitive to ibuprofen, which can cause stomach ulcers and kidney failure even at small doses. Never give it to a pet, and call your veterinarian right away if one swallows some.
Can I take ibuprofen on an empty stomach?
It is better taken with food or milk, which can lower the chance of stomach upset.

name: Imatinib
uses: Certain cancers, including mast cell tumors in pets.
side: Vomiting, diarrhea, decreased appetite; hazardous drug.
how: Blocks specific tyrosine kinase enzymes that drive some cancers.
avoid: Pregnancy and liver disease. Hazardous drug: handle with gloves.
about: Imatinib was approved as Gleevec in 2001 and became one of the first targeted cancer medicines, blocking enzymes that drive the growth of certain cancers. Veterinarians use it off-label for some mast cell tumors in dogs and cats, particularly those with certain KIT gene changes. Compounded oral liquids or capsules can provide doses for smaller patients, and because it is a hazardous drug, careful handling is required.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for sudden weight gain or swelling, shortness of breath, fever or signs of infection, unusual bleeding or bruising, black stools, yellowing of the skin or eyes, a severe rash, or a pet that stops eating or has pale gums.
interactions: Ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin and grapefruit can raise imatinib levels, while rifampin, some seizure medicines and St. John's wort can lower them; it can also raise levels of warfarin and simvastatin and add to liver strain from acetaminophen. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Not used in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby; use effective birth control during treatment and for 2 weeks after, and do not breastfeed during treatment or for 1 month after the last dose.
petNotes: Wear disposable gloves when giving it and when cleaning up vomit, urine or feces, and keep pregnant household members from handling it. Dogs are watched closely for liver changes and stomach upset.
tips: Give it with a meal and a glass of water to reduce stomach upset.
Wear gloves when handling capsules or liquid, and wash your hands after.
Do not open capsules unless your prescriber or pharmacist says to.
Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check blood counts, liver and kidney function regularly, especially in the first months of treatment.
faqs: Why must imatinib be handled with gloves?
It is classified as a hazardous drug because it can harm healthy cells and may affect pregnancy, so caregivers should limit skin contact.
Is imatinib chemotherapy?
It is a targeted cancer medicine rather than traditional chemotherapy, but it is still handled with the same safety precautions.
Can imatinib be given with food?
Yes. Giving it with a meal is recommended to reduce nausea and stomach upset.

name: Imipenem
uses: Resistant bacterial ear infections in pets.
how: A carbapenem antibiotic that breaks down bacterial cell walls, reserved for resistant infections.
avoid: Pets with a beta-lactam allergy.
about: Imipenem is a carbapenem antibiotic, a class first introduced in the 1980s that covers a very wide range of bacteria. In people it is given by injection, combined with cilastatin, for serious hospital infections. In veterinary medicine, imipenem may be compounded into ear packs for multidrug-resistant ear infections, often Pseudomonas, when culture results show that other antibiotics will not work, helping keep this important class effective.
conditions: Resistant Pseudomonas ear infections in dogs
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for a head tilt, loss of balance, seizures, facial swelling or hives.
interactions: Very little is absorbed from the ear, so interactions are unlikely, but tell your veterinarian if your pet takes seizure medicines, and do not add other ear products unless directed. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Veterinarians reserve imipenem for infections that a culture shows are resistant, to protect its usefulness for serious infections in pets and people. Cats may be more sensitive to ear medicines, so the veterinarian decides whether it fits.
tips: Do not clean or flush the ears after treatment unless your veterinarian says to.
Keep the ears dry during treatment.
Keep recheck visits so your veterinarian can confirm the infection has cleared.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck the ears, often with a repeat cytology or culture, to make sure the resistant infection is gone.
faqs: Why is imipenem saved for resistant infections?
Overusing powerful antibiotics lets bacteria become resistant to them. Reserving imipenem for infections that need it helps keep it working when it matters most.
Why does my veterinarian need an ear culture first?
A culture identifies the bacteria and which antibiotics can kill them, so the veterinarian can choose imipenem only when it is truly needed.

name: Itraconazole
uses: Fungal infections including ringworm.
how: Blocks the fungal enzyme needed to build the fungal cell membrane.
avoid: People or pets with liver disease or heart failure.
about: Itraconazole is a triazole antifungal used since the early 1990s for fungal infections of the skin, nails, lungs and other organs. A veterinary product, Itrafungol, is approved for ringworm in cats, and veterinarians use itraconazole off-label for deeper fungal infections in dogs and cats. Compounded flavored suspensions and capsules provide doses for small pets, and nasal sprays may be prescribed off-label for chronic fungal sinus problems.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for shortness of breath, leg swelling or sudden weight gain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, loss of appetite, skin sores on the legs in dogs, or hearing loss or tingling in the hands or feet.
interactions: Itraconazole strongly blocks the CYP3A4 enzyme and should not be combined with cisapride, simvastatin, lovastatin, certain heart rhythm medicines or some sedatives; it raises levels of cyclosporine, digoxin and many others, and acid reducers can lower absorption of capsules. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Generally avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and not used for nail infections in anyone who is or may become pregnant; talk to your prescriber first.
petNotes: Cats and dogs on itraconazole may lose their appetite, which can be an early sign of liver strain. Dogs occasionally develop skin sores on the legs from blood vessel inflammation, which should be reported promptly.
tips: Give capsules with a full meal; follow the label for liquids, which may be given differently.
Shake liquids well before each dose.
Separate it from antacids, and finish the full course.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check liver tests periodically during longer courses.
faqs: How long is ringworm treatment in cats?
Treatment often lasts several weeks and continues until fungal cultures come back negative, along with cleaning the home and sometimes medicated baths.
Should itraconazole be taken with food?
Capsules are absorbed better with a full meal, while some liquid forms are meant for an empty stomach. Follow the instructions on your label.

name: Ivermectin
uses: Parasites in animals; rosacea creams in people.
side: Neurologic effects in sensitive dog breeds; local irritation topically.
how: Paralyzes parasites by acting on their nerve and muscle channels; topically it calms rosacea.
avoid: Collies, Australian shepherds and other herding breeds with the MDR1 gene (oral use), and young animals.
about: Ivermectin is an antiparasitic medicine discovered in the 1970s and used in animals since 1981; its discovery was recognized with a Nobel Prize in 2015. It is a common ingredient in heartworm preventives for dogs and cats, and a cream form is used for rosacea in people. Compounded flavored suspensions and capsules provide pet-specific doses, while compounded rosacea creams may combine it with ingredients such as metronidazole, azelaic acid or brimonidine.
conditions: Heartworm prevention in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a pet with wobbliness, dilated pupils, drooling, tremors, blindness, slow breathing or collapse, or a person with a severe skin reaction or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: In dogs, combining it with spinosad (found in some flea products) or drugs that block P-glycoprotein, such as ketoconazole or cyclosporine, raises the risk of toxicity; with rosacea cream, interactions are unlikely. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical ivermectin has not been well studied in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: Collies, Australian shepherds and other herding breeds with the MDR1 gene can have severe reactions to doses used for mange, even though heartworm preventive doses are generally safe; a cheek-swab test can check for the gene. Never give livestock or horse products to pets.
tips: Apply rosacea cream in a thin layer to clean, dry skin, avoiding the eyes and lips.
Give pet doses exactly as prescribed, and keep your veterinarian updated on your pet's weight.
Shake liquid suspensions well before each dose.
monitoring: Dogs and cats on heartworm prevention usually have yearly heartworm tests, and pets treated for mange often have repeat skin scrapings.
faqs: Can I give my dog horse or cattle ivermectin?
No. Livestock products are very concentrated, and small measuring errors can poison a dog, especially breeds with the MDR1 gene. Use only what your veterinarian prescribes.
What is the MDR1 gene?
It is a gene change, common in herding breeds, that lets more ivermectin reach the brain. A simple cheek-swab test can tell you whether your dog carries it.
How long does ivermectin cream take to work for rosacea?
Improvement is gradual, often over several weeks, and your prescriber will judge results after a few months.

name: Ketoconazole
uses: Fungal and yeast infections of skin, scalp and ears.
side: Local irritation; liver effects with oral use.
how: Blocks the fungal enzyme needed to build the fungal cell membrane; orally it also lowers cortisol.
avoid: People or pets with liver disease (oral use), and anyone taking cisapride.
about: Ketoconazole is an imidazole antifungal introduced in the early 1980s. Because of liver risks, oral ketoconazole in people is now reserved for serious infections, while creams and shampoos remain widely used. Veterinarians use it in dogs and cats for yeast and fungal infections, and sometimes off-label to lower cortisol or to reduce the dose of cyclosporine needed. Compounded ear packs, serums, oral liquids and transdermal gels allow targeted or pet-friendly forms.
conditions: Fungal infections in cats and dogs
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, vomiting, loss of appetite, extreme tiredness, a fast or irregular heartbeat, or severe weakness or collapse.
interactions: Oral ketoconazole should not be combined with cisapride, certain statins, some heart rhythm medicines or some sedatives; it raises cyclosporine levels, and acid reducers can lower its absorption. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Oral ketoconazole is generally avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding; topical forms absorb little, but check with your prescriber first.
petNotes: Cats are more prone than dogs to loss of appetite and liver effects from oral ketoconazole. In dogs, it can occasionally lighten coat color, and it may be paired with cyclosporine so a lower cyclosporine dose can be used.
tips: Give oral doses with food, which helps absorption and eases stomach upset.
Shake liquids well, and wear gloves when applying transdermal gel or serum.
Separate oral doses from antacids by about 2 hours.
For ear products, follow your veterinarian's directions on cleaning before and after use.
monitoring: With oral use, your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check liver tests before and during treatment; topical use usually needs no monitoring.
faqs: Why is ketoconazole given with cyclosporine in dogs?
Ketoconazole slows how fast the body clears cyclosporine, so the veterinarian may use it to lower the cyclosporine dose needed. Both medicines need careful monitoring.
Are topical ketoconazole products as risky as oral?
No. Very little ketoconazole is absorbed from creams, serums or ear products, so the liver risks of oral use are much less of a concern.

name: Ketoprofen
uses: Anti-inflammatory used in topical pain creams.
how: An NSAID that blocks COX enzymes to reduce inflammation and pain.
avoid: People with NSAID allergies or ulcers. Keep topical forms away from pets.
about: Ketoprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that has been used for decades for pain and swelling. Oral capsules are sold in the US, but topical ketoprofen creams are not available as commercial products here, so prescribers often ask for it compounded into creams, often blended with other pain ingredients, to treat a specific area while limiting how much reaches the rest of the body.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction (hives, swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing), an asthma attack, or a blistering or spreading rash, especially on skin that has been in the sun.
interactions: Avoid using other NSAIDs at the same time unless your prescriber says so, and use caution with blood thinners, steroids, lithium, methotrexate and blood pressure medicines, even though topical forms reach the blood in smaller amounts. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: NSAIDs, including topical ones, are usually avoided in the second half of pregnancy because they can affect the baby's heart and kidneys; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only to clean, unbroken skin and wash your hands afterward unless your hands are the area being treated.
Keep treated skin out of direct sunlight and tanning beds during treatment and for a while afterward, because ketoprofen can cause sun-related rashes.
Do not cover the area with tight wraps or heating pads unless your prescriber tells you to.
Keep the cream where pets cannot lick it or rub against treated skin, since cats and dogs are very sensitive to NSAIDs.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for topical use, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Can I use ketoprofen cream if I take ibuprofen or naproxen?
Using more than one NSAID at a time can add to the risk of stomach and kidney side effects, so ask your prescriber before combining them.
Why should I avoid the sun with ketoprofen cream?
Ketoprofen can make treated skin react to sunlight with a red, itchy or blistering rash, so covering the area and avoiding tanning beds is recommended.
Is ketoprofen cream safe around pets?
Pets, especially cats, can be poisoned by NSAIDs, so keep the tube put away and do not let pets lick treated skin.

name: Ketotifen
uses: Mast cell stabilizer for allergies and mast cell activation.
how: Stabilizes mast cells so they release less histamine and also blocks histamine receptors.
avoid: People with seizure disorders or diabetes (some forms).
drugClass: Mast cell stabilizer and H1 antihistamine
about: Ketotifen is an older medicine that both calms mast cells and blocks histamine. It has been sold as an oral medicine in many countries for years, but in the US it is only available commercially as allergy eye drops. Because of that, prescribers who want an oral form for conditions such as mast cell activation syndrome often ask for compounded capsules, which is an off-label use.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, a seizure, unusual bruising or bleeding, or severe drowsiness or confusion.
interactions: Ketotifen can add to the drowsiness of alcohol, sleep aids, other antihistamines and sedating medicines, and a drop in platelets has been reported when it is taken with oral diabetes medicines. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited safety information for oral ketotifen in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Take it at the same times each day, with or without food.
Because it can cause drowsiness, many prescribers start with a bedtime dose; don't drive until you know how it affects you.
Benefits for mast cell symptoms often build slowly, so keep taking it as directed rather than stopping after a few days.
If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check in on how your symptoms respond, and may check blood counts if you also take diabetes medicines.
faqs: How long does ketotifen take to work?
Some people notice changes within a few weeks, but it can take a couple of months to see the full effect for mast cell symptoms.
Will ketotifen make me sleepy?
Drowsiness is common at first and often eases after a week or two; your prescriber may adjust the timing of doses.
Is oral ketotifen the same as ketotifen eye drops?
No. The eye drops are a commercial product for itchy eyes, while compounded oral capsules are prescribed off-label for body-wide allergy and mast cell symptoms.

name: Kojic acid
uses: Brightening creams for dark spots.
how: Blocks tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes skin pigment.
avoid: People with sensitive skin.
about: Kojic acid is a natural substance made by certain fungi, including those used in fermenting rice for sake and soy sauce. It has been used in skin-care products for years to fade dark spots. Prescribers often ask for it compounded into creams alongside other brightening ingredients so the blend and strength can be matched to a person's skin and specific pigment concerns.
conditions: Dark marks after acne or injury
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, such as hives, swelling of the face or lips, or trouble breathing, or for a blistering or severe rash where the cream was applied.
interactions: Kojic acid is applied to the skin and is not known to interact with medicines taken by mouth, but using it with other strong skin products, such as retinoids, acids or peels, can increase irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Little is known about kojic acid in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber before using it if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer only to the dark areas or as directed, and wash your hands afterward.
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day, because sun exposure can undo lightening results.
Try a small test area first if you have sensitive skin, and stop if burning or redness gets worse.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules so they can check progress and irritation.
faqs: How long does kojic acid take to fade dark spots?
Changes are gradual and often take several weeks to a few months of daily use along with sun protection.
Can kojic acid be used with tretinoin or vitamin C?
It is often combined with other brightening ingredients, but layering several active products can irritate skin, so follow your prescriber's plan.

name: L-Arginine
uses: Amino acid used in topical circulation and sexual-health creams.
how: An amino acid the body uses to make nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels.
avoid: People with low blood pressure or a history of cold sores that flare easily.
about: L-arginine is an amino acid found in protein foods that the body uses to make nitric oxide, a natural signal that relaxes and widens blood vessels. In compounding, it is added to topical creams, often with other ingredients, to support local blood flow. These uses are generally off-label, and the prescriber decides whether a topical blend containing it is a good fit.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, dizziness or fainting, chest pain, or a painful erection lasting more than four hours if the cream contains other blood flow ingredients.
interactions: Use caution if you take nitrates, sildenafil-type medicines or other blood pressure medicines, since combined effects on blood vessels can lower blood pressure. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Topical arginine blends have not been well studied in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only the amount directed to clean, dry skin, and wash your hands afterward.
Avoid broken or irritated skin, and stop using it if a rash develops.
If you are prone to cold sores, let your prescriber know, since arginine may trigger flares in some people.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: How quickly does an arginine cream work?
Topical blends are usually applied a short time before activity, and your prescriber will explain timing for your specific cream.
Is topical L-arginine the same as an arginine supplement?
Both contain the same amino acid, but the cream is meant for local effects on the skin and tissues rather than body-wide use.

name: L-Methionine
uses: Urinary acidifier for pets.
how: An amino acid that makes the urine more acidic.
avoid: Cats and dogs with liver or kidney disease, and young kittens.
about: L-methionine is an essential amino acid that, when given as a supplement, is broken down in a way that makes urine more acidic. Veterinarians have used it for many years to help manage certain bladder stones and crystals that form in alkaline urine. Compounded capsules let the veterinarian choose a strength suited to a pet's size, since commercial options are limited.
conditions: Struvite crystals and stones in dogs and cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for weakness, wobbliness, pale gums, fast breathing, vomiting that won't stop, or a pet that seems confused or dull.
interactions: It should not be combined with other urinary acidifiers or acidifying prescription diets unless your veterinarian plans it, and it can change how some urinary antibiotics work. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Cats are more sensitive than dogs and high amounts can cause a type of anemia, so dosing for cats is especially careful. It is not used in young kittens or in pets with liver or kidney disease.
tips: Give with food to reduce stomach upset.
Keep fresh water available at all times so your pet keeps making plenty of urine.
Do not switch your pet's food while on methionine without asking your veterinarian, since diet also affects urine acidity.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck a urine sample to see whether the urine pH and crystals are changing, and may run blood tests in some pets.
faqs: Can L-methionine dissolve bladder stones in cats or dogs?
Making urine more acidic may help manage struvite crystals and some struvite stones, but other stone types do not respond, and your veterinarian decides the plan.
Is L-methionine safe for cats?
It can be used in adult cats under veterinary guidance, but cats are more sensitive to side effects, so never give it without your veterinarian's direction.

name: Lansoprazole
uses: Reduces stomach acid.
how: A proton pump inhibitor that shuts down the stomach's acid pumps.
avoid: Long-term use can affect vitamin B12 and magnesium.
about: Lansoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that has been prescribed since the 1990s to lower stomach acid. Commercial capsules and dissolving tablets exist, but some people, including children and people with feeding tubes, need a liquid. Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for dogs and cats, and a flavored suspension makes dosing small patients easier.
conditions: Ulcer protection with NSAIDs or steroids
Stomach ulcers in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe or watery diarrhea that won't stop, black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, muscle cramps or an irregular heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Lansoprazole can lower the absorption of medicines that need stomach acid, such as ketoconazole, itraconazole and iron, and may affect methotrexate, warfarin and some HIV medicines; sucralfate should be given separately. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; acid reducers are sometimes used in pregnancy when the benefit is clear.
petNotes: In dogs and cats, other PPIs such as omeprazole are used more often, and lansoprazole is an off-label choice. Giving it on an empty stomach before a meal tends to work best.
tips: Give or take it on an empty stomach, about 30 minutes before a meal, usually breakfast.
Shake the suspension well before each dose and measure with the syringe provided.
Don't stop long-term use suddenly without asking your prescriber or veterinarian, since acid symptoms can rebound.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: With long-term use, your prescriber or veterinarian may check magnesium and vitamin B12 levels from time to time.
faqs: How long does lansoprazole take to work?
It starts lowering acid within a day, but it can take a few days of regular use to feel the full effect on heartburn.
Can dogs and cats take lansoprazole?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label to reduce stomach acid in pets; only give it under your veterinarian's direction.
Is it safe to take lansoprazole long-term?
Long-term use can affect magnesium, vitamin B12 and bone health in some people, so your prescriber will review whether you still need it.

name: Leucovorin
uses: Folate supplement that protects against some medication side effects.
how: A ready-to-use form of folate.
avoid: People with untreated B12 deficiency.
about: Leucovorin, also called folinic acid, is a form of folate the body can use directly without first converting it. It has been used for decades alongside medicines that block folate, such as methotrexate and pyrimethamine, to reduce their side effects. Compounded oral liquids help with small or precise doses for children, people who cannot swallow tablets and pets.
conditions: Protozoal infection treatment support in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction (hives, swelling, trouble breathing) or for a seizure.
interactions: Leucovorin can lower the effect of some seizure medicines such as phenobarbital, phenytoin and primidone, and it increases the effects and side effects of fluorouracil. Timing with methotrexate matters, so follow the schedule exactly. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Folate is important in pregnancy, but leucovorin is usually given for a specific medical reason; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In dogs and cats, leucovorin is sometimes given alongside pyrimethamine or other folate-blocking medicines for protozoal infections. A liquid makes small doses easier to give accurately.
tips: Give or take it exactly on the schedule your prescriber or veterinarian sets, especially when it is paired with methotrexate.
Measure the liquid with an oral syringe rather than a kitchen spoon.
Do not use it to treat a vitamin B12 deficiency, since it can hide the anemia while nerve damage continues.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood counts and other labs, especially when leucovorin is given with methotrexate or pyrimethamine.
faqs: What is the difference between leucovorin and folic acid?
Folic acid must be converted by the body before it can be used, while leucovorin is already in an active form, which matters when other medicines block that conversion.
Why is leucovorin given with methotrexate?
It can help protect healthy cells from methotrexate side effects, and the timing is chosen carefully by your prescriber.

name: Levetiracetam
uses: Seizure control in people, dogs and cats.
how: Binds a protein on nerve endings (SV2A) that controls the release of signals, calming abnormal electrical activity.
avoid: People with kidney disease or a history of depression or mood changes.
about: Levetiracetam is a seizure medicine first approved for people in 1999 and now widely used. It is also prescribed off-label by veterinarians for dogs and cats because it is generally well tolerated and does not rely heavily on the liver. Compounded flavored liquids, treats and capsules help match doses to small pets and to people who need a different form.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for seizures that get worse or don't stop, severe sleepiness or trouble walking, signs of an allergic reaction or a severe skin rash, or in people, thoughts of self-harm, aggression or sudden mood changes.
interactions: Levetiracetam has few drug interactions, but alcohol, sedatives and other medicines that cause drowsiness can add to its effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Seizure control is important in pregnancy, so do not stop levetiracetam on your own; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs often need doses several times a day with the regular form, so slow-release capsules may be prescribed to reduce how often they are given; these should not be opened or crushed. Cats can find the taste bitter, so a flavored liquid or treat often helps.
tips: Give or take it at evenly spaced times every day, with or without food.
Never stop it suddenly, because that can trigger seizures; your prescriber or veterinarian will taper it if needed.
Swallow or give slow-release capsules whole; do not open, crush or chew them.
Keep a seizure log with dates and times to share at follow-up visits.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check kidney function and adjust the dose, and will review your seizure log at follow-up visits.
faqs: How long does levetiracetam take to work?
It begins working within hours to a few days, but it may take a few weeks of steady dosing to judge how well seizures are controlled.
Can I give levetiracetam to my dog or cat?
Veterinarians prescribe it off-label for seizures in dogs and cats; only give the form and dose your veterinarian prescribes.
Can I drink alcohol while taking levetiracetam?
Alcohol can increase drowsiness and dizziness and may affect seizure control, so ask your prescriber before drinking.

name: Levocetirizine
uses: Allergy relief.
how: An antihistamine that blocks H1 receptors.
avoid: People with kidney disease.
about: Levocetirizine is the active half of the cetirizine molecule, an antihistamine that has been used for allergies since the 2000s. It is sold over the counter as tablets and an oral solution. Prescribers sometimes ask for it compounded into capsules when a person needs a specific strength, a dye-free form, or a combination with cetirizine.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, trouble urinating, or severe drowsiness; also tell your prescriber about severe itching that starts after stopping long-term use.
interactions: Alcohol, sleep aids and other sedating medicines can add to drowsiness, and some medicines such as theophylline and ritonavir may change levocetirizine levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; antihistamines are sometimes used in pregnancy when needed.
tips: It is usually taken once in the evening, with or without food, which can help if it makes you sleepy.
Avoid alcohol and use caution driving until you know how it affects you.
Ask your prescriber before stopping after months of daily use, since some people get rebound itching.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules; people with kidney disease may need dose changes.
faqs: What is the difference between levocetirizine and cetirizine?
Levocetirizine is the active part of cetirizine, so it works the same way; some people tolerate one better than the other.
Can stopping levocetirizine cause itching?
Some people who stop after long-term daily use report intense itching, so talk with your prescriber about how to stop.

name: Levothyroxine (T4)
uses: Thyroid hormone replacement for hypothyroidism in people and dogs.
