side: Signs of too much thyroid hormone: fast heartbeat, restlessness, weight loss.
how: A synthetic form of T4, the main hormone the thyroid gland makes.
avoid: People or pets with untreated adrenal insufficiency or heart disease (start low).
about: Levothyroxine is a man-made version of thyroxine (T4), the main hormone made by the thyroid gland, and has been the standard treatment for an underactive thyroid for decades. It is also widely used in dogs with hypothyroidism. Compounded capsules can leave out dyes and fillers some people react to, slow-release capsules or combinations with T3 may be prescribed, and transdermal gels help pets that are hard to pill.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, severe shaking or restlessness, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Calcium, iron, antacids, magnesium, sucralfate, cholestyramine and soy or high-fiber foods can block absorption, and levothyroxine can change the effects of blood thinners and diabetes medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Thyroid hormone is important for a developing baby and needs often change in pregnancy, so do not stop it; tell your prescriber right away if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Hypothyroidism is common in dogs but rare in cats, which more often have an overactive thyroid. For transdermal gel, wear gloves and apply to the hairless inner ear, rotating ears as directed.
tips: Take it the same way every day, ideally on an empty stomach with water, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
Separate it by several hours from calcium, iron, antacids and other supplements.
Do not switch between products or forms without your prescriber, since small changes can affect your levels.
If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check thyroid blood levels a few weeks after starting or changing the dose, then periodically.
faqs: How long does levothyroxine take to work?
Some people feel better within a couple of weeks, but it often takes about six weeks for blood levels to settle, which is why labs are rechecked then.
Should I take levothyroxine in the morning or at night?
Most people take it in the morning on an empty stomach, but some prescribers allow bedtime dosing; consistency matters most.
Is levothyroxine used in dogs?
Yes, it is the usual treatment for hypothyroidism in dogs, and your veterinarian will adjust the dose based on blood tests.

name: Lidocaine
uses: Numbing for skin, mouth and procedures; in pain creams and mouthwashes.
side: Temporary numbness, local irritation. Use only as directed on large areas.
how: Blocks sodium channels in nerves to stop pain signals temporarily.
avoid: Applying to large areas, broken skin or under wraps unless directed. Too much can affect the heart and nervous system.
about: Lidocaine is a numbing medicine that has been used since the 1940s on the skin, in the mouth and for medical procedures. Many commercial creams, patches and gels exist. Prescribers ask for it compounded to combine it with other numbing or pain ingredients, to make mouthwashes, nasal sprays and suppositories, or to prepare forms suited to specific procedures or to pets.
conditions: Numbing before needle procedures or cosmetic treatments
Skin and mouth discomfort in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for ringing in the ears, metallic taste, numb lips or tongue that spreads, confusion, shaking, seizures, slow or irregular heartbeat, bluish skin or lips, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Using other numbing products at the same time adds to the total amount absorbed, and heart rhythm medicines such as amiodarone or mexiletine and some beta blockers can increase the risk of side effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical lidocaine used as directed is generally considered low risk in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but talk to your prescriber first.
petNotes: Cats are more sensitive to lidocaine than dogs, so only use products made for your pet and prevent licking of treated areas. Never use human numbing creams on pets without veterinary direction.
tips: Use only the amount directed and only on the area prescribed; don't spread it over large areas or cover it with plastic wrap or heat unless told to.
After using a mouth rinse, avoid eating or hot drinks until the numbness wears off so you don't bite or burn yourself.
Wash your hands after applying unless your hands are being treated.
Store out of reach of children and pets, since swallowing lidocaine can be dangerous.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How long does lidocaine cream take to work?
Numbing often starts within 20 to 60 minutes, depending on the product and where it is applied; follow the timing your prescriber gives you.
Can lidocaine cream be used on broken skin?
Broken skin absorbs more lidocaine, so only use it on wounds or open sores if your prescriber specifically directs it.
Is lidocaine safe for cats and dogs?
Veterinarians use lidocaine in pets, but cats are especially sensitive, so only use products and amounts your veterinarian prescribes.

name: Linezolid
uses: Resistant bacterial infections.
how: Blocks bacterial protein production; reserved for resistant infections.
avoid: Anyone taking MAO inhibitors or serotonin medicines.
about: Linezolid is an oxazolidinone antibiotic approved in 2000 for serious bacterial infections, especially those resistant to other antibiotics such as MRSA and VRE. It is kept in reserve to help slow resistance. Compounded capsules may be prescribed for specific doses, and veterinarians may use it off-label in pets with resistant infections when culture results show few other options.
conditions: Resistant skin and soft tissue infections
Resistant infections in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fever with confusion, agitation or muscle twitching, unusual bruising or bleeding, vision changes, numbness or tingling, fast breathing, or severe or bloody diarrhea.
interactions: Linezolid can cause dangerous reactions with MAO inhibitors, antidepressants and other serotonin medicines, some opioid pain medicines, decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, and large amounts of tyramine-rich foods like aged cheese and cured meats. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Information on use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Use in pets is off-label and generally limited to infections proven resistant by culture. Pets on behavior medicines or amitraz tick products need special review before starting.
tips: Finish the full course even if you or your pet feel better.
Give or take it with or without food at evenly spaced times.
Limit high-tyramine foods such as aged cheeses, cured meats, soy sauce and tap beer while taking it.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: For courses longer than about two weeks, your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check blood counts weekly and watch for vision or nerve changes.
faqs: Why is linezolid reserved for resistant infections?
Limiting its use helps keep bacteria from becoming resistant to it, so it stays available for infections that other antibiotics cannot treat.
Can I take antidepressants with linezolid?
Combining linezolid with serotonin-affecting antidepressants can cause serotonin syndrome, so your prescriber must review these first.

name: Liothyronine (T3)
uses: Thyroid hormone replacement, sometimes combined with T4 in custom capsules.
how: A synthetic form of T3, the active thyroid hormone.
avoid: People with heart disease or untreated adrenal insufficiency.
about: Liothyronine is a man-made form of triiodothyronine (T3), the active thyroid hormone the body makes from T4. It has been available for decades and acts faster and for a shorter time than levothyroxine. Prescribers sometimes ask for it compounded into slow-release capsules for steadier levels, or combined with T4 in a single capsule at a ratio they choose.
conditions: Hypothyroidism needing T4 and T3 together
Thyroid hormone support before thyroid scans
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat, shortness of breath, severe anxiety or shaking, fainting, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Calcium, iron, antacids and cholestyramine can block absorption, and liothyronine can change the effects of blood thinners, diabetes medicines and heart medicines such as digoxin. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Thyroid needs change in pregnancy and many prescribers prefer levothyroxine during this time; tell your prescriber right away if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Take it at the same times each day, and separate it by several hours from calcium, iron and antacids.
Swallow slow-release capsules whole; do not open or crush them.
Do not take extra doses for energy or weight changes; too much thyroid hormone can strain the heart.
If a dose is missed, take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check thyroid blood tests and may ask about heart rate and symptoms after any dose change.
faqs: What is the difference between T3 and T4?
T4 (levothyroxine) is the storage form the body converts as needed, while T3 (liothyronine) is the active form and works faster; some people are prescribed both.
Why would my prescriber choose slow-release T3?
Regular T3 is absorbed quickly, so a slow-release capsule may be prescribed to give steadier levels through the day.

name: Loratadine
uses: Allergy relief.
how: A non-drowsy antihistamine that blocks H1 receptors.
avoid: People with liver disease (lower dose). Some commercial forms contain decongestants unsafe for pets.
about: Loratadine is a non-drowsy antihistamine that has been used for allergies since the 1990s and is sold over the counter. Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for itchy dogs and cats. Compounded flavored liquids and capsules allow doses for small pets and remove ingredients pets should not have, such as xylitol sweeteners or added decongestants.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast or pounding heartbeat, fainting, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Some medicines, such as ketoconazole, erythromycin and cimetidine, can raise loratadine levels, and combining it with other antihistamines or sedatives can increase drowsiness. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Loratadine is one of the antihistamines more often considered in pregnancy, but talk to your prescriber first if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Never give pets loratadine products labeled D, because they contain pseudoephedrine, which can be life-threatening to dogs and cats. Antihistamines alone may not control itching in many pets, so your veterinarian may combine treatments.
tips: Give or take it once a day at about the same time, with or without food.
Shake the suspension well and measure with the syringe provided.
Check labels on any store-bought allergy medicine before giving it to a pet, and avoid products with decongestants or xylitol.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Can I give my dog Claritin?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe loratadine off-label for dogs, but never use Claritin-D or other products with decongestants, and let your veterinarian choose the dose.
Does loratadine cause drowsiness?
It is less likely to cause drowsiness than older antihistamines, though some people and pets still feel sleepy.

name: Lovastatin
uses: Topical cream with cholesterol for porokeratosis and other rare skin conditions.
how: Blocks cholesterol production in the skin, used with topical cholesterol for rare genetic skin conditions.
avoid: Pregnancy.
about: Lovastatin is a statin that has been taken by mouth to lower cholesterol since the 1980s. Dermatologists found that applying it to the skin together with cholesterol can help correct a cholesterol-building problem in the skin seen in some rare inherited conditions. No commercial cream exists, so this topical use is off-label and requires compounding.
conditions: Other rare inherited scaling skin conditions (off-label)
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction or a blistering, spreading or painful rash where the cream is applied.
interactions: Very little is expected to be absorbed through the skin, so interactions with medicines taken by mouth are unlikely, but using other irritating skin products on the same area can increase redness. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Avoid using it if you are pregnant, as with oral statins; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to the affected patches as directed and wash your hands afterward.
Use it consistently, since results tend to develop over several weeks.
Protect treated skin from the sun, especially if porokeratosis appears on sun-exposed areas.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits with your dermatologist to check how the skin is responding.
faqs: Why is cholesterol added to lovastatin cream?
In some rare conditions the skin cannot build cholesterol properly, so the cream supplies cholesterol while lovastatin reduces buildup of other substances that can damage skin.
How long until lovastatin cream shows results?
Many people need several weeks to a few months of regular use, and your dermatologist will judge progress.

name: Magic mouthwash
uses: Blends of an antihistamine, antacid, numbing agent and sometimes antifungal or steroid for mouth sores, including from chemotherapy.
side: Temporary numbness, altered taste. Do not eat or drink right after use.
how: Combines a numbing agent, an antacid coating and an antihistamine, sometimes with an antifungal or steroid, to soothe mouth sores.
avoid: Swallowing the rinse when directed to spit, and eating or drinking before the numbness wears off.
about: Magic mouthwash is a general name for prescription mouth rinses that mix several medicines, such as an antihistamine, an antacid, a numbing agent and sometimes an antifungal, steroid or coating agent. There is no single standard recipe, so prescribers choose the ingredients for each patient. It has long been used to ease painful mouth sores during cancer treatment and other mouth conditions.
conditions: Mouth sores from chemotherapy or radiation
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, trouble swallowing or choking, or for mouth sores with fever, white patches that keep spreading or sores that bleed heavily.
interactions: Interactions depend on the ingredients; blends with diphenhydramine can add to drowsiness from alcohol and sedating medicines, and blends with an antacid can affect absorption of other medicines taken at the same time. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Whether a mouthwash is suitable in pregnancy depends on its ingredients; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Shake well before each use and swish for the time directed, then spit or swallow exactly as your prescriber instructs.
Wait until numbness wears off before eating or drinking hot liquids to avoid choking, biting or burns.
Space doses from other medicines taken by mouth by about an hour unless told otherwise.
Check the label for storage, as some blends need to be refrigerated and have a short beyond-use date.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but tell your care team if mouth sores are not improving or make it hard to eat or drink.
faqs: Do I swallow or spit out magic mouthwash?
It depends on the ingredients and what is being treated, so follow the swish-and-spit or swish-and-swallow directions on your label.
How often can I use magic mouthwash?
Your prescriber sets how often to use it, often a few times a day before meals; do not use more than directed because some ingredients can build up.
Can children use magic mouthwash?
Some blends are used in children, but young children may swallow too much numbing medicine, so only use a product prescribed for the child.

name: Magnesium
uses: Magnesium supplement.
how: A mineral needed for muscle, nerve and heart function.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease.
about: Magnesium is an essential mineral that helps muscles, nerves and the heart work normally. Low levels can happen with poor intake, digestive problems, some medicines such as diuretics and acid reducers, and certain conditions in pets. Compounded capsules let a prescriber or veterinarian choose a specific magnesium salt and amount without fillers, or combine it with other nutrients.
conditions: Magnesium loss from diuretics or acid reducers
Low magnesium in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for muscle weakness, a slow or irregular heartbeat, very low energy, confusion or trouble breathing, which can mean magnesium levels are too high, especially with kidney disease.
interactions: Magnesium can block absorption of some antibiotics (tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones), osteoporosis medicines (bisphosphonates), levothyroxine and some HIV medicines, so these need to be spaced apart. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Magnesium from food and standard supplements is commonly used in pregnancy, but talk to your prescriber about the right amount if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Pets with kidney disease can build up magnesium, so supplements should only be given under veterinary direction. Capsules can be opened and mixed into a small amount of food if your veterinarian approves.
tips: Give or take it with food to reduce stomach upset and diarrhea.
Space it at least a few hours apart from antibiotics, thyroid medicine and other medicines it can bind.
If diarrhea develops, contact your prescriber or veterinarian, as a different magnesium form may be better tolerated.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood magnesium and kidney function, especially with kidney disease or long-term use.
faqs: Which form of magnesium is best?
Forms differ in how well they are absorbed and how likely they are to cause diarrhea, so your prescriber chooses based on the reason you need it.
Can I take magnesium at bedtime?
Many people take it in the evening, but the best timing depends on your other medicines, which may need to be spaced apart.

name: Marbofloxacin
uses: Bacterial infections in pets.
how: A fluoroquinolone that blocks bacterial DNA copying.
avoid: Young growing dogs and pets with seizures.
about: Marbofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic developed for veterinary use and approved for dogs and cats in the US. It is used for skin, urinary and soft tissue infections and is often chosen based on culture results. Veterinarians may ask for it compounded into flavored liquids, chewable treats or ear packs when tablets are hard to give or a different dose or form is needed.
conditions: Skin and soft tissue infections in dogs and cats
Urinary tract infections in dogs and cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for seizures, wobbliness, dilated pupils or vision changes, lameness or joint swelling, severe vomiting or diarrhea, or signs of an allergic reaction such as facial swelling or hives.
interactions: Antacids, sucralfate, iron, zinc and calcium supplements can block absorption, and marbofloxacin may raise theophylline levels; NSAIDs may increase the risk of seizures in some pets. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Fluoroquinolones can affect cartilage in young, growing dogs, especially large breeds, so they are usually avoided in puppies. Cats should receive only the dose prescribed, since high doses of drugs in this class have been linked to vision problems in cats.
tips: Give with or without food, but space it at least two hours apart from antacids, sucralfate or mineral supplements.
Finish the full course even if your pet looks better.
Shake suspensions well and keep chewable treats out of reach so pets don't eat extras.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may recheck the infected area or a urine culture after treatment to confirm the infection has cleared.
faqs: Is marbofloxacin safe for cats?
It is approved for cats at prescribed doses; cats should never get more than directed because high doses of this drug class can affect vision.
How quickly does marbofloxacin work?
Many pets look better within a few days, but the full course is needed to clear the infection.
Can puppies take marbofloxacin?
It is usually avoided in young, growing dogs because it may affect developing joints; your veterinarian decides if it is needed.

name: Maropitant
uses: Vomiting and motion sickness in dogs and cats.
how: Blocks substance P at the vomiting center in the brain.
avoid: Very young puppies and pets with liver disease.
about: Maropitant is an anti-nausea medicine developed for dogs and cats and approved in the US in 2007. It works in the brain's vomiting center and is used for vomiting from many causes and for motion sickness in dogs. Compounded flavored liquids, treats, transdermal gels and other forms help when tablets are hard to give or a pet needs a dose tablets can't provide.
conditions: Nausea with kidney disease in cats (off-label)
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for repeated vomiting despite the medicine, blood in vomit or stool, a swollen or painful belly, extreme tiredness, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Maropitant is highly protein bound, so veterinarians use care with other highly protein-bound medicines such as NSAIDs, some heart medicines, seizure medicines and behavior medicines. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Because maropitant stops vomiting but does not fix the cause, call your veterinarian if your pet keeps vomiting or swallowed something it shouldn't have. For motion sickness, it is usually given ahead of travel on a light meal, and gel forms should be applied with gloves.
tips: For car trips, give it ahead of travel as your veterinarian directs, with a small amount of food rather than on a totally empty stomach.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to the inner ear and wipe away old gel before the next dose.
Shake liquids well and store treats out of reach.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses, but your veterinarian may run tests to find and treat the cause of vomiting.
faqs: Can maropitant be used for car sickness in dogs?
Yes, it is commonly used for motion sickness in dogs, given ahead of travel as your veterinarian directs.
Is maropitant safe for cats?
It is approved for vomiting in cats and is also used off-label for nausea in some cats with ongoing illness, under veterinary guidance.
Does maropitant help with appetite?
By easing nausea, some pets eat better, but it is not an appetite stimulant itself.

name: Mastic gum
uses: Traditional supplement for stomach support.
how: A plant resin traditionally used to soothe the stomach.
avoid: People allergic to pistachio or mastic trees.
about: Mastic gum is a resin from the mastic tree, which grows mainly on the Greek island of Chios. It has been used for centuries as a chewing gum and as a traditional remedy for stomach complaints. It is a dietary supplement rather than a prescription medicine, and a compounded oral liquid can be useful for people who want a measured amount in a form that is easy to take.
conditions: Stomach support with H. pylori care (supplemental)
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the lips or throat, or trouble breathing, especially if you have tree nut or pistachio allergies.
interactions: Interactions with medicines are not well studied, so tell your prescriber before using it with stomach medicines, blood thinners or other supplements. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is not enough safety information for mastic gum in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so avoid it unless your prescriber says it is okay.
tips: Shake the liquid well and measure each dose with an oral syringe or dosing cup.
Take it at the times directed, often before meals for stomach support.
Let your prescriber know if stomach symptoms continue or get worse, since ongoing indigestion should be checked.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Can mastic gum replace treatment for H. pylori?
No. Mastic gum is a supplement and should not replace antibiotic treatment your prescriber recommends for H. pylori.
Is mastic gum the same as pistachio?
Mastic comes from a close relative of the pistachio tree, so people allergic to pistachios may react to it.

name: Mebendazole
uses: Intestinal worms.
how: Blocks worms from absorbing sugar, which kills them.
avoid: Pregnancy and liver disease.
about: Mebendazole is a dewormer that has been used since the 1970s to treat intestinal worms such as pinworms, roundworms, hookworms and whipworms. Commercial chewable tablets are available for people, and related drugs are more common in pets. Compounded capsules may be prescribed when a specific dose is needed, the commercial product is hard to get, or a veterinarian prescribes it for a pet.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a seizure, yellowing of the skin or eyes, a severe or blistering rash, or fever with sore throat, which can be signs of a rare blood problem.
interactions: Taking mebendazole with metronidazole has been linked to severe skin reactions and should be avoided, and cimetidine can raise mebendazole levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Mebendazole is generally avoided in pregnancy, especially the first trimester; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians more often use related drugs such as fenbendazole in pets. Rare liver reactions have been reported in dogs given mebendazole, so give only as prescribed.
tips: Taking it with food, especially a meal with some fat, can help it work in the gut.
For pinworms, wash bedding and underwear in hot water and have everyone wash hands often to prevent reinfection.
A second dose a couple of weeks later is sometimes prescribed; follow your label exactly.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses, but longer treatment may include blood counts and liver tests.
faqs: Does the whole family need treatment for pinworms?
Pinworms spread easily in households, so prescribers often treat everyone in the home at the same time.
Can dogs take mebendazole?
It is sometimes prescribed off-label for dogs, but other dewormers are more common; only give it under your veterinarian's direction.

name: Meclizine
uses: Motion sickness and vertigo.
how: An antihistamine that calms the inner ear and vomiting center.
avoid: People with glaucoma or urinary retention.
about: Meclizine is an antihistamine that has been used for decades to prevent motion sickness and ease dizziness from inner ear problems. It is sold as tablets, some over the counter. Veterinarians also prescribe it off-label for dogs and cats with motion sickness or balance problems, and a flavored liquid makes dosing easier for pets and for people who can't swallow tablets.
conditions: Vestibular disease in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a fast or irregular heartbeat, severe confusion, trouble urinating, eye pain with blurred vision, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Alcohol, sleep aids, other antihistamines and sedating medicines can add to drowsiness, and other medicines with drying (anticholinergic) effects can increase dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Meclizine has been used for nausea in pregnancy, but talk to your prescriber before taking it if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In pets, meclizine is used off-label for nausea and dizziness from vestibular disease and travel. Some pets become sleepy or have a dry mouth; let your veterinarian know if your pet stops eating.
tips: For motion sickness, give or take it about an hour before travel.
Shake the suspension well and measure with the syringe provided.
Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how drowsy it makes you.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules, especially if dizziness continues.
faqs: Can I give my dog meclizine for car sickness?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for car sickness and dizziness in dogs; ask your veterinarian for the right form and dose.
Does meclizine make you sleepy?
It can cause drowsiness, though usually less than some other motion sickness medicines.

name: Melatonin
uses: Sleep support in people; hair loss and anxiety support in dogs.
how: Mimics the hormone the body makes to signal nighttime and regulate sleep cycles.
avoid: People with autoimmune conditions or seizure disorders. Some commercial products contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.
about: Melatonin is a hormone the brain releases at night to signal that it is time to sleep. It is sold as a dietary supplement for people and is used off-label by veterinarians for certain types of hair loss and for anxiety in dogs. Compounded flavored liquids let doses be measured precisely and avoid xylitol and other ingredients found in some store products that can harm pets.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, severe confusion or unusual behavior, or a seizure.
interactions: Melatonin can add to the effects of sedatives and alcohol, may affect blood thinners, diabetes medicines and immune-suppressing medicines, and fluvoxamine can greatly raise melatonin levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is not enough safety information on melatonin supplements in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber before using it.
petNotes: Never give pets melatonin products that contain xylitol, which can cause dangerously low blood sugar and liver damage in dogs. For hair loss, results in dogs can take a few months to show.
tips: For sleep, take it a short time before bedtime and keep lights low afterward.
Shake the suspension well and measure with the syringe provided.
Avoid driving or other tasks that need alertness after a dose.
For noise anxiety in dogs, your veterinarian may suggest giving it before an expected event like fireworks or storms.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Is melatonin safe for dogs?
Veterinarians often recommend it off-label for dogs, but products with xylitol are dangerous; use a pet-safe product and the dose your veterinarian gives.
Can I take melatonin every night?
Many people use it short term; talk to your prescriber about long-term use and about any sleep problem that lasts more than a few weeks.
How long does melatonin take to work?
It often takes 30 minutes to two hours to cause sleepiness, while effects on hair coat in dogs may take months.

name: Meloxicam
uses: Arthritis and pain.
how: An NSAID that blocks COX-2 more than COX-1 to reduce inflammation.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease, ulcers or dehydration, or taking steroids.
about: Meloxicam is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used since the 1990s for arthritis pain and inflammation in people, and approved separately for dogs and, in limited situations, cats. Because pets need very precise doses based on weight, veterinarians often prescribe a flavored liquid, and compounding can provide strengths or flavors that suit a specific animal.
conditions: Joint pain in cats (off-label, closely monitored)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, stomach pain, decreased urination or increased thirst, yellowing of the skin, eyes or gums, chest pain, weakness on one side, or a severe skin rash.
interactions: Do not combine meloxicam with other NSAIDs, aspirin or steroids such as prednisone, and use caution with blood thinners, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, SSRIs, lithium and methotrexate. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: NSAIDs are usually avoided from around the middle of pregnancy on because they can affect the baby's kidneys and heart, and they may make it harder to get pregnant; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats are very sensitive to NSAIDs, and repeated dosing has been linked to kidney injury, so long-term use in cats is a careful veterinary decision. Never give a pet a human NSAID or switch between products without your veterinarian.
tips: Give or take it with food to lower the chance of stomach upset.
Shake the suspension well and use the exact syringe or dropper provided, since pet doses are very small.
Make sure pets have plenty of fresh water, and stop and call the veterinarian if your pet stops eating or vomits.
Allow a washout time, as your prescriber or veterinarian directs, when switching from another NSAID or a steroid.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will usually check kidney and liver bloodwork before and during long-term use.
faqs: Can I give my dog meloxicam meant for people?
No. Pet doses are much smaller and must be measured precisely, so only use the meloxicam product your veterinarian prescribes.
How long does meloxicam take to work?
Pain relief may start within a few hours, but it can take a week or two of regular use to see the full effect on arthritis.
Is meloxicam safe for cats?
Cats are especially sensitive to NSAIDs; veterinarians may use it carefully in some cats with close kidney monitoring.

name: Metformin
uses: Type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance.
how: Lowers the liver's sugar production and helps the body respond to insulin.
avoid: People with kidney disease, severe liver disease or heavy alcohol use, and before contrast X-ray studies.
about: Metformin is a biguanide that has been a first-choice medicine for type 2 diabetes for decades. Taken by mouth, it lowers blood sugar and improves the body's response to insulin. Prescribers also ask for it compounded into topical creams, often with other ingredients, for skin and hair concerns; topical use is off-label and less studied than oral use.
conditions: Melasma and dark spots in topical blends (off-label)
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of lactic acidosis with oral metformin, such as unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, stomach pain with vomiting, unusual sleepiness, dizziness or a slow or irregular heartbeat, or for signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: With oral metformin, avoid heavy alcohol use and tell your care team before any scan that uses iodinated contrast dye; topiramate, some heart and acid medicines and other diabetes medicines can also affect it. Topical creams reach the blood in much smaller amounts. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Oral metformin is sometimes used in pregnancy under close supervision, and less is known about topical metformin; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply the cream as a thin layer only to the area prescribed and wash your hands afterward.
Use sunscreen daily when using metformin in skin-lightening blends.
If you also take metformin by mouth, tell your prescriber so they know your full exposure.
monitoring: With oral use, your prescriber checks blood sugar, kidney function and sometimes vitamin B12; routine monitoring is usually not needed for topical creams.
faqs: Why would metformin be used in a skin cream?
Some prescribers use topical metformin off-label for dark spots or hair thinning because of its effects on skin cell signaling; research is still limited.
Does topical metformin lower blood sugar?
Much less reaches the bloodstream from a cream than from a tablet, but tell your prescriber if you have diabetes or take other diabetes medicines.

name: Methenamine hippurate
uses: Helps prevent recurring urinary tract infections.
how: Turns into formaldehyde in acidic urine, which prevents bacteria from growing.
avoid: People or pets with kidney or liver disease, or taking sulfa drugs.
about: Methenamine hippurate has been used for many decades to help prevent repeat urinary tract infections. In acidic urine it slowly releases formaldehyde, which keeps bacteria from growing in the bladder, and bacteria do not readily become resistant to it. It is not used to treat an active infection. Compounded capsules may help when commercial tablets are unavailable or a pet needs a specific dose.
conditions: Recurring bladder infections in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, blood in the urine, painful urination that gets worse, or fever and back pain, which can mean an active kidney infection.
interactions: Sulfa drugs can form crystals in the urine with methenamine and should not be combined, and urine-alkalinizing products such as potassium citrate, sodium bicarbonate and some antacids can stop it from working. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding; methenamine has been used in pregnancy, but your prescriber should weigh it for you.
petNotes: Use in dogs and cats is off-label, usually to help prevent repeat bladder infections. It needs acidic urine to work, so your veterinarian may consider your pet's diet and urine pH.
tips: Give or take it at evenly spaced times; it works best when used every day without gaps.
Drink plenty of fluids, but avoid large amounts of citrus juices, antacids and baking soda that make urine less acidic.
Do not use it in place of antibiotics for an active infection; call your prescriber or veterinarian if UTI symptoms return.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check urine tests periodically and, with long-term use, liver tests.
faqs: Is methenamine an antibiotic?
It is a urinary antiseptic rather than a traditional antibiotic, and bacteria are not known to become resistant to it the same way.
How long does methenamine take to work?
It works only while it is in acidic urine, so it is taken regularly as prevention rather than for quick relief of an active infection.

name: Methimazole
uses: Hyperthyroidism in cats, including transdermal gel applied to the ear.
side: Vomiting, decreased appetite, facial itching; requires blood monitoring.
how: Blocks the thyroid gland from making thyroid hormone.
avoid: Cats with kidney disease need close monitoring, since treating hyperthyroidism can reveal kidney problems.
about: Methimazole blocks the thyroid gland from making too much hormone and has been the most common medicine for hyperthyroid cats for many years. Commercial tablets exist, including a veterinary-approved product, but many cats are difficult to pill. Compounded transdermal gel rubbed on the inner ear, flavored liquids and chewable treats make daily dosing easier for cats and their owners.
conditions: Stabilizing cats before radioiodine or surgery
Hyperthyroidism with kidney disease in cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for severe facial itching or scratching wounds, yellow gums or eyes, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever, extreme tiredness, or vomiting and not eating for more than a day.
interactions: Methimazole can change the effects of blood thinners, theophylline, digoxin and some heart medicines such as beta blockers as thyroid levels come down. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: For transdermal gel, wear gloves, apply to the hairless inner ear flap, alternate ears and gently wipe away old gel before the next dose. People who are pregnant should avoid handling methimazole, and children and other pets should not touch the cat's treated ear right after dosing.
tips: Give it at the same times each day; transdermal gel should be rubbed in until absorbed.
Wear gloves when handling gel or crushing treats, and wash your hands afterward.
Watch for redness or crusting on the ear and tell your veterinarian if it develops.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check thyroid levels, kidney values, blood counts and liver enzymes a few weeks after starting and after dose changes, then regularly.
faqs: Does methimazole ear gel work as well as pills for cats?
Many cats do well on transdermal gel, though some may take longer to reach target levels; your veterinarian will adjust based on blood tests.
Will my cat need methimazole for life?
Methimazole controls hyperthyroidism but does not make it go away, so it is usually given long term unless the cat has radioiodine treatment or surgery.
Why does my cat's kidney value change after starting methimazole?
An overactive thyroid can hide kidney disease, so kidney values may rise once thyroid levels drop; your veterinarian monitors this closely.

name: Methocarbamol
uses: Muscle spasm.
how: A muscle relaxant that acts on the central nervous system.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease (injectable forms).
about: Methocarbamol is a muscle relaxant used since the 1950s for painful muscle spasms in people, and it is also approved for dogs and cats. Veterinarians use it for back and muscle injuries and to help control tremors from certain poisonings. Compounded flavored liquids and capsules make it easier to give accurate doses to pets and to people who can't swallow tablets.
conditions: Muscle tremors from toxins in pets
Muscle strain in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for extreme sleepiness, trouble breathing, fainting, a seizure, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Alcohol, sleep aids, sedatives, opioid pain medicines and other drowsiness-causing medicines can add to its sedating effects. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been well established, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians sometimes use it to help control tremors in cats exposed to permethrin dog flea products, which should never be used on cats. Some pets drool or become wobbly; let your veterinarian know if this happens.
tips: Give or take it with food if it upsets the stomach.
Don't drive or do risky tasks until you know how drowsy it makes you.
Urine may turn dark brown, black or green; this is harmless but tell your prescriber if you are concerned.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Is methocarbamol a narcotic?
No. It is a muscle relaxant, not an opioid, but it can still cause drowsiness.
Why did my urine change color on methocarbamol?
Methocarbamol can turn urine dark brown, black, blue or green, which is usually harmless.
Can dogs and cats take methocarbamol?
Yes, it is approved for use in dogs and cats, and your veterinarian sets the dose.

name: Metoclopramide
uses: Nausea and slow stomach emptying.
how: Blocks dopamine to reduce nausea and speeds stomach emptying.
avoid: People or pets with a bowel blockage, seizures or pheochromocytoma.
about: Metoclopramide has been used since the 1980s to reduce nausea and help the stomach empty faster. It is prescribed for people with slow stomach emptying and reflux and is used by veterinarians for vomiting and stomach motility problems in dogs and cats. Compounded oral liquids, flavored suspensions and transdermal gels help with precise dosing and with pets that won't take tablets.
conditions: Acid reflux not helped by other medicines
Vomiting and stomach motility problems in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for uncontrolled or repeated movements of the face, tongue or limbs, muscle stiffness with high fever, confusion, a seizure, or in people, depression or thoughts of self-harm.
interactions: Avoid combining it with other dopamine-blocking medicines such as antipsychotics, and use caution with sedatives, alcohol and serotonin medicines; opioid pain medicines and anticholinergic medicines can work against its effect on the gut. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Metoclopramide has been used for nausea in pregnancy, but talk to your prescriber first if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Some pets become restless, anxious or show behavior changes, which should be reported to your veterinarian. It should not be used if a blockage of the stomach or intestines is suspected, such as after swallowing a toy.
tips: Give or take it about 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime, or as directed.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to pets and rotate ears.
In people, long-term use beyond a few months is generally avoided because of the risk of a movement disorder.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will watch for abnormal movements, mood or behavior changes and decide how long treatment should continue.
faqs: How long can I take metoclopramide?
Use in people is usually limited to 12 weeks or less because longer use raises the risk of a lasting movement disorder.
Can my dog take metoclopramide for vomiting?
Veterinarians often use it in dogs, but only after ruling out a blockage, so call your veterinarian before giving it.

name: Metronidazole
uses: Anaerobic and parasitic infections and diarrhea; also in topical creams.
side: Nausea, metallic taste, decreased appetite; bitter taste in pets.
how: Damages DNA in anaerobic bacteria and some parasites.
avoid: Pregnancy (early), liver disease, and alcohol use. High doses can cause neurologic signs in pets.
about: Metronidazole is an antibiotic and antiparasitic medicine used since the 1960s for infections caused by anaerobic bacteria and parasites such as Giardia. It is widely used in dogs and cats, often off-label for diarrhea. The tablets taste very bitter, so compounded flavored liquids and treats make it easier to give, and topical creams are prescribed for skin conditions such as rosacea.
conditions: C. difficile and other anaerobic infections
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a seizure, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, a severe or blistering rash, confusion, or in pets, a head tilt, wobbly walking, flicking eye movements or trouble standing.
interactions: Do not drink alcohol during treatment and for a few days after, and avoid disulfiram; metronidazole can increase the effects of warfarin, lithium and busulfan. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Metronidazole is usually avoided in the first trimester and its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is a prescriber decision; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Neurologic signs are more likely with high doses or long courses, and they usually improve after the medicine is stopped; call your veterinarian if they appear. The bitter taste causes drooling and food refusal, which flavored forms can help reduce.
tips: Give or take it with food to reduce stomach upset.
Finish the full course even if symptoms improve.
Shake liquids well, and do not crush or split tablets for pets, which makes the taste worse.
For topical creams, apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin and avoid the eyes.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for short courses, but your prescriber or veterinarian may recheck stool or symptoms after treatment.
faqs: Can I drink alcohol while taking metronidazole?
No. Alcohol can cause flushing, nausea, vomiting and a fast heartbeat with metronidazole, so avoid it during treatment and for a few days after.
Why does my pet drool after taking metronidazole?
The medicine is very bitter; flavored suspensions or treats can make it easier to give.
How fast does metronidazole work for diarrhea in dogs?
Many dogs improve within a few days, but your veterinarian may want to find the underlying cause if diarrhea continues.

name: Mexiletine
uses: Heart rhythm disorders in people and dogs.
how: Blocks sodium channels in the heart to steady abnormal rhythms.
avoid: People or pets with certain heart blocks or liver disease.
about: Mexiletine is an oral heart rhythm medicine related to lidocaine that has been used since the 1980s for dangerous ventricular rhythm problems. The original brand was discontinued in the US, and veterinarians also use it off-label in dogs, such as Boxers and Dobermans with heart rhythm disease. Compounded capsules and liquids allow specific doses for dogs and for people who need a different form.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, a new or worse irregular heartbeat, chest pain, shortness of breath, a seizure, yellowing of the skin or eyes, a severe rash with fever, or unusual bruising or infections.
interactions: Theophylline levels can rise with mexiletine, and medicines such as cimetidine and fluvoxamine can raise mexiletine levels, while phenobarbital, phenytoin and rifampin can lower them; other heart rhythm medicines need careful planning. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Information on use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In dogs, it is often given with another heart medicine such as sotalol or atenolol. Giving it with food helps prevent vomiting and loss of appetite, which are common in dogs.
tips: Give or take it with food or milk to reduce stomach upset.
Use evenly spaced doses every day and do not stop suddenly without your prescriber or veterinarian.
Swallow or give slow-release capsules whole.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check heart rhythm with ECGs or Holter monitors and may check liver tests and blood counts.
faqs: Why is mexiletine used in Boxer dogs?
Boxers can develop a heart muscle disease that causes dangerous rhythms, and veterinarians may prescribe mexiletine off-label to help control them.
What should I do if my dog vomits after mexiletine?
Giving it with a meal often helps; call your veterinarian if vomiting continues or your dog stops eating.

name: Milk thistle
uses: Liver support supplement.
how: Contains silymarin, an antioxidant thought to protect liver cells.
avoid: People with ragweed allergies.
about: Milk thistle is a flowering plant whose seeds contain silymarin, a group of antioxidant compounds. It has been used for centuries as a traditional liver remedy and is sold today as a dietary supplement for people and pets. Veterinarians often recommend it alongside other liver support such as SAM-e, and compounded liquids and capsules allow measured doses for different-sized patients.
conditions: Liver disease in dogs and cats (supportive)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, yellowing of the skin, eyes or gums, dark urine, or vomiting that won't stop.
interactions: Milk thistle may lower blood sugar and add to the effect of diabetes medicines, and it may affect how the liver processes some medicines, including blood thinners. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is not enough safety information on milk thistle in pregnancy or breastfeeding, so avoid it unless your prescriber recommends it.
petNotes: Milk thistle is commonly used as supportive care for dogs and cats with liver disease, but it does not replace a diagnosis and treatment plan. Absorption is better on an empty stomach, though giving it with a little food is fine if your pet's stomach gets upset.
tips: Shake liquids well and measure with the syringe provided.
Give or take it consistently each day for the best chance of benefit.
Tell your prescriber or veterinarian before starting it if you or your pet has diabetes or takes daily medicines.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may recheck liver bloodwork to follow the underlying condition.
faqs: Is milk thistle safe for dogs and cats?
It is generally well tolerated in pets and commonly used by veterinarians, but give it under veterinary guidance.
What is the difference between milk thistle and silymarin?
Silymarin is the main group of active compounds extracted from milk thistle seeds; products vary in how much they contain.

name: Minocycline
uses: Bacterial infections, acne and rosacea.
how: A tetracycline antibiotic that stops bacteria from making proteins.
avoid: Children under 8 and pregnancy.
about: Minocycline is a tetracycline antibiotic used since the 1970s for bacterial infections and, especially in people, for acne and rosacea, where it also calms inflammation. Veterinarians use it in dogs and cats, sometimes as an alternative to doxycycline for tick-borne diseases. A compounded flavored suspension makes dosing easier for children, people who can't swallow pills and pets.
conditions: Bacterial infections in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a severe headache with vision changes, a severe rash or blistering skin, joint pain with fever or rash, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or severe or bloody diarrhea.
interactions: Antacids, calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc and dairy can block absorption, and it should not be combined with isotretinoin; minocycline may also increase the effect of blood thinners. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Minocycline is not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding because it can affect a baby's developing teeth and bones; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant or planning pregnancy.
petNotes: Liquid forms should be followed by food or a little water to help it pass through the esophagus, especially in cats. Dogs may vomit if it is given on an empty stomach.
tips: Give or take it with a full glass of water or followed by food, and stay upright for a while afterward.
Space it two to three hours from dairy, antacids and mineral supplements.
Use sunscreen and avoid tanning beds, since it can make skin more sensitive to sun.
Finish the full course for infections even if you or your pet feel better.
monitoring: For long-term use, such as for acne, your prescriber may check liver tests and watch for skin or nail color changes.
faqs: How long does minocycline take to work for acne?
Improvement is usually gradual over several weeks, and your prescriber will decide how long to continue.
Can minocycline cause skin discoloration?
Long-term use can cause blue-gray discoloration of the skin, nails or teeth in some people, so tell your prescriber if you notice it.

name: Minoxidil
uses: Hair regrowth, as topical solutions or low-dose oral capsules.
side: Scalp irritation, unwanted hair growth; oral forms can cause fluid retention or fast heartbeat.
how: Widens blood vessels and extends the hair's growth phase, which can thicken thinning hair.
avoid: People with heart disease or low blood pressure (oral forms). Very toxic to cats; keep topical forms away from pets.
about: Minoxidil was first used in the 1970s as a blood pressure pill, and its side effect of hair growth led to topical products for hair loss. Prescribers now also use very low oral doses off-label for thinning hair. Compounding allows topical solutions, foams and creams combined with other hair ingredients, without certain alcohols or propylene glycol, and oral capsules in strengths not sold commercially.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, a fast or pounding heartbeat, shortness of breath, swelling of the hands, feet or face, sudden weight gain, or fainting, especially with oral minoxidil.
interactions: Oral minoxidil can add to the effect of other blood pressure medicines and diuretics; topical products are less absorbed but should not be used with other scalp products that increase absorption unless directed. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Minoxidil is not recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply topical forms to a dry scalp, let them dry fully before bed, and wash your hands afterward.
Keep topical minoxidil away from pets, including on pillows and hands, since even small amounts can be fatal to cats.
Expect some extra shedding in the first weeks; this often settles as new growth begins.
Take oral capsules at the same time daily and report swelling or a racing heart.
monitoring: With oral use, your prescriber may check blood pressure, heart rate and weight; routine monitoring is usually not needed for topical use.
faqs: How long does minoxidil take to work?
Hair changes usually take three to six months of regular use, and stopping it often leads to loss of the new growth.
Is minoxidil dangerous to cats?
Yes. Cats can be poisoned by very small amounts of topical minoxidil, even from licking a person's skin or bedding, so keep it well away from them.
What is the difference between oral and topical minoxidil?
Topical minoxidil works on the scalp, while low-dose oral minoxidil is prescribed off-label and acts through the whole body, so it needs more monitoring.

name: Mirtazapine
uses: Depression and sleep in people; appetite stimulation and nausea control in cats and dogs, including transdermal gels.
side: Drowsiness, increased appetite, vocalization in cats.
how: Increases serotonin and norepinephrine signaling and blocks histamine, which boosts appetite and reduces nausea.
avoid: Pets or people with liver or kidney disease (lower doses needed), and anyone on MAO inhibitors.
about: Mirtazapine is an antidepressant approved in the 1990s for people, where its sleepiness and appetite effects can help some patients. Veterinarians use it as an appetite stimulant and anti-nausea medicine in cats and dogs, and an ear ointment is approved for cats that are not eating well and losing body condition. Compounded transdermal gels and flavored suspensions allow small doses and avoid pilling sick pets.
conditions: Nausea in pets with kidney disease (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fever with agitation, shaking or muscle stiffness, fever or sore throat that may mean low white blood cells, a severe rash, or in people, thoughts of self-harm or sudden mood changes.
interactions: Never combine it with MAO inhibitors, and use caution with other serotonin medicines such as SSRIs, triptans and some opioid pain medicines, as well as alcohol and sedatives; in pets, amitraz tick products, selegiline and cyproheptadine also matter. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding, since untreated depression and the medicine both carry risks.
petNotes: Cats may become vocal, restless or more affectionate after a dose, which usually passes. For ear gel, wear gloves and alternate ears, and lower or less frequent doses are often needed for cats with kidney or liver disease.
tips: In people, it is usually taken at bedtime because it causes sleepiness.
Do not stop it suddenly without your prescriber, since withdrawal symptoms can occur.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to pets and wash your hands afterward.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check how mood and sleep respond, and your veterinarian will follow your pet's appetite and weight and may check kidney values.
faqs: How fast does mirtazapine increase a cat's appetite?
Many cats start eating within hours to a day, but your veterinarian will want to know if your cat still isn't eating.
Does mirtazapine make you sleepy?
Yes, sleepiness is common, especially when starting, so it is usually taken at bedtime.
Why is my cat meowing more on mirtazapine?
Vocalizing and restlessness are known side effects in cats; tell your veterinarian, who may adjust the dose.

name: Montelukast
uses: Asthma and allergies.
how: Blocks leukotrienes, inflammatory signals that tighten airways.
avoid: People with a history of depression or mood changes.
about: Montelukast is a leukotriene blocker approved in the late 1990s to help control asthma and allergy symptoms. It is taken daily and is not a rescue medicine. Commercial tablets, chewables and granules exist; prescribers sometimes ask for compounded capsules for a specific strength or to avoid dyes or other ingredients, and it is sometimes prescribed off-label for mast cell conditions.
serious: Get medical help right away for mood or behavior changes such as agitation, aggression, depression, nightmares, sleepwalking or thoughts of self-harm, or for a worsening rash with numbness, tingling or breathing trouble.
interactions: Montelukast has few drug interactions, though phenobarbital and rifampin can lower its levels. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Montelukast is sometimes continued in pregnancy when asthma control requires it; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Take it once a day, usually in the evening for asthma, with or without food.
Do not use it for sudden asthma attacks; keep your rescue inhaler with you.
Family members should watch for mood or sleep changes, especially in children, and report them promptly.
monitoring: Your prescriber will review asthma control and ask about mood, sleep and behavior at follow-up visits.
faqs: What are the mood side effects of montelukast?
Some people have reported agitation, bad dreams, depression or suicidal thoughts, which led to an FDA boxed warning; contact your prescriber right away if these occur.
Why is montelukast taken at night?
For asthma it is often taken in the evening, but your prescriber may choose a different time for allergies or exercise symptoms.

name: Mupirocin
uses: Topical and nasal preparations for bacterial skin infections, including MRSA.
how: Blocks an enzyme bacteria need to make proteins.
avoid: Usually well tolerated; for skin and nasal use only.
about: Mupirocin is a topical antibiotic used since the 1980s for skin infections such as impetigo and to clear staph, including MRSA, from the nose. Commercial ointment and cream exist; compounding allows nasal sprays, ear packs for pets and combinations with other ingredients. Veterinarians use it on dogs and cats for bacterial skin infections, including resistant staph.
conditions: Resistant staph skin infections in pets
Ear infections in combination ear packs (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling or trouble breathing, a severe rash, or severe or ongoing diarrhea.
interactions: Mupirocin is applied to the skin or nose and has no meaningful interactions with medicines taken by mouth, but avoid applying other products to the same spot unless directed. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Very little mupirocin is absorbed, and it is generally considered low risk, but talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Try to keep pets from licking treated areas for a while after application, and use a cone if needed.
tips: Wash and gently dry the area first, then apply a thin layer and wash your hands.
For nasal use, use only the amount directed and press the sides of the nose together to spread it.
Use it only for the number of days prescribed, since long use can lead to resistance.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but tell your prescriber or veterinarian if the infection doesn't improve within a few days.
faqs: Can I use mupirocin on my dog?
Veterinarians do prescribe mupirocin for dogs, but use only the product and plan your veterinarian gives and prevent licking.
How long should I use mupirocin?
It is usually used for a short course, often up to about 10 days; follow your prescriber's directions.

name: Mycophenolate
uses: Immune-mediated diseases.
how: Blocks the growth of immune cells.
avoid: Pregnancy, and people or pets with serious infections.
about: Mycophenolate is an immune-suppressing medicine first approved in the 1990s to prevent rejection after organ transplants. It is also prescribed off-label for autoimmune diseases in people and immune-mediated diseases in dogs and cats, such as immune-mediated anemia. Compounded flavored suspensions and capsules help match doses to pets and to patients who cannot take commercial forms.
conditions: Immune-mediated skin and blood disorders in pets (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fever, chills or other signs of infection, unusual bruising or bleeding, bloody or black stools, severe diarrhea, new confusion or weakness, or skin changes such as a new or changing mole.
interactions: Antacids with magnesium or aluminum, cholestyramine and some acid reducers can lower absorption, and live vaccines should be avoided; azathioprine is generally not combined with it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Mycophenolate can cause miscarriage and serious birth defects, so it must not be used in pregnancy and reliable birth control is required; tell your prescriber right away if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Diarrhea is the most common problem in dogs and can be dose-limiting, so report it promptly. Caregivers who are pregnant should not handle the medicine, and gloves should be worn when giving it.
tips: Give or take it on a regular schedule, usually twice a day, as directed.
Do not open capsules or let the liquid touch skin; wear gloves and wash any spills with soap and water.
Avoid people who are sick and practice good hand-washing, since infections can be more serious.
Use sun protection, since immune-suppressing medicines raise skin cancer risk in people.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check blood counts and other labs regularly, especially early in treatment.
faqs: Can I get vaccines while taking mycophenolate?
Live vaccines should be avoided, and other vaccines may work less well, so check with your prescriber first.
Is mycophenolate used in dogs?
Veterinarians prescribe it off-label for some immune-mediated diseases in dogs, often with other immune-suppressing medicines.

name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
uses: Antioxidant support; mucus thinning.
how: Replenishes glutathione, the body's main antioxidant, and breaks up thick mucus.
avoid: People with asthma (inhaled forms) or bleeding disorders.
about: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) is a form of the amino acid cysteine that helps the body make glutathione, a key antioxidant. It has been used in hospitals for decades to treat acetaminophen overdose and to thin mucus. It is also sold as a supplement and used in pets for liver support; compounded capsules, liquids and creams allow measured doses and taste-masked options.
conditions: Liver support in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction, wheezing or trouble breathing, or vomiting that won't stop.
interactions: NAC can increase the effects of nitroglycerin, which may cause headaches and low blood pressure, and activated charcoal can block its absorption. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: NAC is used in pregnancy for acetaminophen overdose, but routine supplement use has less safety information; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats are extremely sensitive to acetaminophen (Tylenol), and even one tablet can be deadly; if exposure happens, it is an emergency that needs a veterinarian, not home NAC. For ongoing liver support, give it with food if it causes stomach upset.
tips: Take or give it with food if it upsets the stomach.
The sulfur smell is normal and does not mean the medicine has gone bad.
Drink plenty of fluids when using it to help thin mucus.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when remembered unless it is almost time for the next one; don't double up.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed for supplement use, but your prescriber or veterinarian may recheck liver tests when it is used for liver support.
faqs: Why does NAC smell like rotten eggs?
NAC contains sulfur, which gives it a strong smell; this is normal.
Can I give my cat NAC if it ate Tylenol?
Acetaminophen poisoning in cats is an emergency; go to a veterinarian immediately rather than treating at home.

name: Naltrexone (including low-dose)
uses: Low-dose naltrexone (LDN) is prescribed off-label for chronic pain, inflammation and autoimmune conditions; standard doses treat alcohol and opioid dependence.
side: Vivid dreams, trouble sleeping, headache, nausea. Blocks opioid pain relievers.
how: At standard doses it blocks opioid receptors. At low doses it briefly blocks them, which is thought to prompt the body to make more of its own endorphins and to calm certain immune cells.
avoid: Anyone taking opioid pain medicine or who needs opioids for surgery, and people with liver disease.
about: Naltrexone is an opioid blocker approved in the 1980s to help people with alcohol or opioid dependence. In much smaller amounts, called low-dose naltrexone or LDN, it is prescribed off-label for chronic pain and immune-related conditions. Because no commercial product comes in these low strengths, LDN is compounded into tablets, capsules, liquids and topical forms, and the prescriber decides the dose.
serious: Get medical help right away for yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or severe stomach pain, sudden opioid withdrawal symptoms, or signs of an allergic reaction. After stopping naltrexone, a person's sensitivity to opioids can return, which raises the risk of a dangerous overdose.
interactions: Naltrexone blocks opioid pain medicines and opioid-containing cough, diarrhea and anesthesia medicines, and taking it while opioids are in the system can cause sudden withdrawal. Tell every doctor, surgeon and dentist that you take it. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Information on naltrexone in pregnancy and breastfeeding is limited; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: LDN is often taken at bedtime; if vivid dreams or sleep problems bother you, ask your prescriber about taking it in the morning.
Take it at the same time each day and keep a simple symptom diary to share at follow-up visits.
Carry a card or note saying you take naltrexone in case of emergency care.
Stop it only as your prescriber directs before any planned surgery.
monitoring: At standard doses your prescriber may check liver tests; with LDN, follow-up visits focus on how symptoms change.
faqs: How long does LDN take to work?
Some people notice changes in a few weeks, but it can take two to three months to judge whether LDN is helping; your prescriber decides how long to try it.
Can I take LDN with opioid pain medicine?
No. Naltrexone blocks opioids and can cause withdrawal, so tell your prescriber about any opioid use before starting.
What is the difference between LDN and regular naltrexone?
They are the same medicine, but LDN uses a much smaller amount and is prescribed off-label for different reasons than standard naltrexone.

name: Neomycin
uses: Topical and ear preparations for bacterial infections.
how: An aminoglycoside that stops bacteria from making proteins.
avoid: Ruptured eardrums (ear products); some people develop skin allergies to it.
about: Neomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic discovered in the 1940s. Because it is poorly absorbed and can harm the kidneys and hearing if it reaches the blood in large amounts, it is mainly used on the skin, in the ears and in the gut. It appears in many commercial combination ointments and ear products, and veterinarians often ask for it in compounded ear packs with steroids and antifungals.
conditions: Bacterial ear infections in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for hearing loss, ringing in the ears, loss of balance or head tilt, or signs of an allergic reaction such as spreading redness, swelling or hives.
interactions: Topical neomycin rarely interacts with medicines taken by mouth, but combining it with other aminoglycosides or medicines that affect hearing or kidneys can add to risk if the eardrum is damaged or large areas are treated. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Very little topical neomycin is absorbed through intact skin, but talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Your veterinarian should check that the eardrum is intact before placing an ear pack with neomycin. Watch for a new head tilt, imbalance or apparent hearing loss after treatment, and report it right away.
tips: Do not clean or put anything in your pet's ear after an ear pack is placed unless your veterinarian says so.
Wash your hands after handling ear packs or treated skin.
Stop and call your prescriber if redness, itching or swelling gets worse, since neomycin allergy is fairly common.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck the ear at a follow-up visit after an ear pack to make sure the infection has cleared.
faqs: How long do neomycin ear packs last in a dog's ear?
Long-acting ear packs are designed to stay in the ear for a period your veterinarian sets, and a recheck visit is usually scheduled.
Why do some people react to neomycin?
Neomycin is a common cause of allergic skin reactions, so stop using it and call your prescriber if the area gets redder or itchier.

name: Niacinamide
uses: Skin tone, barrier and redness support in creams; vitamin B3.
how: A form of vitamin B3 that strengthens the skin barrier and evens tone.
avoid: Usually well tolerated.
about: Niacinamide is a form of vitamin B3 that has long been used in skin care. Applied to the skin, it helps support the protective barrier, calm redness and even out tone. Prescribers ask for it compounded into creams, serums, gels and ointments, often combined with brightening, anti-aging or acne ingredients, and veterinarians may use it in topical preparations for pets.
conditions: Dark spots and uneven skin tone
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or trouble breathing.
interactions: Topical niacinamide has no meaningful interactions with medicines taken by mouth, and it is often combined with other skin ingredients, though layering many actives can increase irritation. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical niacinamide is generally considered low risk in pregnancy and breastfeeding, but talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians sometimes give niacinamide by mouth with certain antibiotics for immune-mediated skin disease in dogs; this page covers the topical forms. Keep pets from licking treated skin until the product has absorbed.
tips: Apply to clean, dry skin as directed, and wash your hands afterward.
Use daily sunscreen if it is part of a brightening routine.
If you notice flushing or stinging, apply less often and let your prescriber know.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How long does niacinamide take to improve skin?
Many people see gradual changes in tone or redness after several weeks of regular use.
Is niacinamide the same as niacin?
Both are forms of vitamin B3, but niacinamide does not usually cause the flushing that niacin can cause.

name: Nifedipine
uses: Topical ointments for anal fissures and hemorrhoid pain.
how: Relaxes smooth muscle, easing the spasm that keeps anal fissures from healing.
avoid: People with very low blood pressure.
about: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker that has been taken by mouth for decades for blood pressure and chest pain. When mixed into an ointment or cream and applied near the anus, it relaxes the ring of muscle around the anal opening. No commercial topical nifedipine product is sold in the US, so prescribers order it compounded for anal fissures, an off-label use.
