serious: Get medical help right away for fainting, a very fast or pounding heartbeat, severe dizziness, heavy rectal bleeding, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives or swelling of the face or throat.
interactions: Some of the medicine can be absorbed, so tell your prescriber if you take blood pressure medicines, other calcium channel blockers or nitrates. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on topical nifedipine in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Wash your hands before and after each application, and use a finger cot or glove if your prescriber suggests one.
Apply only the small amount your prescriber directs, around or just inside the anal opening as instructed.
Eating more fiber, drinking water and avoiding straining can help a fissure heal while you use the ointment.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check how the fissure is healing at a follow-up visit after several weeks of use.
faqs: How long does nifedipine ointment take to work for a fissure?
Many people notice less pain within a few days to a couple of weeks, but full healing often takes several weeks of regular use. Your prescriber decides how long to continue.
Is nifedipine ointment different from nitroglycerin ointment for fissures?
Both relax the anal sphincter, but they work in different ways. Nifedipine ointment may cause fewer headaches for some people; your prescriber chooses which fits you.
Will nifedipine ointment lower my blood pressure?
Only a small amount is absorbed through the skin, so large drops in blood pressure are uncommon. Tell your prescriber if you feel dizzy or lightheaded.

name: Nipple cream (APNO)
uses: A combination of an antibiotic, steroid and antifungal for sore, cracked nipples while breastfeeding, applied after feeding as directed.
how: Combines an antibiotic, a steroid and an antifungal to treat infection and inflammation of the nipple.
avoid: Wipe off before feeding only if your provider directs; use for the shortest time needed.
about: All-purpose nipple ointment, often called APNO, is a compounded mix of an antibiotic, a mild steroid and an antifungal in one cream. It was popularized by breastfeeding specialists for nipples that are sore, cracked or slow to heal. No single commercial product combines these ingredients, so prescribers order it compounded for nursing parents.
serious: Get medical help right away for spreading redness, a hard or painful breast lump, fever or chills, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives or swelling of the face or throat.
interactions: Because it is applied to a small area of skin, interactions with other medicines are unlikely. Avoid putting other creams on the same spot unless your provider says so. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: This cream is meant for use while breastfeeding; follow your provider's directions about how much to apply and whether to remove it before your baby feeds.
tips: Apply a thin layer after feeding, as directed, rather than a thick coat.
Wash your hands before and after applying the cream.
If your baby also has white patches in the mouth, tell your baby's doctor so both of you can be treated.
Tell your provider if your nipples are not improving after the first week or two.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or lactation provider schedules.
faqs: Do I need to wipe off nipple cream before breastfeeding?
It depends on your provider's directions. Many providers say a thin layer does not need to be removed, while others prefer you gently wipe it off.
How long should I use APNO?
It is usually used for a short time, often a couple of weeks. Long use of a steroid on thin skin is avoided, so ask your provider before continuing.
Is a lactation consultant helpful along with the cream?
Often, yes. Sore nipples are commonly caused by latch or positioning problems, and fixing these may help the skin heal and keep the pain from coming back.

name: Nitrofurantoin
uses: Urinary tract infections.
how: Damages bacterial DNA and proteins, concentrated in the urine.
avoid: People or pets with kidney disease, and people near the end of pregnancy.
about: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that has been used since the 1950s to treat and prevent bladder infections. It collects in the urine, where it acts on bacteria, while reaching only low levels in the blood. Commercial capsules and a liquid exist for people, and veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats, sometimes as a flavored liquid that is easier to give.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble breathing, a lasting cough or chest pain, yellow skin or eyes, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, severe diarrhea, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Antacids containing magnesium can lower absorption, and some gout medicines may reduce how well it reaches the urine. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It is often avoided near the end of pregnancy and when nursing a newborn or a baby with G6PD deficiency; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Nitrofurantoin is used off-label in dogs and cats, usually for bladder infections caused by bacteria that resist other antibiotics. Giving it with a meal can ease stomach upset, and a flavored liquid is often easier for small pets.
tips: Take or give it with food or milk, which may improve absorption and lessen nausea.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring each dose.
Finish the full course even if symptoms improve, unless the prescriber or veterinarian says to stop.
Brown or dark yellow urine is expected and harmless.
monitoring: For short courses, monitoring is usually not needed; for long-term prevention, your prescriber may check lung, liver and nerve health.
faqs: Why does nitrofurantoin turn urine dark?
The medicine itself can color urine dark yellow or brown. This is harmless and goes away after stopping.
Is nitrofurantoin used for kidney infections?
Usually not. It reaches high levels in the bladder but not in the kidneys or blood, so prescribers choose other antibiotics for kidney infections.
Can dogs take nitrofurantoin?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for dogs and cats with bladder infections. Your veterinarian chooses the dose based on your pet's weight and kidney health.

name: Nitroglycerin
uses: Topical ointment for anal fissures.
how: Releases nitric oxide, relaxing the anal sphincter muscle and improving blood flow to help fissures heal.
avoid: Anyone taking sildenafil, tadalafil or similar medicines. Headaches are common.
about: Nitroglycerin is a nitrate that has been used for more than a century to treat chest pain. Applied as a weak ointment around the anus, it relaxes the anal sphincter and brings more blood flow to the area, which can help a fissure heal. A commercial rectal ointment exists, and prescribers may order it compounded in a strength or base not available commercially.
serious: Get medical help right away for fainting, chest pain, a severe or lasting headache, a very fast or uneven heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Never use it with erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension medicines such as sildenafil, tadalafil or vardenafil, or with riociguat, because blood pressure can drop dangerously. Alcohol and other blood pressure medicines can add to dizziness. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Use a finger cot or glove to apply, and wash your hands well afterward so the medicine does not absorb through your fingers.
Sit or lie down for a few minutes after applying if you tend to feel dizzy.
Acetaminophen may help with headaches; ask your prescriber what pain reliever is right for you.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will usually check how the fissure is healing at a follow-up visit after several weeks of use.
faqs: Why does nitroglycerin ointment give me a headache?
Nitroglycerin widens blood vessels, including those in the head, which commonly causes headaches. They often get milder after the first days of use.
Can I use nitroglycerin ointment if I take Viagra or Cialis?
No. Combining nitrates with these medicines can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. Tell your prescriber about every medicine you take.
How long do I need to use it?
Many people use it for several weeks while the fissure heals. Your prescriber decides how long to continue.

name: Nystatin
uses: Yeast infections of the mouth and skin, including mouthwash and ointments.
how: Binds to the yeast cell wall and makes it leak, killing the yeast.
avoid: Usually well tolerated; not absorbed into the body when swallowed.
about: Nystatin is an antifungal discovered in the 1950s that works mainly against Candida yeast. It is barely absorbed from the gut or skin, so it acts right where it is applied or swallowed. It is a common ingredient in compounded mouthwashes, ointments and vaginal preparations, and prescribers or veterinarians may order it in a form, flavor or combination that is not sold commercially.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, or for a rash that blisters or spreads.
interactions: Because so little is absorbed, nystatin has few drug interactions. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Because very little is absorbed, it is often considered an option during pregnancy and breastfeeding, but check with your prescriber first.
petNotes: Veterinarians use nystatin in dogs, cats and birds, often in ear and skin ointments combined with other ingredients. Flavored liquids can make oral doses easier for small animals.
tips: For mouthwash or oral liquid, swish it around the mouth and hold it as long as directed before swallowing or spitting, as your prescriber instructs.
Shake liquid forms well before each use.
Keep using it for the full time prescribed, often a few days after symptoms clear, so the yeast does not come back.
Wash your hands after applying creams or ointments.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How fast does nystatin work for thrush?
Many people see improvement within a few days, but treatment often continues for some days after the white patches clear.
Should I eat or drink right after using nystatin mouthwash?
Many prescribers suggest waiting a short while after using it so the medicine stays in contact with the mouth. Follow your prescriber's directions.
Does nystatin work on ringworm?
No. Nystatin works on Candida yeast, not on the fungi that cause ringworm or athlete's foot, which need other antifungals.

name: Omeprazole
uses: Reduces stomach acid for reflux and ulcers.
how: A proton pump inhibitor that shuts down the stomach's acid pumps.
avoid: Long-term use can affect vitamin B12 and magnesium; interacts with clopidogrel.
about: Omeprazole was the first proton pump inhibitor, introduced in the late 1980s, and is among the most widely used acid reducers. It is sold as capsules and tablets for people and as an oral paste for horses. Prescribers and veterinarians may order it compounded as a liquid or small-strength capsule for children, people with feeding tubes, or pets who need a size or flavor that is not commercially available.
conditions: Stomach ulcers in dogs and cats
Protection during steroid or NSAID use
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe or watery diarrhea, black or bloody stools, muscle cramps or a racing heartbeat (possible low magnesium), or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: It can lower the effect of clopidogrel and change levels of drugs such as methotrexate, certain HIV medicines and some antifungals. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Omeprazole is often considered acceptable during pregnancy and breastfeeding when it is needed, but talk to your prescriber first.
petNotes: Omeprazole is used off-label in dogs and cats to reduce stomach acid and protect against ulcers. It works best given on an empty stomach before the first meal of the day.
tips: Take or give it before a meal, usually breakfast, for best effect.
Shake liquid forms well and keep them stored as labeled.
Don't stop long-term use suddenly without talking to your prescriber, because acid can rebound.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: With long-term use, your prescriber may check magnesium and vitamin B12 levels from time to time.
faqs: How long does omeprazole take to work?
It may start reducing acid within a day, but full relief often takes several days of regular use.
Can dogs take omeprazole?
Veterinarians commonly prescribe it off-label for dogs and cats. The dose depends on your pet's weight, so use only what your veterinarian prescribes.
Is it OK to take omeprazole long term?
Some people need it long term, but extended use has been linked to low magnesium, low B12 and other concerns. Your prescriber decides whether to continue.

name: Ondansetron
uses: Nausea and vomiting.
how: Blocks serotonin (5-HT3) receptors that trigger nausea.
avoid: People or pets with heart rhythm problems, and anyone taking apomorphine.
about: Ondansetron is an anti-nausea medicine introduced in the early 1990s, first to prevent nausea from chemotherapy and surgery. It is sold as tablets, dissolving tablets and liquid for people. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats, and compounded flavored liquids, small-strength forms or transdermal gels can help when a patient cannot swallow pills or keep them down.
conditions: Nausea and vomiting in dogs and cats
Nausea in cats with kidney disease
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, a fast or uneven heartbeat, severe constipation or belly pain, signs of an allergic reaction, or agitation with fever, shaking and muscle stiffness (possible serotonin syndrome).
interactions: Avoid apomorphine, and use caution with other medicines that affect heart rhythm or raise serotonin, such as certain antidepressants and some pain medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Some studies have raised questions about use in early pregnancy, so talk with your prescriber about benefits and risks if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Ondansetron is used off-label in dogs and cats and is generally well tolerated. Transdermal gel may be absorbed less reliably than oral forms, so your veterinarian will watch how your pet responds.
tips: It can be taken with or without food.
For rapid-dissolve tablets, place on the tongue with dry hands and let it melt before swallowing.
When it is used to prevent nausea, take it at the time your prescriber directs, often before chemotherapy or travel.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to your pet, and rotate between the inner ear tips as directed.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but people with heart rhythm or electrolyte problems may need an ECG or blood tests.
faqs: How quickly does ondansetron work?
It often starts working within about 30 minutes to an hour by mouth.
Can ondansetron be given to cats?
Veterinarians use it off-label in cats, including those with kidney disease or pancreatitis. Your veterinarian decides the dose.
Why does ondansetron cause constipation?
It slows the movement of the gut along with blocking nausea signals. Drinking fluids and eating fiber may help; tell your prescriber if it is severe.

name: Oxymetazoline
uses: Facial redness from rosacea.
how: Narrows blood vessels in the skin to reduce redness.
avoid: Use as directed; overuse can cause rebound redness.
about: Oxymetazoline narrows small blood vessels. It has long been used in nasal sprays for congestion, and a commercial cream was later approved for the persistent facial redness of rosacea. Dermatology prescribers may order it compounded into a cream together with other rosacea ingredients, such as ivermectin or azelaic acid, so one product treats both redness and bumps.
serious: Get medical help right away for signs of an allergic reaction such as hives or swelling of the face, chest pain, a racing heartbeat, or new vision symptoms such as eye pain.
interactions: Very little is absorbed, but tell your prescriber if you take blood pressure medicines, heart medicines or MAO inhibitors. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, dry skin, usually once a day, as your prescriber directs.
Keep it out of your eyes, mouth and the inside of your nose, and wash your hands after applying.
Use sunscreen and avoid known rosacea triggers such as heat, spicy food and alcohol.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: How long does oxymetazoline cream take to reduce redness?
The effect on redness often appears within hours of applying and lasts for part of the day. It does not treat the cause of rosacea, so redness returns when it wears off.
What is rebound redness?
Some people notice redness that comes back stronger after the cream wears off, especially with overuse. Tell your prescriber if this happens.
Is it the same ingredient as Afrin nasal spray?
Yes, the active ingredient is the same, but the cream is made for skin and should not be used in the nose.

name: Oxytocin
uses: A naturally occurring hormone that some prescribers order off-label as rapid-dissolve tablets or troches. Your prescriber decides whether it is right for you.
how: Acts like the body's own oxytocin, a hormone made in the brain.
avoid: Pregnancy.
about: Oxytocin is a hormone made in the brain and released by the pituitary gland. It plays a role in childbirth and breastfeeding, and the commercial injection is used in hospitals to start or strengthen labor. Some prescribers order it off-label as compounded rapid-dissolve tablets or troches. Evidence for these uses is limited, and your prescriber decides whether it is right for you.
serious: Get medical help right away for a severe headache, confusion, seizures, a fast or uneven heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Tell your prescriber about any medicines that affect blood pressure, heart rhythm or fluid and sodium balance. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used during pregnancy because it can cause the uterus to contract; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Let a troche or rapid-dissolve tablet dissolve fully between the cheek and gum or under the tongue instead of swallowing it whole.
Avoid eating or drinking until it has fully dissolved.
Use it only at the times your prescriber directs.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Why is it given as a troche or dissolving tablet?
Oxytocin is broken down in the stomach, so it is absorbed through the lining of the mouth instead of being swallowed.

name: Pantoprazole
uses: Reduces stomach acid, including suspensions for feeding tubes.
how: A proton pump inhibitor that shuts down the stomach's acid pumps.
avoid: Long-term use can affect vitamin B12 and magnesium.
about: Pantoprazole is a proton pump inhibitor that has been widely used since the 2000s to reduce stomach acid. Commercial tablets are delayed-release and should not be crushed, and the commercial granules can clog feeding tubes. Prescribers and veterinarians may order a compounded oral liquid for people with feeding tubes, children, or pets who cannot take a tablet.
conditions: Stomach acid reduction in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe or watery diarrhea, black or bloody stools, muscle cramps or a racing heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: It can change the absorption of medicines that need stomach acid, such as some antifungals and certain HIV medicines, and may raise methotrexate levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Pantoprazole is often considered acceptable in pregnancy and breastfeeding when needed, but talk to your prescriber first.
petNotes: Pantoprazole is used off-label in dogs and cats, most often in the hospital or for pets that cannot take omeprazole. An oral liquid can be easier to give than tablets.
tips: Take or give it before a meal, usually breakfast, unless directed otherwise.
Shake the liquid well and flush feeding tubes with water before and after each dose as instructed.
Store the liquid as labeled and discard it after the beyond-use date.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: With long-term use, your prescriber may check magnesium and vitamin B12 levels from time to time.
faqs: Can pantoprazole be given through a feeding tube?
Commercial tablets cannot be crushed, so a compounded liquid is often used for feeding tubes. Follow your care team's flushing directions.
What is the difference between pantoprazole and omeprazole?
Both are proton pump inhibitors that reduce stomach acid. They differ in some drug interactions, and your prescriber chooses which one fits you.

name: Paroxetine
uses: Anxiety and depression; behavior problems in pets.
how: An SSRI that increases serotonin available in the brain.
avoid: Anyone taking MAO inhibitors or other serotonin medicines, and those who are pregnant.
about: Paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used since the early 1990s for depression and several anxiety disorders. Veterinarians use it off-label in cats and dogs for behavior problems such as anxiety, aggression and urine marking. Compounded flavored liquids, chewable treats or transdermal gels can help when a pet will not take a tablet or needs a small dose.
conditions: Anxiety and behavior problems in pets
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for thoughts of self-harm, agitation with fever, shaking or muscle stiffness, unusual bleeding, seizures, or in pets, severe restlessness or dilated pupils with a racing heartbeat.
interactions: Never combine with MAO inhibitors (including selegiline and amitraz flea and tick products for pets), and use caution with other serotonin medicines, triptans, certain pain medicines, blood thinners, NSAIDs, tamoxifen and thioridazine. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Paroxetine is generally avoided in pregnancy, especially early pregnancy, because it has been linked to heart defects; talk to your prescriber before stopping or starting it if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Paroxetine is used off-label in pets, more often in cats. It can take weeks to see a change, and it works best alongside a behavior plan; transdermal gel may be absorbed less predictably than oral forms.
tips: It can be taken or given with or without food; with food may lessen nausea.
Do not stop it suddenly; your prescriber or veterinarian will taper it to avoid withdrawal effects.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to your pet.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber will check how you are doing, especially in the first weeks and after dose changes; veterinarians may check blood work in older pets.
faqs: How long does paroxetine take to work?
Some effects may appear within a couple of weeks, but full benefits often take four to six weeks or longer.
Can I drink alcohol while taking paroxetine?
Alcohol can add to drowsiness and may worsen depression or anxiety. Ask your prescriber before drinking.
Is paroxetine used in cats?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for cats with anxiety, aggression or urine marking. Your veterinarian decides the dose and form.

name: Pentoxifylline
uses: Circulation support; used in topical sexual-health creams and in dogs for some skin and vascular conditions.
how: Makes red blood cells more flexible and blood less sticky, which improves circulation in small vessels.
avoid: People with recent bleeding or stroke, and those sensitive to caffeine or theophylline.
about: Pentoxifylline is a xanthine derivative, related to caffeine and theophylline, that has been used since the 1980s to improve blood flow through small vessels. Commercial tablets are made for leg pain from poor circulation. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs for certain skin and blood vessel conditions, and it is also an ingredient in compounded topical creams that combine blood-flow ingredients.
conditions: Ear tip and skin vessel disease in dogs
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for unusual bleeding or bruising, black stools, chest pain, a fast or uneven heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Bleeding risk may rise with blood thinners, aspirin and NSAIDs, and it can raise theophylline levels; cimetidine may raise pentoxifylline levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information in pregnancy, and it passes into breast milk, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Pentoxifylline is used off-label in dogs, often for weeks to months before improvement is seen. Giving it with food can lessen vomiting.
tips: Take or give oral forms with food to reduce stomach upset.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
For cream, wash your hands after applying unless your hands are the treatment area.
Limit caffeine if you notice jitteriness or a fast heartbeat.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber or veterinarian may check for bleeding problems if you take other blood thinners.
faqs: How long does pentoxifylline take to work in dogs?
Skin and vessel conditions often take several weeks to a few months to improve. Your veterinarian will judge progress at follow-up visits.
Why is pentoxifylline in a cream?
In compounded creams it is combined with other ingredients to increase local blood flow where the cream is applied. This is an off-label use.

name: Phenobarbital
uses: Long-standing seizure medication for dogs and cats.
side: Sedation, increased thirst, appetite and urination; requires liver monitoring.
how: Boosts the brain's main calming signal (GABA), reducing seizure activity.
avoid: Pets with liver disease. Needs regular blood level and liver monitoring.
about: Phenobarbital is one of the oldest seizure medicines, in use for more than a hundred years. It remains a common first choice for seizures in dogs and cats because it is effective for many pets and can be given long term. Veterinarians may order it compounded as a flavored liquid, small-strength capsule or transdermal gel when tablets are hard to split or a pet refuses pills.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for yellow gums or eyes, extreme sleepiness or trouble walking, unusual bleeding or bruising, skin sores, or any seizure lasting more than a few minutes or several seizures in a row.
interactions: It speeds up the breakdown of many drugs, including steroids, some antibiotics and heart medicines, and it adds to the effects of other sedatives and potassium bromide. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Dogs and cats often seem sleepy or wobbly for the first couple of weeks, which usually improves. Cats generally tolerate it well, and transdermal gel can be absorbed less reliably than oral forms, so blood levels guide the dose.
tips: Give it at the same times every day to keep blood levels steady.
Never stop it suddenly, which can trigger severe seizures.
Keep a seizure diary with dates and lengths to share with your veterinarian.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel and store all forms safely away from people and other pets.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check phenobarbital blood levels and liver values a few weeks after starting and then regularly, often every six to twelve months.
faqs: How long does phenobarbital take to work in dogs?
It takes about two to three weeks for blood levels to become steady, so seizures may not be fully controlled right away.
Will my dog always be sleepy on phenobarbital?
Sleepiness and wobbliness are common at first and often fade within a few weeks. Tell your veterinarian if they continue.
Can my pet ever stop phenobarbital?
Some pets can be tapered off after a long seizure-free period, but only under your veterinarian's direction.

name: Phenoxybenzamine
uses: Urethral spasm and urine retention in cats and dogs.
how: Blocks alpha receptors to relax the urethra and blood vessels.
avoid: Pets with low blood pressure or heart disease.
about: Phenoxybenzamine is an alpha blocker that has been used for decades in people for a rare adrenal tumor. Veterinarians use it off-label in cats and dogs to relax the smooth muscle of the urethra, especially after a urinary blockage. Commercial capsules can be expensive and come in one strength, so veterinarians may order smaller compounded capsules sized for cats and small dogs.
conditions: Recovery after urinary blockage in cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for collapse, severe weakness, a very fast heartbeat, straining with little or no urine, or vomiting that does not stop.
interactions: Other medicines that lower blood pressure, such as prazosin, ACE inhibitors and some sedatives, can add to its effects. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Cats are most often treated after a urinary blockage, and the medicine may take several days to reach full effect. Some pets get a stuffy nose or red eyes because blood vessels widen.
tips: Give it with food to lessen stomach upset.
Watch your pet's litter box or bathroom habits closely and report straining right away.
Let your pet rise slowly after resting if they seem weak or wobbly.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may check blood pressure and urination at follow-up visits.
faqs: How long does phenoxybenzamine take to work in cats?
It may take several days to reach its full effect, which is why veterinarians sometimes use other medicines alongside it.
Is a blocked cat an emergency?
Yes. A cat straining with little or no urine needs to see a veterinarian right away, whether or not it is on this medicine.

name: Phenylephrine
uses: Constricts blood vessels; used in numbing ointments and hemorrhoid care.
how: Narrows blood vessels, which reduces swelling and bleeding.
avoid: People with high blood pressure or heart disease (larger amounts).
about: Phenylephrine is a decongestant that narrows blood vessels. It is found in nasal sprays, cold medicines and over-the-counter hemorrhoid ointments, where it shrinks swollen tissue. Prescribers may order it compounded into a numbing ointment with local anesthetics such as lidocaine or tetracaine, which may also help reduce minor bleeding and make numbing last longer.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, a pounding or uneven heartbeat, severe headache, rectal bleeding that does not stop, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Larger amounts may interact with MAO inhibitors, some antidepressants, and blood pressure or heart medicines. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on topical use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only the amount your prescriber directs, and only to the area you are treating.
Wash your hands before and after applying.
Do not use on broken or bleeding skin unless your prescriber says to.
Tell your prescriber if symptoms last more than about a week.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Why is phenylephrine combined with numbing medicines?
By narrowing blood vessels, it may keep the numbing medicine in place longer and reduce minor bleeding and swelling.
Can I use phenylephrine ointment if I have high blood pressure?
Small amounts on the skin are usually low risk, but ask your prescriber first if you have high blood pressure or heart disease.

name: Phenylpropanolamine
uses: Urinary incontinence in dogs.
side: Restlessness, high blood pressure, decreased appetite.
how: Tightens the muscle that keeps the bladder closed.
avoid: Dogs with high blood pressure, heart disease or glaucoma.
about: Phenylpropanolamine, often called PPA, tightens the muscle at the neck of the bladder. It was once in human cold medicines but was removed from human products in the US in 2000. It is still widely used in dogs for urinary leaking, and a veterinary product is approved for dogs. Veterinarians may order it compounded as a flavored liquid or custom capsule for very small or very large dogs.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for collapse, a racing or uneven heartbeat, severe agitation, seizures, or signs of eye pain or sudden vision change.
interactions: Avoid MAO inhibitors, including selegiline and amitraz flea and tick products, and use caution with other stimulants, NSAIDs and some antidepressants. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Most dogs respond well, and results are often seen within days. Use in cats is off-label and less common; keep flavored products away from children and other pets because an overdose can be dangerous.
tips: Give it at about the same times each day.
Giving it with a meal may lessen stomach upset.
Watch for restlessness or changes in appetite and report them to your veterinarian.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may check blood pressure before starting and periodically, especially in older dogs.
faqs: How fast does PPA work for dog incontinence?
Many dogs improve within a few days to a week.
Is phenylpropanolamine safe for dogs long term?
Many dogs take it for years. Your veterinarian may check blood pressure and heart health over time.
Why was PPA removed from human medicines?
It was linked to a higher risk of a type of stroke in people. This did not change its veterinary use in dogs.

name: Pilocarpine
uses: Dry mouth (lollipops and troches) and dry eye.
how: Stimulates saliva and tear glands.
avoid: People with asthma, glaucoma of certain types, or heart disease.
about: Pilocarpine is a plant-derived medicine that has been used for well over a century, first as eye drops for glaucoma. Taken by mouth, it stimulates the salivary and tear glands. Commercial tablets are prescribed for dry mouth, and prescribers may order compounded lollipops or troches that dissolve slowly in the mouth. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs for certain types of dry eye.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble breathing or wheezing, a slow or uneven heartbeat, severe sweating, vomiting or diarrhea, or confusion or tremors.
interactions: Beta blockers can add to heart rhythm effects, and medicines with anticholinergic effects (some antihistamines, bladder medicines and antidepressants) may work against it. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information on its use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: In dogs, veterinarians sometimes give tiny amounts by mouth, often mixed in food, for dry eye caused by nerve problems. Signs of too much include drooling, vomiting or diarrhea.
tips: Let lollipops and troches dissolve slowly in the mouth rather than chewing them.
Sip water during the day and use sugar-free products to protect your teeth.
Be careful driving at night, since it can blur vision in dim light.
Taking it with meals may lessen stomach upset.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How long does pilocarpine take to work for dry mouth?
Saliva may increase within about 30 minutes of a dose, though full benefit can take several weeks of regular use.
Why does pilocarpine make me sweat?
It stimulates sweat glands along with salivary glands. Mild sweating is common; tell your prescriber if it is heavy.

name: Pimobendan
uses: Congestive heart failure and certain heart diseases in dogs, and sometimes cats.
how: Strengthens the heart's squeeze and widens blood vessels, reducing the heart's workload.
avoid: Dogs with certain heart conditions where increasing the heart's force is harmful, such as some obstructive diseases.
about: Pimobendan helps the heart pump more strongly and widens blood vessels, which lowers the heart's workload. It is approved for dogs with congestive heart failure and for certain dogs before heart failure develops. Veterinarians use it off-label in cats. Compounded forms such as flavored liquids, chewable treats, small capsules or transdermal gel help with small patients and pets that refuse tablets.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for fainting or collapse, faster or harder breathing at rest, a cough that gets worse, blue or pale gums, or a swollen belly.
interactions: It is often given with heart medicines such as furosemide and ACE inhibitors; calcium channel blockers and beta blockers may change how it works. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: It is usually given on an empty stomach, about an hour before food, for better absorption. In cats it is off-label and used with care, especially when the heart muscle is thickened.
tips: Give it about an hour before meals, at the same times each day.
Count your pet's breathing rate while sleeping and tell your veterinarian if it rises.
Never stop it without talking to your veterinarian.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck heart health with exams, chest X-rays, an ultrasound or blood work over time.
faqs: How long can a dog live on pimobendan?
It varies a lot with the type and stage of heart disease. Pimobendan may help some dogs feel better and stay well longer; your veterinarian can discuss your dog's outlook.
Why give pimobendan on an empty stomach?
Food can reduce how much is absorbed, so it is usually given about an hour before meals.
Can cats take pimobendan?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for cats with heart failure. Your veterinarian decides whether it fits your cat's type of heart disease.

name: Piroxicam
uses: Some bladder cancers and pain in dogs.
how: An NSAID that reduces inflammation and has anti-tumor effects in some cancers.
avoid: Pets with ulcers or kidney disease, or taking steroids.
about: Piroxicam is a long-acting nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used in people for arthritis since the early 1980s. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs, most often as part of treatment for bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinoma) and some other tumors. Because dogs need much smaller amounts than the commercial capsules contain, veterinarians may order compounded capsules or flavored liquids sized to a pet's weight.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, not eating, much more or less drinking and urination, yellow gums or eyes, or sudden weakness.
interactions: Never give it with steroids such as prednisone or other NSAIDs, including aspirin, because ulcer and bleeding risk rises sharply. Use caution with diuretics, ACE inhibitors and some chemotherapy drugs. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Dogs and especially cats are sensitive to NSAIDs, so only use the dose your veterinarian prescribes and never give human pain relievers. Give it with food, and wash your hands after handling capsules.
tips: Give it with food to protect the stomach.
Never switch to or add another pain reliever without asking your veterinarian.
Keep it away from children and other pets, since even a few capsules can be dangerous.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually check kidney and liver blood work and urine before starting and periodically during treatment.
faqs: Why is piroxicam used for bladder cancer in dogs?
It has anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor effects in some cancers and is often used alone or with chemotherapy. It does not cure cancer, but it may help slow it and ease symptoms.
Can I give my dog piroxicam with prednisone?
No. Combining an NSAID with a steroid greatly raises the risk of stomach ulcers. Your veterinarian will advise a safe gap if switching.

name: Polymyxin B
uses: Topical and ear preparations for bacterial infections.
how: Disrupts the outer membrane of bacteria.
avoid: Ruptured eardrums (ear products).
about: Polymyxin B is an antibiotic discovered in the 1940s that acts mainly on gram-negative bacteria such as Pseudomonas. It is found in common first aid ointments, eye drops and ear drops, often paired with neomycin or bacitracin. Veterinarians may order it compounded into ear packs or other topical blends with steroids or antifungals for dogs and cats with ear infections.
conditions: Ear infections in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for sudden hearing loss, balance problems or a head tilt after using an ear product, or for swelling, blistering or a spreading rash.
interactions: Very little is absorbed from the skin or ear, so interactions are unlikely, but avoid using other ear products at the same time unless directed. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Little is absorbed from the skin or ear, but check with your prescriber before using it if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Ear packs are placed by the veterinarian and slowly release medicine over days to weeks, so do not clean the ear unless told to. Tell your veterinarian right away if your pet shows a head tilt or loss of balance.
tips: Do not put cotton swabs or cleaners in the ear after an ear pack is placed unless your veterinarian says to.
Keep the ear dry, and avoid bathing or swimming as directed.
For skin products, apply a thin layer to clean skin and wash your hands afterward.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will usually recheck the ear at a follow-up visit to make sure the infection has cleared.
faqs: How long does an ear pack last in a dog's ear?
It slowly releases medicine and usually dries and falls out over one to several weeks, depending on the product. Your veterinarian will tell you when to come back.
Why should ear drops not be used with a ruptured eardrum?
Some ingredients can harm the inner ear if they pass through a hole in the eardrum, which may affect hearing or balance.

name: Ponazuril
uses: Coccidia and protozoal infections in pets.
how: Blocks the energy production of protozoa such as coccidia.
avoid: Usually well tolerated.
about: Ponazuril is an antiprotozoal medicine approved for horses with a nerve infection called EPM. Veterinarians use it off-label in puppies, kittens, dogs and cats to treat coccidia, tiny intestinal parasites that cause diarrhea, especially in young animals and shelters. The horse paste is very concentrated, so veterinarians may order a compounded flavored liquid or capsule that is easier to measure for small pets.
conditions: Coccidia diarrhea in dogs and cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for bloody diarrhea, repeated vomiting, weakness, not eating, or signs of dehydration such as sunken eyes and sticky gums.
interactions: Few drug interactions are known. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Ponazuril is used off-label in dogs and cats and is often given for a short course. Coccidia spreads in feces, so clean up promptly and treat all affected pets as your veterinarian advises.
tips: Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
It can usually be given with or without food.
Pick up feces right away and clean bedding to help prevent reinfection.
Recheck stool samples if your veterinarian recommends it.
monitoring: Your veterinarian may recheck a stool sample after treatment to confirm the infection has cleared.
faqs: How long does ponazuril take to work for coccidia?
Many pets improve within a few days, but the full course is still needed.
Can people catch coccidia from puppies?
The common coccidia of dogs and cats generally do not infect people, but good handwashing after cleaning up is always wise.

name: Potassium bromide
uses: Seizure control in dogs.
side: Sedation, increased thirst and appetite, wobbliness.
how: Bromide replaces chloride in nerve cells, making them less excitable.
avoid: Cats (it can cause serious lung problems), and dogs with kidney disease or on low-salt diets.
about: Potassium bromide is one of the oldest seizure medicines and is still used in dogs, either alone or with phenobarbital. No FDA-approved animal product is sold in the US, so veterinarians rely on compounded capsules or liquids. It builds up slowly, often taking months to reach steady levels, and is cleared by the kidneys, so salt intake and kidney health affect how it works.
conditions: Dogs with liver concerns needing a seizure medicine
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for severe stumbling or weakness, extreme sleepiness, confusion, vomiting that does not stop, or any long or clustered seizures.
interactions: Changes in salt intake, salty treats, IV fluids and diuretics such as furosemide can change bromide levels. It adds to the sedation of phenobarbital and other sedatives. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Do not use in cats, which can develop serious lung inflammation. In dogs, keep the diet and treats consistent because more or less salt changes blood levels; giving it with food can reduce stomach upset.
tips: Give it with food to lessen stomach upset.
Keep your dog's food and treats the same, and ask your veterinarian before switching diets.
Never stop it suddenly; seizures can return.
Keep a seizure diary to share at checkups.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check bromide blood levels periodically, often a few months after starting and after any diet or dose change.
faqs: Why does potassium bromide take so long to work?
It stays in the body a long time, so blood levels rise slowly over weeks to months. Your veterinarian may use a higher starting dose or another medicine during that time.
Can I change my dog's food while on potassium bromide?
Talk to your veterinarian first. Foods with different salt levels can raise or lower bromide levels.
Is potassium bromide safe for cats?
It is generally not used in cats because it can cause serious lung problems.

name: Potassium chloride
uses: Potassium supplementation.
how: Replaces potassium.
avoid: People or pets with high potassium or kidney failure.
about: Potassium chloride is the most common prescription potassium supplement. Potassium is a mineral that nerves, muscles and the heart need to work normally. Commercial tablets and liquids exist, and prescribers or veterinarians may order slow-release capsules compounded in a strength or size that better fits a patient, such as a child, a small pet, or someone who cannot swallow large tablets.
conditions: Potassium loss from vomiting or diarrhea
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a slow or uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness or paralysis, severe stomach pain, black or bloody stools, or vomiting that looks like coffee grounds.
interactions: Potassium can build up when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, other potassium-sparing diuretics or salt substitutes. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It is generally used in pregnancy and breastfeeding when needed to correct low potassium, under your prescriber's care.
petNotes: Cats with kidney disease more often receive potassium gluconate, but potassium chloride may be used in some pets. Give it with food to reduce stomach upset.
tips: Take or give it with a meal and a full glass of water.
Swallow slow-release capsules whole unless your prescriber says otherwise.
Do not use salt substitutes unless your prescriber approves, since many contain potassium.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check potassium and kidney function with blood tests.
faqs: What are signs of low potassium?
Weakness, muscle cramps, tiredness, constipation and an irregular heartbeat can be signs. In pets, weakness and a drooping head in cats may be seen.
Can I get enough potassium from food instead?
Foods such as bananas, potatoes and beans contain potassium, but they may not be enough to correct a low level. Your prescriber decides whether you need a supplement.

name: Potassium citrate
uses: Helps prevent certain kidney and bladder stones.
how: Makes urine less acidic and adds citrate, which blocks certain stones from forming.
avoid: People or pets with high potassium, kidney failure or stomach ulcers.
about: Potassium citrate makes urine less acidic and raises citrate, a natural stone blocker. It is prescribed to help prevent certain kidney and bladder stones in people and pets. Commercial tablets are made for people, and prescribers or veterinarians may order a compounded liquid or flavored suspension for children, people who cannot swallow large tablets, or pets that need a smaller dose.
conditions: Calcium oxalate bladder stones in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a slow or uneven heartbeat, muscle weakness, severe stomach pain, black or bloody stools, or vomiting.
interactions: Potassium can build up when combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics or salt substitutes. Medicines that slow the gut, such as anticholinergics, may raise the risk of stomach irritation. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians use it in dogs and cats to help prevent calcium oxalate stones, often along with a special diet. Mixing it into food helps with taste and stomach upset.
tips: Take or give it with meals or a snack.
Drink plenty of fluids to help keep urine dilute, unless told otherwise.
Mix liquid forms with water or juice if directed, and shake suspensions well.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check potassium, kidney function and urine pH, and sometimes take X-rays to look for stones.
faqs: Does potassium citrate dissolve kidney stones?
It may help dissolve uric acid stones and help prevent new stones, but it usually does not dissolve calcium oxalate stones. Your prescriber decides the plan.
Why is my urine pH being checked?
Urine pH shows whether the medicine is making urine less acidic, which helps your prescriber adjust treatment.

name: Potassium gluconate
uses: Potassium supplement for cats and dogs with low potassium, often from kidney disease.
how: Replaces potassium lost through the kidneys.
avoid: Pets with high potassium or urinary blockage.
about: Potassium gluconate is a potassium supplement commonly used in cats and dogs. Pets with chronic kidney disease often lose potassium in their urine, which can cause weakness and a poor appetite. Potassium gluconate tends to be gentle on the stomach, and veterinarians may order a compounded flavored suspension so the dose can be measured easily and mixed into food.
conditions: Low potassium in cats with kidney disease
Potassium loss from vomiting or poor appetite
Muscle weakness from low potassium in cats
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for a slow or uneven heartbeat, collapse, severe weakness, vomiting that does not stop, or straining to urinate with little or no urine.
interactions: Potassium levels can rise too high when given with ACE inhibitors such as benazepril, spironolactone or other potassium sources. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Cats with kidney disease are the most common patients. Low potassium in cats may show as weakness or a drooping head, and the supplement is usually mixed into a small amount of food.
tips: Mix it with a small amount of food your pet will finish.
Shake the suspension well before measuring.
Keep regular recheck appointments, since potassium needs can change over time.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will check potassium and kidney values with blood tests periodically.
faqs: Why do cats with kidney disease need potassium?
Damaged kidneys may let too much potassium leave in the urine, and low potassium can make kidney disease and weakness worse.
Can I give my cat potassium gluconate long term?
Many cats with kidney disease take it for months or years, with blood tests to make sure levels stay in range.

name: Praziquantel
uses: Tapeworms and flukes in pets.
how: Makes tapeworm and fluke membranes leak calcium, paralyzing them.
avoid: Very young puppies and kittens.
about: Praziquantel is a dewormer that has been used since the 1970s against tapeworms and flukes. It is found in many veterinary dewormers for dogs and cats, often combined with other dewormers, and a commercial tablet is used in people. Veterinarians may order a compounded flavored liquid or capsule for small or picky pets, or when a combination product is not a good fit.
conditions: Liver and lung flukes in pets
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for repeated vomiting, severe weakness, wobbliness, collapse, or swelling of the face or hives.
interactions: Some seizure medicines such as phenobarbital, and steroids, can lower praziquantel levels. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Fleas spread the most common tapeworm, so flea control is part of treatment. It is usually given once, and drooling in cats is often due to the bitter taste.
tips: Give it with or without food as your veterinarian directs.
Treat all pets for fleas to prevent reinfection.
Pick up feces promptly and wash your hands after cleaning up.
Repeat treatment only if your veterinarian advises.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your veterinarian schedules.
faqs: How do I know if my pet has tapeworms?
Small segments that look like rice grains may be seen around the tail or in the stool. Your veterinarian can confirm it.
Will I see worms after giving praziquantel?
Usually not. The worms are often digested after they die, so you may not see them pass.

name: Prazosin
uses: Urinary blockage and urethral spasm in cats and dogs; blood pressure and nightmares in people.
how: Blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing smooth muscle in blood vessels and the urethra.
avoid: People or pets with low blood pressure.
about: Prazosin is an alpha-1 blocker that has been used since the 1970s for high blood pressure. Prescribers also use it off-label for nightmares related to PTSD. Veterinarians use it off-label in cats and dogs to relax the urethra after a urinary blockage. Commercial capsules come in strengths too large for many pets, so veterinarians may order compounded liquids or smaller capsules.
conditions: Recovery after urinary blockage in cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for fainting, a very fast or pounding heartbeat, chest pain, a painful erection lasting more than a few hours, or straining to urinate with little or no urine.
interactions: Other blood pressure medicines, erectile dysfunction medicines such as sildenafil, other alpha blockers and alcohol can add to dizziness and low blood pressure. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information in pregnancy, and small amounts pass into breast milk, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats are often sent home on it after a urinary blockage. Watch the litter box closely, because straining with little urine is an emergency.
tips: The first dose can cause dizziness, so it is often taken at bedtime; stand up slowly.
Avoid alcohol until you know how it affects you.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check blood pressure at visits; your veterinarian will watch urination and may check blood pressure.
faqs: Why is prazosin used for nightmares?
It blocks some of the stress chemicals that may be linked to nightmares in PTSD. This is an off-label use, and your prescriber decides whether it fits.
Why does prazosin make me dizzy when I stand up?
It lowers blood pressure, which can drop further when you stand. This is most common after the first doses or a dose increase.
Is prazosin used in blocked cats?
Veterinarians often prescribe it off-label after a urinary blockage to help relax the urethra.

name: Prednisolone
uses: Inflammation, allergies and immune conditions; preferred over prednisone in cats.
side: Increased thirst, urination and appetite, panting, mood changes.
how: A steroid that calms inflammation and the immune system.
avoid: People or pets with diabetes, infections or stomach ulcers, or taking NSAIDs. Do not stop suddenly after long use.
about: Prednisolone is a corticosteroid that has been used since the 1950s to calm inflammation and an overactive immune system. It is the active form of prednisone, so it does not need the liver to convert it, which is why it is preferred in cats and people with liver problems. Prescribers and veterinarians may order compounded flavored liquids, chewable treats or transdermal gels for children and pets.
conditions: Some cancers in pets (with other treatment)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, signs of infection such as fever, severe mood changes, vision changes, or extreme weakness or collapse after missing doses.
interactions: NSAIDs raise the risk of stomach ulcers, and diabetes medicines, blood thinners, some seizure medicines, certain antifungals and live vaccines may also interact. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It may be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding when the benefits outweigh the risks; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats convert prednisone poorly, so prednisolone is the usual choice for them. Dogs often drink, urinate and pant more; never combine it with NSAIDs such as carprofen or meloxicam.
tips: Take or give it with food to protect the stomach.
Morning dosing is common for dogs and people; cats are often dosed in the evening, as your veterinarian directs.
Do not stop suddenly after long use; your prescriber will taper the dose.
Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to your pet.
monitoring: With long-term use, your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood sugar, blood pressure, eyes, bones or blood work.
faqs: What is the difference between prednisolone and prednisone?
Prednisone is changed into prednisolone by the liver. Prednisolone is already active, which is why it is preferred for cats and people with liver problems.
Why is my dog so thirsty on prednisolone?
Increased thirst, urination and appetite are common steroid effects. Provide plenty of water and take your dog outside more often.
Can prednisolone be stopped suddenly?
After more than a short course, stopping suddenly can cause serious problems. Your prescriber or veterinarian will taper the dose.

name: Prednisone
uses: Inflammation, allergies and immune conditions.
side: Increased thirst, urination and appetite, mood changes.
how: A steroid the liver converts to prednisolone to calm inflammation and the immune system.
avoid: Cats and people with liver disease (prednisolone is preferred), and anyone with diabetes, infections or ulcers.
about: Prednisone is one of the most widely used corticosteroids, available since the 1950s. It is a prodrug, meaning the liver converts it into the active steroid prednisolone. It calms inflammation and the immune system in people and dogs. Prescribers and veterinarians may order a compounded flavored liquid, small-strength capsule or transdermal gel when tablets are too large, bitter or hard to give.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for black or bloody stools, vomiting blood, signs of infection such as fever, severe mood or behavior changes, vision changes, or extreme weakness after missing doses.
interactions: NSAIDs raise the risk of stomach ulcers, and diabetes medicines, blood thinners, some seizure medicines, certain antifungals and live vaccines may interact. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It may be used during pregnancy and breastfeeding when the benefits outweigh the risks; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs convert prednisone well, but cats and horses do not, so veterinarians usually choose prednisolone for them. Never give it with NSAIDs such as carprofen or meloxicam.
tips: Take or give it with food, usually in the morning for people and dogs.
Do not stop suddenly after long use; your prescriber will taper the dose.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
Avoid people who are sick, since steroids can lower your ability to fight infection.
monitoring: With long-term use, your prescriber or veterinarian may check blood sugar, blood pressure, eyes, bone health or blood work.
faqs: Why does prednisone make me hungry and keep me up at night?
Increased appetite and trouble sleeping are common steroid effects. Taking it in the morning may help with sleep.
Can I take prednisone with ibuprofen?
Combining a steroid with an NSAID raises the risk of stomach ulcers. Ask your prescriber before taking them together.
Why are cats given prednisolone instead of prednisone?
Cats do not convert prednisone to its active form well, so prednisolone is usually preferred.

name: Pregabalin
uses: Nerve pain and fibromyalgia; seizures in pets.
how: Binds calcium channels on nerve cells and reduces the release of pain and excitement signals.
avoid: People with kidney disease, heart failure or a history of misuse.
about: Pregabalin is a nerve pain and seizure medicine related to gabapentin, used in people since the mid-2000s. It is a controlled substance because of its potential for misuse. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats for nerve pain and seizures. Compounded flavored liquids or small capsules can help when a pet needs a smaller dose than commercial capsules provide.
conditions: Nerve pain in dogs and cats (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble breathing, swelling of the face, lips or throat, thoughts of self-harm, unexplained muscle pain or weakness, or extreme sleepiness.
interactions: Opioid pain medicines, sedatives, sleeping pills, alcohol and gabapentin can add to drowsiness and slowed breathing. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: There is limited information on its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Pregabalin is used off-label in dogs and cats, often when gabapentin has not been enough. Sleepiness and wobbliness are the most common effects; doses may need lowering in pets with kidney disease.
tips: Take or give it with or without food, at the same times each day.
Don't drive or use machinery until you know how it affects you.
Do not stop it suddenly; your prescriber will taper it to avoid withdrawal or seizures.
Shake liquid forms well before measuring.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check kidney function, since the dose depends on how well the kidneys clear it.
faqs: What is the difference between pregabalin and gabapentin?
They work in a similar way, but pregabalin is absorbed more predictably. Your prescriber decides which one fits.
How long does pregabalin take to work for nerve pain?
Some people notice relief within the first week, though it can take longer to reach full benefit.
Can I drink alcohol on pregabalin?
Alcohol adds to dizziness and drowsiness and is usually best avoided. Ask your prescriber.

name: Pregnenolone
uses: A hormone precursor occasionally included in hormone therapy plans.
how: A building block the body uses to make other steroid hormones.
avoid: People with hormone-sensitive cancers and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding.
about: Pregnenolone is a natural steroid that the body makes from cholesterol, mainly in the adrenal glands and brain. It is the starting point for other hormones, including DHEA, progesterone, cortisol, testosterone and estrogen. It is sold as a dietary supplement, and some prescribers include it in compounded hormone therapy plans, often with testosterone or DHEA. Evidence for its use is limited.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, a fast or uneven heartbeat, sudden severe headache, breast lumps, unusual bleeding, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: It may add to the effects of other hormone therapies such as DHEA, testosterone, estrogen and progesterone. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Not used during pregnancy or breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Take it at the time of day your prescriber directs; it is often taken in the morning.
Apply creams to clean, dry skin and wash your hands afterward.
Report acne, hair changes or mood changes to your prescriber.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check hormone levels with blood tests at follow-up visits.
faqs: Is pregnenolone a hormone?
Yes, it is a steroid hormone that the body uses as a building block to make other hormones.
Can pregnenolone be taken with DHEA?
Some prescribers include both in a hormone plan, sometimes in one compounded product. Your prescriber decides.

name: Prilocaine
uses: Numbing agent in topical anesthetic creams.
how: Blocks nerve signals to numb the skin.
avoid: Infants and people with methemoglobinemia.
about: Prilocaine is an amide local anesthetic, related to lidocaine, used since the 1960s. It is best known as one half of a lidocaine and prilocaine cream applied before needle sticks and minor skin procedures. It is also used in dental injections. Prescribers may order it compounded with lidocaine, tetracaine and phenylephrine in stronger numbing ointments for cosmetic or dermatology procedures.
conditions: Numbing before injections or IV starts
Numbing before laser and cosmetic procedures
serious: Get medical help right away for blue or gray lips, skin or nails, shortness of breath, headache with tiredness (possible methemoglobinemia), seizures, a slow heartbeat, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Other numbing medicines, nitrates, sulfa drugs, dapsone and some antimalarial drugs can raise the risk of methemoglobinemia. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: There is limited information on topical use in pregnancy and breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply only to the area and for the time your prescriber directs, and do not cover it with plastic or heat unless told to.
Wash your hands after applying, and keep it away from your eyes.
Avoid scratching or bumping the numbed area until feeling returns.
Never use on large areas of skin or on broken skin unless your prescriber says to.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but follow your prescriber's directions closely.
faqs: How long before a procedure should I apply numbing cream?
Timing depends on the product and procedure. Follow your prescriber's directions exactly.
Why is prilocaine not used in young infants?
Infants are more prone to methemoglobinemia, a condition that lowers the blood's ability to carry oxygen.

name: Progesterone
uses: Hormone therapy in women, often alongside estrogen, and for cycle and sleep support as prescribed.
side: Drowsiness, dizziness, breast tenderness, bloating, headache.
how: Replaces the hormone progesterone, which balances the effects of estrogen on the uterus and supports sleep and mood in some women.
avoid: People with a history of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, liver disease or unexplained vaginal bleeding. Can cause drowsiness; oral forms are usually taken at bedtime.
about: Progesterone is a hormone made mainly by the ovaries that prepares the uterus each month and helps balance estrogen. In menopause hormone therapy it is used to protect the lining of the uterus when estrogen is taken. Commercial capsules and vaginal gels exist, and prescribers may order compounded capsules, creams, troches or vaginal forms to fit a woman's needs, often as part of a plan with estrogen.
serious: Get medical help right away for chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, pain or swelling in one leg, sudden severe headache or vision changes, weakness or numbness on one side, yellowing skin or eyes, or a new breast lump.
interactions: Some seizure medicines, rifampin and St. John's wort can lower progesterone levels, and sedatives or alcohol can add to drowsiness. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Progesterone is sometimes prescribed for fertility or early pregnancy support, but hormone therapy products are not for use in pregnancy unless your prescriber directs; tell your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Oral capsules are usually taken at bedtime because they can cause drowsiness.
Apply creams to clean, thin skin such as the inner arm and rotate sites, washing your hands afterward.
Let troches and rapid-dissolve tablets dissolve fully without chewing or swallowing.
Report unexpected vaginal bleeding to your prescriber.
monitoring: Your prescriber will schedule follow-up visits and may check hormone levels, breast health and the uterine lining.
faqs: Why is progesterone taken with estrogen?
Estrogen alone can thicken the lining of the uterus, which raises the risk of uterine cancer. Progesterone helps protect the lining in women who have a uterus.
Why does progesterone make me sleepy?
Oral progesterone has calming effects in the brain, which is why it is often taken at bedtime.
Can men use progesterone?
Progesterone hormone therapy is mainly prescribed for women. Your prescriber decides whether it fits your plan.

name: Pyridostigmine
uses: Myasthenia gravis (muscle weakness) in people and dogs.
how: Slows the breakdown of acetylcholine, the chemical that tells muscles to contract.
avoid: People with bowel or urinary blockages or asthma.
about: Pyridostigmine slows the breakdown of acetylcholine, the chemical messenger nerves use to tell muscles to move. It has been used since the 1950s for myasthenia gravis in people, and veterinarians use it off-label for acquired myasthenia gravis in dogs, which often causes weakness and megaesophagus. A compounded flavored suspension can make doses easier to measure and swallow.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for trouble breathing or swallowing, severe muscle weakness or twitching, a very slow heartbeat, heavy drooling or sweating, or vomiting and diarrhea that do not stop.
interactions: Some antibiotics (aminoglycosides), beta blockers, steroids, magnesium and anticholinergic medicines may change its effect. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It is sometimes used in pregnancy and breastfeeding to manage myasthenia gravis under close care; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs with megaesophagus may need upright feeding and special handling, and some need doses mixed with food. Too much can cause weakness similar to the disease, so report any change.
tips: Take or give it at evenly spaced times as directed, often with food to lessen stomach upset.
Shake the suspension well before measuring.
Keep a log of strength and symptoms to share with your prescriber or veterinarian.
For dogs with megaesophagus, follow feeding instructions such as keeping them upright after meals.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check strength and symptoms regularly; dogs may have antibody blood tests and chest X-rays.
faqs: How quickly does pyridostigmine work?
It often starts working within an hour, and the effect lasts a few hours, which is why it is given several times a day.
Can dogs recover from myasthenia gravis?
Some dogs with the acquired form go into remission over months. Your veterinarian will guide treatment and testing.

name: Quetiapine
uses: Mood disorders and sleep, as prescribed.
how: Blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors and has sedating antihistamine effects.
avoid: Older adults with dementia, and people with heart rhythm problems or diabetes.
about: Quetiapine is an atypical antipsychotic used since the late 1990s for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and with an antidepressant for depression. Because it is sedating, some prescribers use small amounts off-label for sleep, though this carries risks. Prescribers may order a compounded capsule or oral liquid when a patient needs a dose or form that commercial tablets do not provide.
serious: Get medical help right away for high fever with stiff muscles and confusion, fainting or a fast or uneven heartbeat, uncontrolled movements of the face or body, thoughts of self-harm, or very high blood sugar symptoms such as extreme thirst.
interactions: Some antifungals, certain antibiotics, HIV medicines and grapefruit can raise its levels, and some seizure medicines lower them. Alcohol, sedatives and other medicines that affect heart rhythm can add to its effects. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Use in late pregnancy may cause effects in newborns, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: It is often taken in the evening because it causes drowsiness.
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness, especially when starting.
Do not stop suddenly; talk to your prescriber first.
Avoid alcohol and do not drive until you know how it affects you.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check weight, blood sugar, cholesterol and blood pressure, and sometimes an ECG or eye exam.
faqs: Is quetiapine used for sleep?
Some prescribers use small amounts off-label for sleep, but it can cause weight gain and other effects. Your prescriber weighs the risks.
Why does quetiapine cause weight gain?
It can increase appetite and affect blood sugar and fat levels. Healthy eating, activity and lab checks help.

name: Rivaroxaban
uses: Prevents and treats blood clots.
how: Blocks factor Xa, a key step in blood clotting.
avoid: People or pets with active bleeding or severe liver disease.
about: Rivaroxaban is an oral blood thinner introduced in 2011 that blocks factor Xa, a key step in clotting. It is used to treat and prevent clots without the routine blood tests needed for warfarin. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats at risk of clots, such as cats with heart disease. A compounded flavored suspension helps when tablets are too large or a pet will not take them.
conditions: Clot prevention after hip or knee surgery
Clot prevention in cats with heart disease (off-label)
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for bleeding that will not stop, blood in urine or stool, black stools, vomiting blood, a severe headache, sudden weakness, or in pets, pale gums or sudden back-leg pain.
interactions: Other blood thinners, aspirin, NSAIDs, some antidepressants and certain antifungals or seizure medicines can raise bleeding risk or change its levels. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: It is not usually recommended during pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians use it off-label, often in cats with heart disease to lower the risk of a clot in the back legs. Watch for bleeding and sudden leg weakness or pain.
tips: Take or give it at the same time each day; some strengths are taken with food, so follow the label.
Tell every doctor, dentist and veterinarian that you or your pet take a blood thinner.
Do not stop it without talking to your prescriber, because clot risk can rise.
If a dose is missed, give or take it when you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose; don't double up.
monitoring: Your prescriber may check kidney and liver function and blood counts from time to time.
faqs: Do I need regular blood tests on rivaroxaban?
Routine clotting tests are not needed as with warfarin, but your prescriber may check kidney function and blood counts.
Can I take ibuprofen with rivaroxaban?
NSAIDs such as ibuprofen raise bleeding risk. Ask your prescriber before taking any pain reliever.
Is rivaroxaban used in cats?
Veterinarians sometimes prescribe it off-label for cats at risk of blood clots. Your veterinarian decides the dose.
