interactions: Avoid using other irritating products on the same area, such as benzoyl peroxide (unless directed), salicylic acid, alcohol-based toners, harsh scrubs or waxing, and use caution with other drugs that increase sun sensitivity. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Tretinoin is avoided in pregnancy because retinoids can harm a developing baby, and its use while breastfeeding should be discussed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer to clean, completely dry skin at night, about 20 to 30 minutes after washing.
Start slowly, every other night if needed, and use a moisturizer to reduce dryness.
Wear broad-spectrum sunscreen every day and avoid tanning beds.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits so your prescriber can adjust the strength or how often you use it.
faqs: What is retinization or the tretinoin purge?
In the first few weeks, skin may get dry, red or break out more before it improves. This often settles as skin adjusts.
How long does tretinoin take to work?
Acne often improves over about 6 to 12 weeks, while changes in fine lines and tone may take several months.
What is the difference between tretinoin and retinol?
Retinol is an over-the-counter ingredient the skin must convert to retinoic acid, while tretinoin is retinoic acid itself and is prescription only.

avoid: Pregnancy. Long-term continuous hydroquinone use, which can darken skin. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover, hydroquinone blocks tyrosinase (the enzyme that makes skin pigment), niacinamide reduces pigment transfer and supports the skin barrier, and hyaluronic acid holds moisture.
name: Tretinoin and hydroquinone chest cream
side: Dryness, peeling, irritation and sun sensitivity.
uses: Sun damage, dark spots and fine lines on the chest. Made with tretinoin 0.01%, hydroquinone 7%, niacinamide 3% and hyaluronic acid 0.5%.
about: This chest cream combines tretinoin, a prescription retinoid, with hydroquinone, a skin-lightening agent, plus niacinamide and hyaluronic acid. The chest and upper chest (decolletage) often show sun damage, spots and crepey lines, but the skin there can be more sensitive than the face. Prescribers order this combination so patients can use one product instead of layering several.
serious: Get medical help right away for severe blistering, burning or swelling, or a blue-black or gray darkening of the skin (possible ochronosis), or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Avoid benzoyl peroxide, hydrogen peroxide and other irritating or peeling products on the same area, which can irritate the skin or cause temporary staining. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: This cream is not used in pregnancy because it contains a retinoid, and hydroquinone use while breastfeeding should also be avoided unless your prescriber approves; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer at night to clean, dry skin, and avoid the nipples and any broken skin.
Start a few nights a week and increase as your skin tolerates it.
Wear sunscreen on your chest every day and cover up in strong sun.
Use it for the time your prescriber advises, since hydroquinone is usually used in cycles with breaks.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits so your prescriber can check progress and decide when to take a break from hydroquinone.
faqs: How long until I see results on my chest?
Changes in spots and tone often start after about 8 to 12 weeks of regular use.
Why does hydroquinone need breaks?
Using it continuously for a long time can, rarely, cause darkening of the skin, so prescribers often plan breaks between courses.

avoid: Pregnancy. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover and supports collagen, niacinamide supports the skin barrier and evens tone, and hyaluronic acid holds moisture.
name: Tretinoin neck cream
side: Dryness, peeling, redness or sun sensitivity.
uses: Fine lines, crepey texture and uneven tone on the neck. Made with tretinoin 0.03%, niacinamide 3% and hyaluronic acid 0.5%.
about: This neck cream pairs tretinoin, a prescription retinoid, with niacinamide and hyaluronic acid in a formula meant for the thinner, more sensitive skin of the neck. The neck often shows lines, crepey texture and uneven tone but is easily irritated by stronger face products. Prescribers order this combination so patients can treat the neck with a single product.
serious: Get medical help right away for severe blistering, crusting or swelling of the skin, or signs of an allergic reaction such as hives or trouble breathing.
interactions: Avoid using other retinoids, acids, scrubs or waxing on the same area, which can increase irritation. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: This cream is not used in pregnancy because it contains a retinoid, and use while breastfeeding should be discussed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Apply a thin layer at night to clean, dry skin on the neck, smoothing upward.
Start every other night and increase as your skin tolerates it, using a moisturizer if dry.
Use sunscreen on your neck daily, not just your face.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Can I use my face tretinoin on my neck?
Neck skin is thinner and more easily irritated, so prescribers often prefer a formula made for the neck; ask before using a face product there.
How long does it take to see a difference in neck skin?
Texture and tone changes usually take a few months of regular use.

avoid: Pregnancy. Getting it in the eyes. Use sunscreen daily.
how: Tretinoin speeds skin cell turnover, caffeine tightens small blood vessels to reduce darkness and puffiness, hyaluronic acid holds moisture, and niacinamide supports the skin barrier and evens tone.
name: Tretinoin under-eye serum
side: Dryness, mild peeling, redness or sun sensitivity.
uses: Dark circles and fine wrinkles under the eyes. A gentle serum made with tretinoin 0.001%, caffeine 1%, hyaluronic acid 2% and niacinamide 2%.
about: This under-eye serum combines a very low strength of tretinoin with caffeine, hyaluronic acid and niacinamide in a lightweight base made for the delicate skin around the eyes. The under-eye area is thin and easily irritated, so standard tretinoin products are often too strong there. Prescribers order this combination to target dark circles, puffiness and fine lines in one gentle product.
serious: Get medical help right away for eye pain, vision changes, severe swelling of the eyelids, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Avoid using other retinoids, acids or strong eye products in the same area unless your prescriber directs. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: This serum is not used in pregnancy because it contains a retinoid, and use while breastfeeding should be discussed; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Pat a tiny amount along the orbital bone with your ring finger, staying away from the lash line.
If serum gets in your eye, rinse with plenty of water.
Start a few nights a week, and wear sunglasses and sunscreen during the day.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Can I use this serum on my eyelids?
No. Apply it only to the under-eye area along the bone, not on the eyelids or near the lashes.
Why does it have caffeine?
Caffeine tightens small blood vessels for a short time, which may make dark circles and puffiness look less noticeable.

name: Triamcinolone
uses: Steroid for skin and ear inflammation, including vet ear packs.
how: A medium-strength steroid that reduces inflammation.
avoid: Untreated skin or ear infections; avoid long use on thin skin.
about: Triamcinolone is a corticosteroid used since the 1950s to calm inflammation and itching. It is available commercially in creams, ointments, dental paste, nasal sprays and injections. Compounding lets prescribers and veterinarians use it in ear packs, oral liquids or transdermal gels, sometimes combined with antibiotics or antifungals, when standard products do not fit the patient or pet.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for signs of infection where it is used, eye pain or vision changes, severe increased thirst and urination, black or bloody stools, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: With oral or transdermal use, avoid combining with NSAIDs because of stomach ulcer risk, and use caution with diabetes medicines and other steroids; topical products used on small areas have few interactions. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Short-term topical use on small areas is generally considered low risk, while oral use is decided by your prescriber; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Cats generally tolerate steroids better than dogs, but cats can develop diabetes with long-term use. Never give a steroid with an NSAID such as carprofen or meloxicam unless your vet directs it.
tips: Wear gloves when applying transdermal gel to your pet, and rotate ears as directed.
Shake oral liquid well before each dose and give it with food.
Do not stop oral steroids suddenly after long use; your prescriber or veterinarian will taper them.
monitoring: Short courses usually need no special labs, but pets or people on long-term steroids may have blood sugar, liver values and other blood work checked.
faqs: Can steroids make my dog thirsty?
Yes. Increased thirst, urination and appetite are common with steroids in dogs. Tell your vet if they are severe.
How long can triamcinolone be used on the skin?
It is usually used for limited periods, especially on thin skin like the face or folds, to avoid thinning. Your prescriber decides how long.

name: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA)
uses: A strong acid applied by a clinician in the office for chemical peels and to treat warts and some skin lesions.
side: Burning, redness and peeling; for professional application only.
how: Causes controlled peeling of the outer skin layers.
avoid: Home use. For application by a trained clinician only.
about: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a strong acid that has been used by dermatologists for decades for chemical peels and to remove warts and some skin growths. It works by causing controlled damage to the outer skin layers, which then peel and heal with new skin. Clinicians order compounded solutions in the specific strength they need for in-office procedures; it is never used at home.
serious: Get medical help right away for spreading redness, pus, fever, severe pain, blistering beyond the treated area, or any signs of infection after a treatment.
interactions: Tell your clinician if you use tretinoin, other retinoids, exfoliating acids or recently took isotretinoin, since these may need to be stopped before a peel. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Your clinician decides whether TCA treatment is appropriate in pregnancy or breastfeeding; some clinicians use it for genital warts in pregnancy, but cosmetic peels are often postponed, so tell your clinician if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Follow your clinician's aftercare instructions carefully, including gentle cleansing and moisturizing.
Do not pick or peel flaking skin; let it come off on its own.
Avoid sun and use sunscreen daily while skin heals, to lower the risk of dark spots.
monitoring: Your clinician will schedule follow-up visits to check healing and decide if more treatments are needed.
faqs: How long does it take to heal after a TCA peel?
Healing time depends on the depth of the peel, ranging from several days for light peels to a week or more for deeper ones.
Why can't TCA be used at home?
It is a strong acid that can cause burns and scarring if not applied correctly, so only trained clinicians should use it.

name: Trilostane
uses: Cushing's disease (hyperadrenocorticism) in dogs.
side: Lethargy, decreased appetite, vomiting; requires monitoring.
how: Blocks an enzyme in the adrenal gland to lower cortisol production.
avoid: Dogs with kidney or liver disease, and pregnant dogs.
about: Trilostane blocks an enzyme in the adrenal glands that is needed to make cortisol. It is approved in the US for dogs with Cushing's disease (hyperadrenocorticism) and is now one of the most common treatments for it. Veterinarians may ask for compounded capsules or flavored suspensions when a dog needs a strength that the commercial capsules don't come in, especially small dogs.
conditions: Excessive thirst and urination from Cushing's
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for weakness, collapse, repeated vomiting or diarrhea, not eating, or shaking, which may be signs of low cortisol (an Addisonian crisis).
interactions: Use caution with ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, and potassium supplements, which can raise potassium, and with other drugs that affect the adrenal glands. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Trilostane is given with food, which helps absorption. Use in cats is off-label and less common, and pregnant women should wear gloves when handling it.
tips: Give it with a meal, at the same time each day.
Keep a log of your dog's water drinking, appetite and energy to share with your vet.
Wash hands after handling, and do not split or open capsules unless your vet says so.
monitoring: Your veterinarian will run blood tests (often an ACTH stimulation test or cortisol levels) and electrolytes within a few weeks after starting or changing the dose and periodically after that.
faqs: How long does trilostane take to work?
Excessive thirst and appetite often improve within the first few weeks, while skin and coat changes may take a few months.
Why does my dog need so many blood tests on trilostane?
The dose that controls cortisol without dropping it too low varies a lot between dogs, so testing helps your vet adjust it safely.
Should trilostane be given with food?
Yes. It is absorbed better with food, so give it with a meal.

name: Tylosin
uses: Chronic diarrhea and colitis in dogs.
how: A macrolide antibiotic that also changes gut bacteria in dogs with chronic diarrhea.
avoid: Horses and rabbits. Extremely bitter, so it is usually compounded into capsules.
about: Tylosin is a macrolide antibiotic developed for veterinary use that is widely used off-label in dogs with chronic diarrhea that responds to antibiotics, sometimes called tylosin-responsive diarrhea. It is commonly sold as a very bitter powder for livestock. Because of its taste, veterinarians often ask for it compounded into capsules, flavored suspensions or chewable treats measured for each dog or cat.
serious: Call your veterinarian right away for repeated vomiting, bloody diarrhea, not eating, swelling of the face, hives or trouble breathing.
interactions: Tylosin may raise blood levels of digoxin and can interact with other macrolides or drugs processed by the liver. Tell your veterinarian about every medicine, supplement and flea or tick product your pet gets.
petNotes: Tylosin is used off-label in dogs and cats, and it is dangerous for horses and rabbits, so keep it away from them. If the bitter powder touches a cat's mouth it can cause heavy drooling, which is why capsules and flavored forms help.
tips: Give it with food if it upsets the stomach.
Do not open capsules or mix the raw powder into food, since the bitter taste can lead to food refusal.
Keep giving it for as long as your veterinarian directs, even after stools firm up.
monitoring: Routine lab monitoring is usually not needed, but your veterinarian will follow stool quality and may try lowering or stopping the dose over time.
faqs: How long does tylosin take to firm up stool?
Many dogs improve within a few days, but your veterinarian will decide how long to continue.
Is tylosin safe for long-term use in dogs?
Some dogs take it for long periods for chronic diarrhea under veterinary supervision; your vet balances benefits with concerns about antibiotic resistance.

name: Urea
uses: Thick, dry or cracked skin and nails; ear flush ingredients.
how: Draws water into skin and softens thick, rough areas.
avoid: Broken or irritated skin.
about: Urea is a natural compound found in skin that attracts and holds water. In creams, it softens and loosens thick, rough or scaly skin and nails, and higher strengths are used to soften thickened nails. Prescribers and veterinarians may ask for compounded urea creams in a specific strength or combined with other ingredients, or for ear flush blends used for pets.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe burning, blistering, swelling or signs of skin infection, or for signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Urea can increase how much of other topical medicines soak into the skin, so use other creams on the same area only as directed; it has few other interactions. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical urea is minimally absorbed and generally considered low risk in pregnancy and breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Urea is used in some veterinary ear cleaners and skin products. Do not put creams into a pet's ear unless your veterinarian tells you to, especially if the eardrum may be damaged.
tips: Apply to clean skin, and for heels or nails, soaking first can help it work better.
Wash your hands after applying unless you are treating your hands.
Avoid the eyes, mouth and any open cuts, where it can sting.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Why does urea cream sting?
It can sting on cracked or broken skin. This usually eases as the skin heals; stop and call your prescriber if it is severe.
Is the urea in creams from urine?
No. Urea in skin products is made in a lab, although the same compound is naturally found in skin and urine.

name: Ursodiol
uses: Liver and gallbladder conditions and gallstones.
how: A natural bile acid that makes bile thinner and protects liver cells.
avoid: People or pets with a blocked bile duct.
about: Ursodiol, also called ursodeoxycholic acid, is a natural bile acid used since the 1980s to dissolve some gallstones and treat certain liver conditions. It thins bile and helps protect liver cells from damage. Veterinarians use it off-label in dogs and cats with liver disease and gallbladder sludge, and compounded flavored suspensions, capsules and chewable treats make dosing easier for pets and people who can't swallow tablets.
conditions: Liver disease in dogs and cats
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for yellow skin, eyes or gums, severe belly pain, vomiting that won't stop, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Aluminum antacids, cholestyramine and colestipol can bind ursodiol and should be spaced apart, and estrogens may reduce its effect on gallstones. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Ursodiol is sometimes prescribed during pregnancy for certain liver conditions, but only under a prescriber's care; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Give it with food, which helps absorption. It should not be used in pets with a blocked bile duct or gallbladder rupture, so your vet will check this first.
tips: Take or give it with food.
Space it at least two hours from aluminum antacids or bile-acid binders.
Shake the suspension well before measuring.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian will check liver values periodically and may repeat ultrasounds to check gallstones or sludge.
faqs: How long does ursodiol take to dissolve gallstones?
Dissolving gallstones can take months to years, and it works only on certain types of stones.
Is ursodiol safe for dogs and cats?
Veterinarians commonly use it off-label in dogs and cats with liver and gallbladder conditions, and it is usually well tolerated.

name: Valacyclovir
uses: Herpes infections, cold sores and shingles.
how: Converted to acyclovir, which stops herpesviruses from copying their DNA.
avoid: People with kidney disease (lower dose).
about: Valacyclovir is an antiviral prodrug that the body converts into acyclovir. It has been used since the mid-1990s for herpes simplex infections, including cold sores and genital herpes, and for shingles and chickenpox. Because the commercial tablets are large, prescribers may ask for a compounded oral liquid for children or adults who have trouble swallowing pills.
serious: Get medical help right away for confusion, hallucinations, unusual sleepiness, seizures, decreased urination, unusual bruising or bleeding, or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Use caution with other medicines that can affect the kidneys, such as NSAIDs, some antibiotics and certain chemotherapy drugs. Give your prescriber a full list of medicines and supplements.
pregnancy: Valacyclovir is commonly used in pregnancy when needed and is considered compatible with breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
tips: Start it as soon as possible at the first sign of an outbreak, such as tingling or itching.
Drink plenty of fluids to help protect your kidneys.
Shake the oral liquid well, measure with a dosing syringe, and store it as labeled.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but your prescriber may check kidney function in older adults or people with kidney disease.
faqs: How fast does valacyclovir work for cold sores?
It works best when started at the first tingle, and it may help shorten an outbreak.
Does valacyclovir cure herpes?
No. It helps control outbreaks and may lower the chance of passing herpes to a partner, but the virus stays in the body.
What is the difference between valacyclovir and acyclovir?
Valacyclovir turns into acyclovir in the body but is absorbed better, so it can be taken less often.

name: Vitamin C
uses: Antioxidant in skin creams; vitamin supplement.
how: An antioxidant that brightens skin and supports collagen.
avoid: Usually well tolerated.
about: Vitamin C, or ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin and antioxidant the body needs to build collagen and protect cells. In skin care it is used to brighten dull skin, even tone and support firmness. Because vitamin C breaks down easily in light and air, prescribers may ask for fresh compounded creams or ointments in a specific strength or combined with other skin ingredients.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe burning, swelling, blistering or signs of an allergic reaction.
interactions: Topical vitamin C has few interactions, but using it at the same time as strong acids, benzoyl peroxide or retinoids may increase irritation. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical vitamin C is generally considered safe in pregnancy and breastfeeding; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Dogs and cats make their own vitamin C, so supplements are given only when a veterinarian recommends them. Keep topical products where pets cannot lick them.
tips: Apply it in the morning under sunscreen, which may help boost sun protection.
Store it in a cool, dark place and close the container tightly.
A product that turns dark brown may have broken down; ask your pharmacist.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber schedules.
faqs: Why does vitamin C cream change color?
Vitamin C oxidizes when exposed to light and air, which can turn it yellow or brown and make it less active.
Can I use vitamin C with retinol or tretinoin?
Many people use vitamin C in the morning and a retinoid at night to limit irritation; ask your prescriber.

name: Vitamin E
uses: Antioxidant supplement and skin moisturizer.
how: An antioxidant that protects cell membranes.
avoid: People taking blood thinners (high oral doses).
about: Vitamin E is a fat-soluble vitamin and antioxidant that helps protect cell membranes from damage. In skin and mucous membrane care it is used as a moisturizer and soothing agent. Prescribers may ask for vitamin E in compounded creams, vaginal preparations or suppositories, sometimes with other ingredients, for dryness or irritation such as vaginal dryness after menopause.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for severe itching, burning, swelling or signs of an allergic reaction, and for unusual bleeding or bruising with high oral doses.
interactions: High oral doses may increase bleeding risk with warfarin and other blood thinners or antiplatelet drugs; topical and vaginal forms have few interactions. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Topical and vaginal vitamin E are generally considered low risk, but ask before using vaginal products in pregnancy; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding.
petNotes: Veterinarians sometimes recommend vitamin E for some skin conditions in dogs. Keep creams where pets cannot lick them off.
tips: Insert vaginal suppositories at bedtime and wear a panty liner, since they melt.
Oil-based products may weaken latex condoms and diaphragms.
Store suppositories in a cool place so they stay firm.
monitoring: Routine monitoring is usually not needed, but keep follow-up visits your prescriber or veterinarian schedules.
faqs: Can vitamin E help vaginal dryness?
Some prescribers recommend vaginal vitamin E to moisturize dry tissue, often as a hormone-free option. Your prescriber decides if it fits.
Can I use vitamin E on scars?
Some people use it on healing skin, but results vary and it can cause irritation in some people.

name: Zonisamide
uses: Seizure control, often as an add-on medication.
how: Blocks sodium and calcium channels in nerve cells to reduce abnormal electrical activity.
avoid: Anyone allergic to sulfa drugs, and people with kidney stones or kidney disease.
about: Zonisamide is an anticonvulsant approved in the US since 2000 as an add-on treatment for partial seizures in adults. It is chemically a sulfonamide and acts on sodium and calcium channels in nerve cells. Veterinarians use it off-label for epilepsy in dogs and cats, and compounded liquids, powders and transdermal gels help with pets or people who need a specific strength or cannot take capsules.
serious: Get medical or veterinary help right away for a skin rash or blistering, fever or sore throat, decreased sweating with overheating, kidney stone pain or blood in urine, thoughts of suicide, or yellow skin or eyes.
interactions: Other seizure medicines such as phenobarbital, phenytoin and carbamazepine can lower zonisamide levels, and use care with topiramate, acetazolamide and other sedating medicines. Give your prescriber, or your pet's veterinarian, a full list of medicines, supplements and flea or tick products.
pregnancy: Zonisamide may harm a developing baby, and effective birth control is often advised; talk to your prescriber if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding, and do not stop it on your own.
petNotes: Dogs usually tolerate zonisamide well, but some develop dry eye, liver changes or reduced appetite. Doses for cats and dogs differ, so use only your vet's pet-specific dose.
tips: Give or take it at the same times each day, with or without food.
Do not stop it suddenly, which can trigger seizures.
Drink plenty of water (or keep fresh water available for pets) to lower the risk of kidney stones.
monitoring: Your prescriber or veterinarian may check zonisamide blood levels, kidney and liver values, and blood counts periodically.
faqs: How long does zonisamide take to work?
It takes a few weeks to reach steady levels, so seizure control is usually judged over a few months.
Can I drink alcohol with zonisamide?
Alcohol can increase drowsiness and dizziness and may affect seizure control, so it is best avoided.
Why is zonisamide used in dogs?
Veterinarians use it off-label as a single or add-on seizure medicine, often because it is given less often and is gentler on the liver than some older choices.
